subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception choice when body weight reduces oral efficacy
stem:
You are the doctor in a community sexual health clinic. A 26-year-old woman attends 68 hours after a condom broke. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and today is day 13.

She weighs 104 kg with a body mass index of 38 kg per square metre. She is not using any regular contraception, has never been pregnant, and has no contraindication to any method. She has taken no medication in the past month. She says she does not want to be pregnant under any circumstances, and separately she would like to start something reliable and long lasting today so that she is not back here again. A urine pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg per square metre, abdomen soft and non-tender, no cervical excitation or adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative; nucleic acid testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea taken today

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Give levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally now and start a progestogen only pill
Insert a copper intrauterine device today and screen for infection
Give levonorgestrel 3 mg orally now as a double dose for her weight
Give ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally and start a pill tomorrow morning
Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device today as emergency cover

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth stratified by peak bile acid concentration in cholestasis of pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 31 weeks and 4 days who has had two weeks of intense itching of her palms and soles that is worst after she goes to bed. The only skin findings are linear scratch marks over her forearms and shins.

Her blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg with no proteinuria, and she has no headache, no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain. Hepatitis serology is negative, an autoimmune liver screen is negative and a liver ultrasound is normal. Ursodeoxycholic acid was started a week ago for symptom relief, and fetal growth is on the 45th centile with a normal umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 112 micromol/L (less than 19), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), international normalised ratio 1.0
data_table.Imaging: Liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation and no gallstones

lead_in: What should you advise about the timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 37 to 38 weeks of gestation with weekly liver function tests
Plan birth at 39 weeks of gestation with weekly cardiotocography
Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks of gestation after discussing the risks
Plan immediate birth by caesarean section during this admission
Plan birth at 40 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography monitoring

subtopic_detail: Deciding on repeat antenatal corticosteroid when the first course was given weeks earlier
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 33-year-old woman in her third pregnancy at 31 weeks and 2 days with contractions every four minutes that she cannot talk through. She was admitted at 27 weeks with threatened preterm labour, completed a course of betamethasone then, and was discharged when the contractions settled.

Her membranes are intact and there is no bleeding, no fever, no uterine tenderness and no offensive discharge. Speculum and digital examination show the cervix is 2 cm dilated and 1 cm long, and a repeat examination two hours later shows 3 cm dilatation. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145 beats per minute with normal variability and no decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine culture negative, vaginal swab pending
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound confirms a single cephalic fetus with an estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid management?

options.text: Give no further corticosteroid as she has already completed a course
Give a full two dose course of betamethasone and repeat it weekly
Give magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection instead of corticosteroid
Give a single repeat dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly
Give four doses of dexamethasone 6 mg twelve hours apart from now

subtopic_detail: Choosing a method at three weeks postpartum in a woman who is fully breastfeeding
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman three weeks after a normal vaginal birth of her second child. She is fully breastfeeding on demand, has had no periods since the birth, and tells you she and her partner have resumed sex and that she would be devastated to conceive again this year.

Her lochia has almost stopped and her perineal graze has healed. Her blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg, her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre and she has no history of venous thromboembolism, migraine or liver disease. She wants something she does not have to remember daily and would prefer not to wait for another appointment.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), full blood count otherwise within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Involuted uterus not palpable abdominally, healed perineum, minimal lochia

lead_in: Which contraceptive method should you provide today?

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill at today's visit
Advise lactational amenorrhoea alone until the baby is six months
Insert a copper intrauterine device at today's visit in the clinic
Defer all contraception until the six week postnatal appointment
Insert an etonogestrel implant at today's visit in the clinic

subtopic_detail: Classifying a perineal injury and choosing the setting for its repair
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite after a 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy has had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 3900 g baby following a second stage of 95 minutes. The midwife is concerned about the extent of the perineal injury and has asked you to examine it before any suturing.

With the woman consented and adequately analgesed, you find a tear through the vaginal mucosa and perineal body extending to the anal sphincter complex. On rectal examination the external anal sphincter is disrupted across less than half of its thickness, the internal anal sphincter is intact, and the anorectal mucosa is intact. Blood loss is 350 mL and she is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tear through vaginal mucosa and perineal body, external anal sphincter disrupted across less than half its thickness, internal anal sphincter intact, anorectal mucosa intact
data_table.Analgesia: Epidural sited in labour and still functioning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the injury?

options.text: Repair in theatre under regional anaesthesia with antibiotic cover
Repair in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration now
Leave unrepaired and review in the perineal clinic at six weeks
Refer to colorectal surgery for a delayed repair at six weeks
Perform a defunctioning colostomy before any perineal repair

subtopic_detail: Pathway after a high risk genotype is detected on a self collected screening sample
stem:
You are the general practitioner following up a 38-year-old woman whose cervical screening was four years overdue. She declined a speculum examination because of a history of sexual assault, and at her last visit she collected a vaginal sample herself in the practice bathroom after you explained the technique.

The laboratory reports that oncogenic human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 have been detected, and notes that cytology cannot be performed on a self collected sample. She has never had an abnormal screening result before, has no abnormal bleeding and no pelvic pain, and is not pregnant.

data_table.Screening result: Self collected vaginal sample, oncogenic human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 detected, no cytology performed
data_table.History: Last cervical screening test negative six years ago, no previous abnormal result

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months' time
Refer directly for colposcopy at the local gynaecology service
Arrange a clinician collected sample for reflex liquid based cytology
Return to routine five yearly cervical screening as scheduled
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and review the result in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Treating antiphospholipid syndrome in a new pregnancy after recurrent first trimester loss
stem:
You are the early pregnancy unit registrar seeing a 33-year-old woman who is six weeks pregnant and has had three consecutive first trimester losses at seven, nine and eight weeks. She has no living children and describes the previous appointments as the hardest part of the past two years.

Investigations arranged between pregnancies showed normal parental karyotypes, a normal uterine cavity on three dimensional ultrasound, normal thyroid function and a normal glycated haemoglobin. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart, while anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein I antibodies were negative on both occasions. Today an ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal heart rate of 118 beats per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 218 x10^9/L (150-400), activated partial thromboplastin time prolonged and not correcting on mixing, full blood count and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Single intrauterine gestational sac with a crown rump length consistent with six weeks and a visible fetal heart

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this pregnancy?

options.text: Commence aspirin 100 mg daily alone from the first positive test
Commence prednisolone 10 mg daily with aspirin 100 mg daily now
Commence aspirin 100 mg daily with prophylactic dose enoxaparin
Commence therapeutic dose enoxaparin with aspirin 100 mg daily
Arrange intravenous immunoglobulin infusions each trimester now

subtopic_detail: First line treatment of a scarring vulval dermatosis with malignant potential
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old woman with 18 months of vulval itching that is worst at night and now makes sex painful. She has tried three courses of antifungal cream bought from the pharmacy with no benefit.

There are white, thin, crinkled plaques over the labia minora, clitoral hood and perineum extending around the anus in a figure of eight pattern, with fusion of the skin over the clitoris and loss of the labia minora. There is no ulceration, no fixed lump and no thickened indurated area. The vaginal walls appear normal and a swab for microscopy and culture shows no candida.

data_table.Investigations: Vulvovaginal swab negative for candida and bacterial pathogens, fasting glucose and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Examination: White atrophic plaques in a figure of eight distribution with clitoral hood fusion and resorption of the labia minora, no ulceration or induration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Apply clotrimazole 1 per cent cream twice daily for four weeks
Apply oestriol 0.01 per cent cream three nights a week ongoing
Refer for a vulval punch biopsy before starting any treatment
Apply clobetasol propionate 0.05 per cent ointment nightly
Refer for wide local excision of the affected vulval skin

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection for group B streptococcal prophylaxis when the isolate and the patient both limit options
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy who is in established labour at 39 weeks and 2 days, contracting three times in ten minutes with the cervix 5 cm dilated. Her membranes ruptured two hours ago with clear liquor and she is afebrile.

Her combined vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus, and the laboratory has reported the isolate as resistant to both clindamycin and erythromycin. She tells you that as a teenager penicillin caused her face to swell and her throat to close over, and that she was given an adrenaline injection in the emergency department.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks positive for group B streptococcus with resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 140 beats per minute with normal variability and no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Give intravenous cefazolin 2 g then 1 g every eight hours in labour
Give intravenous clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours in labour
Give intravenous erythromycin 500 mg every six hours in labour
Give no prophylaxis and observe the baby for 48 hours after birth
Give intravenous vancomycin as prophylaxis throughout the labour

subtopic_detail: Planning birth when ultrasound suggests abnormal placental invasion
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman in her fourth pregnancy at 32 weeks who has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal birth. She has had no bleeding, no contractions and no pain, and she attends for a routine growth and placental localisation scan.

The report describes an anterior placenta covering the internal cervical os, loss of the hypoechoic clear zone between placenta and myometrium, multiple placental lacunae with turbulent flow, and interruption of the interface between the uterine serosa and the bladder wall. Fetal growth is on the 55th centile with normal Dopplers, and she lives 40 minutes from a tertiary maternity unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 144 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-300), platelets 236 x10^9/L (150-400), blood group O RhD positive with no atypical antibodies
data_table.Imaging: Anterior placenta covering the internal os with loss of the clear zone, multiple lacunae with turbulent flow and bladder wall interface interruption

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for birth?

options.text: Plan caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks in a specialist centre
Plan caesarean at 39 weeks with attempted manual removal of the placenta
Plan induction of labour at 37 weeks with continuous monitoring
Plan caesarean at 37 weeks with uterine artery embolisation first
Repeat the ultrasound at 36 weeks before making any birth plan

subtopic_detail: Choosing route and progestogen for hormone therapy when thrombotic risk is elevated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53-year-old woman who has had no periods for 14 months and describes more than a dozen drenching hot flushes a day with night sweats that wake her three or four times. She has stopped going to her walking group because of them and says she is exhausted.

Her body mass index is 34 kg per square metre. Eight years ago she had a deep vein thrombosis in the six weeks after a knee arthroscopy, treated with six months of anticoagulation, and a thrombophilia screen at the time was negative. Her uterus is intact, her blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, she has never smoked and her mammogram three months ago was reported as normal.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Screening: Mammogram three months ago reported as normal, cervical screening up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence oral conjugated oestrogen with medroxyprogesterone acetate
Commence transdermal oestradiol with micronised progesterone orally
Commence oral oestradiol 2 mg daily without a progestogen component
Commence tibolone 2.5 mg daily and review the symptoms in three months
Decline menopausal hormone therapy and commence venlafaxine instead

subtopic_detail: Operative decision for adnexal torsion in the second trimester
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks in her first pregnancy who developed severe right sided lower abdominal pain five hours ago while hanging out washing. The pain comes in waves and she has vomited four times.

A 7 cm simple right ovarian cyst was noted at her dating scan and she has had no bleeding. Her abdomen is tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding, and the cervix is closed on speculum examination. Ultrasound today shows an oedematous right ovary measuring 8 cm with follicles displaced to the periphery, a twisted vascular pedicle and no venous flow within the ovary, with a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 152 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 116 g/L (115-155), midstream urine negative
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged oedematous right ovary with peripherally displaced follicles, twisted vascular pedicle and absent intraovarian venous flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Perform laparoscopic oophorectomy of the affected right ovary
Manage conservatively with analgesia and repeat ultrasound in 24 hours
Perform laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary
Perform laparotomy with oophorectomy and salpingectomy on the right
Defer surgery until after 16 weeks when the placenta has taken over

subtopic_detail: Matching treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding to fibroid location when fertility is intended
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 41-year-old woman with two years of periods so heavy that she soaks through a pad each hour on the worst days and passes clots the size of coins. She has been trying to conceive for eight months and has not been pregnant before.

She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and no pelvic pain. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a uterus of ten week size containing a single 3 cm submucosal fibroid that indents the cavity with less than half its volume within the myometrium, an endometrium of 6 mm and normal ovaries. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and her cervical screening is up to date.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Single 3 cm submucosal fibroid indenting the endometrial cavity with less than half its volume intramural, endometrium 6 mm, ovaries normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system in the clinic
Refer for uterine artery embolisation by interventional radiology
Prescribe tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during her periods
Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the submucosal fibroid
Refer for total abdominal hysterectomy and ovarian conservation

subtopic_detail: Fluid and vitamin choices when rehydrating a woman with prolonged pregnancy vomiting
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman at nine weeks in her first pregnancy who has vomited eight to ten times a day for two weeks and has kept nothing down for the past 48 hours. Her booking weight two weeks ago was 68 kg and she now weighs 63 kg.

She is not febrile, has no abdominal pain, no diarrhoea and no urinary symptoms. Her mucous membranes are dry and her skin turgor is reduced. Ultrasound today shows a single viable intrauterine pregnancy with no molar features, and she has taken no antiemetic other than ginger tablets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urinalysis ketones 3 plus
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine at the upper limit of normal and no goitre or eye signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous 5 per cent glucose with intravenous metoclopramide
Prescribe oral pyridoxine with doxylamine and review her in 48 hours
Prescribe oral ondansetron and arrange community midwife review
Admit for enteral feeding through a fine bore nasogastric tube
Admit for intravenous sodium chloride with intravenous thiamine

subtopic_detail: Contraception and human chorionic gonadotrophin surveillance after evacuation of a complete mole
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman two weeks after suction evacuation of the uterus. The histology has returned as a complete hydatidiform mole and the case has been notified to the state registry.

Her bleeding has settled and she feels well. Her human chorionic gonadotrophin was 148 000 IU/L before evacuation and is 8400 IU/L today. She and her partner had been trying for a first pregnancy for a year before this one and she asks how soon they can start again. She takes no regular medication, has no vascular risk factors and does not smoke. Pelvic ultrasound today shows an empty uterus with a normal endometrial line and normal adnexa.

data_table.Examination: Uterus normal size and non-tender, no adnexal masses, minimal vaginal loss
data_table.Investigations: Human chorionic gonadotrophin 8400 IU/L falling from 148 000 IU/L pre evacuation, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: Barrier contraception only with a single hCG check in six months
No contraception needed and a single hCG check at three months
Hormonal contraception with a further uterine evacuation within a week
Hormonal contraception with serial hCG until surveillance is complete
A copper intrauterine device with serial hCG until it is complete

subtopic_detail: Testing immunity before giving immunoglobulin after household varicella exposure
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her 3-year-old daughter developed a widespread blistering rash two days ago that the child health nurse identified as chickenpox, and the two of them have shared a bed since.

She grew up overseas, has no record of having had chickenpox as a child and no vaccination record. She has no rash herself, no fever and no malaise. Her booking bloods included rubella and hepatitis serology but varicella status was not tested. She is otherwise well with an uncomplicated pregnancy to date.

data_table.Examination: No rash on skin or mucous membranes, chest clear, uterus consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 146 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Booking serology showed rubella immune and hepatitis B surface antigen negative, varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not previously tested

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a varicella vaccine dose now and repeat it in four weeks
Start oral valaciclovir now and review her again in seven days
Reassure her and advise review only if a rash develops later
Test varicella antibody now and give immunoglobulin if non immune
Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin now without antibody testing

subtopic_detail: Recognising shock out of proportion to blood loss in the third stage and stopping uterotonics before replacement
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite. A 24-year-old woman gave birth to her first baby 15 minutes ago and the midwife delivered the placenta by controlled cord traction a few minutes later. An oxytocin infusion is running.

The woman screamed with sudden severe lower abdominal pain as the placenta came away and has become grey and clammy. Estimated blood loss is around 500 mL, which does not account for how she looks. On palpating the abdomen you cannot feel the fundus in the usual position and there is a dimple where it should be. On inspecting the perineum there is a firm dark red mass filling the introitus. Two large bore cannulas are already in and fluid is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fundus not palpable abdominally with a suprapubic depression, firm dark red mass visible at the introitus, placenta already delivered and complete
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 500 mL, group and hold on file, blood taken for cross match

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for laparotomy before attempting any manoeuvre
Insert a uterine balloon tamponade device and continue the infusion
Stop the uterotonic infusion and replace the uterus manually now
Continue the infusion and add ergometrine before any manoeuvre
Apply bimanual uterine compression and continue the infusion now

subtopic_detail: Treatment regimen for latent syphilis of unknown duration detected on third trimester screening
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy with the results of her third trimester screening bloods.

Her syphilis enzyme immunoassay is reactive, treponemal particle agglutination is reactive and the rapid plasma reagin titre is 1 in 32. Her booking screen at 11 weeks was non reactive on the same assays. She feels well, has had no rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no genital or oral ulcer and no hair loss, and she has never been diagnosed with or treated for syphilis. She reports no penicillin allergy and has taken amoxicillin previously without difficulty. She has one regular sexual partner.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no genital or oral ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, fundal height consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Syphilis enzyme immunoassay reactive, treponemal particle agglutination reactive, rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32, booking screen at 11 weeks non reactive, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral azithromycin as a single dose with repeat serology later
Repeat the serology in four weeks before starting any treatment
Weekly intramuscular benzathine penicillin for a total of three doses
A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin administered today
Oral doxycycline twice daily for a total of fourteen days now

subtopic_detail: Localising secondary amenorrhoea to the outflow tract when gonadotrophins are normal and withdrawal fails
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman whose periods have not returned to normal since a surgical evacuation of the uterus for retained products seven months ago, performed two weeks after the birth of her first child.

Before that pregnancy her cycles were regular and moderately heavy. For the first three months after the procedure she had only a few hours of light spotting each month, and for the last four months she has had nothing at all. She stopped breastfeeding five months ago. Each month around the time she expects a period she gets cramping lower abdominal pain for a day or two with no bleeding. A urine pregnancy test is negative and a course of oral progestogen followed by cessation produced no bleeding at all.

data_table.Examination: Normal external genitalia, patent vagina and cervix on speculum examination, normal sized mobile uterus, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 5.8 IU/L (2-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 4.6 IU/L (2-10 follicular), oestradiol 342 pmol/L (110-1500 follicular), prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy with adhesiolysis under direct vision
Anti Mullerian hormone measurement and repeat gonadotrophins
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any procedure
A combined oral contraceptive with review again in six months
A repeat progestogen challenge after oestrogen priming first

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dose and quantification after a mid pregnancy sensitising event
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 20 weeks and 3 days who slipped on wet steps yesterday evening and struck her abdomen against the handrail.

She presents 18 hours later because a friend told her she should be checked. She has had no vaginal bleeding, no leaking and no abdominal pain since the fall, and she reports normal fetal movements. Her booking bloods recorded blood group O with a negative red cell antibody screen, and she has not yet had any anti-D this pregnancy. Her uterus is soft and non-tender, and the fetal heart rate is 148 beats per minute on hand held Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, red cell antibody screen negative at booking, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165)
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, fundal height consistent with dates, no bruising over the abdominal wall, no vaginal bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give 625 IU anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer test
Give 250 IU anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer test
Send a Kleihauer test and give anti-D only if the result is raised
Withhold anti-D because more than 12 hours have already elapsed
Repeat the antibody screen and give anti-D if it is still negative

subtopic_detail: Fertility sparing management of atypical endometrial hyperplasia with intensive surveillance
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman in clinic with the result of an endometrial pipelle biopsy taken three weeks ago for eight months of heavy irregular bleeding.

She has polycystic ovary syndrome with a lifelong pattern of four or five periods a year, a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 and no other medical history. She has one child, conceived after ovulation induction, and she and her partner have been trying for a second for the past two years. The histology reports endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis shows an endometrium of 16 mm with no myometrial invasion, no cervical involvement and normal adnexa, and there is no lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, bulky mobile uterus, no adnexal masses, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial biopsy showing hyperplasia with atypia, magnetic resonance imaging with endometrial thickness 16 mm and no myometrial invasion, haemoglobin 106 g/L (115-165), ferritin 12 mcg/L (20-200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Observation with repeat endometrial sampling again in 12 months
A levonorgestrel intrauterine system with three monthly sampling
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo oophorectomy as planned
Cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone with sampling again in one year
A combined oral contraceptive with sampling again in six months

subtopic_detail: First line ovulation induction agent in anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive for 14 months. She has had four or five periods a year since her teens and shaves her chin every second day.

Her body mass index was 34 kg/m2 at her first visit six months ago and is now 31 kg/m2 after a supervised diet and exercise program, and her cycles remain unchanged. Her partner's semen analysis was normal on two occasions. A hysterosalpingogram showed a normal cavity with free spill from both tubes. She is rubella immune, takes folic acid, and her thyroid function and prolactin are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, terminal hair over the chin and lower abdomen, no acanthosis nigricans, normal sized non-tender uterus and adnexae
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 320 mIU/L (less than 500), total testosterone mildly raised, transvaginal ultrasound showing multifollicular ovaries with normal antral morphology, hysterosalpingogram with bilateral free spill

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Ovulation induction with letrozole and follicle tracking by ultrasound
Ovulation induction with clomifene and follicle tracking by ultrasound
Metformin alone with a review of her cycles again in six months
Referral for in vitro fertilisation as the next treatment step
Ovulation induction with injectable gonadotrophins and monitoring

subtopic_detail: Sequencing antibiotics before surgical evacuation in secondary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 26-year-old woman who gave birth 12 days ago. She had a spontaneous vaginal birth at term and the placenta appeared complete at the time.

Her lochia had almost stopped by day eight but for the past two days she has been soaking a maternity pad every hour with bright red blood and passing clots the size of a golf ball. Her partner says the discharge smells offensive. She has had rigors overnight. Her uterus is tender and the fundus is palpable midway between the symphysis and the umbilicus. A transvaginal ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material 22 mm across within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender bulky uterus with the fundus midway to the umbilicus, open cervical os with active bright red loss, offensive discharge, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 122 mg/L (less than 5), high vaginal and endocervical swabs and blood cultures collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation with repeat full blood count and ultrasound in a week
Intravenous antibiotics with evacuation by a senior obstetrician
Immediate evacuation of the uterus before antibiotics are given
Oral antibiotics with discharge and community midwife review
Intramuscular ergometrine with repeat ultrasound in seven days

subtopic_detail: Choosing emergency contraception at four days with a raised body mass index
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman who had unprotected intercourse four days ago, on day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle.

She has been using condoms alone and one broke. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease and no unusual discharge, and a self collected swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea has been sent today with results due tomorrow. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. She tells you she would like something more reliable going forward and is open to any method.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 36 kg/m2, normal sized anteverted uterus, no adnexal tenderness, no cervical motion tenderness, no abnormal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 3 mg orally as a single dose taken today
Reassurance that emergency contraception is no longer effective
A copper intrauterine device inserted within the next 24 hours
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single dose taken today
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single dose taken today

subtopic_detail: Referral for fetoscopic laser at an early stage of twin to twin transfusion syndrome
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 19 weeks and 2 days with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, attending for her routine fortnightly surveillance scan.

She feels well, has no abdominal tightening, no bleeding and no leaking. Her fundal height is larger than expected for dates and she has noticed her abdomen becoming rapidly more distended over the past fortnight. Today's scan reports the first twin with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm and a bladder that is not visible over 60 minutes of observation, and the second twin with a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm and a persistently distended bladder. Umbilical artery Doppler waveforms show positive end diastolic flow in both twins, the ductus venosus waveforms are normal, and neither twin is hydropic.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ultrasound findings: Monochorionic diamniotic twins, twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with non visible bladder, twin two deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with distended bladder, positive end diastolic flow in both umbilical arteries, normal ductus venosus waveforms, no hydrops, cervical length 34 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Serial amnioreduction with weekly ultrasound surveillance instead
Weekly ultrasound surveillance with review again in four weeks
Administer antenatal corticosteroids and plan birth at 26 weeks
Amniotic septostomy with weekly ultrasound surveillance instead
Urgent referral to a fetal therapy centre for laser ablation

subtopic_detail: Antithyroid drug choice by trimester in newly diagnosed hyperthyroidism
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman at 7 weeks in her first pregnancy, referred by her general practitioner with palpitations and weight loss.

She has lost 3 kg since her booking visit despite eating normally and describes her heart racing when she climbs the stairs at work. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist palms and a smooth symmetrically enlarged thyroid with a bruit over it. There is mild retraction of both upper eyelids and slight proptosis. Her vomiting settled at six weeks and she is now keeping food down, and there is no history of a molar pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 38 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 12.4 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody strongly positive
data_table.Examination: Smooth symmetrical goitre with an audible bruit, fine outstretched hand tremor, bilateral lid retraction with mild proptosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start propylthiouracil now and reassess the plan after 16 weeks
Start carbimazole now and reassess the plan again after 16 weeks
Start propranolol alone and reassess the plan after 16 weeks
Arrange radioiodine ablation and reassess the plan after 16 weeks
Withhold treatment now and reassess the plan again after 16 weeks

subtopic_detail: Reduced liquor with a small fetus once membrane rupture has been excluded
stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at 33+4 weeks was referred after a growth scan. She reports normal movements and no fluid loss. Speculum shows no pooling and a point-of-care amniotic fluid test is negative.

data_table.Ultrasound: Estimated weight 3rd centile, abdominal circumference below the 3rd centile, deepest pocket 1.6 cm, umbilical artery pulsatility index above the 95th centile with end diastolic flow present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Erythromycin and expectant management for ruptured membranes
Emergency caesarean birth today for the reduced liquor and growth
Advise increased oral fluid and repeat the growth scan in 4 weeks
Corticosteroids with twice weekly Doppler and cardiotocograph surveillance
Induction of labour after corticosteroids, with continuous monitoring

subtopic_detail: First line investigation of excessive amniotic fluid found on a third trimester scan
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman in her third pregnancy at 30 weeks and 2 days, referred because her abdomen measures 38 cm against a symphysis fundal height expectation of 30 cm. She says she has felt increasingly stretched and breathless lying flat for the last fortnight.

Her two previous babies weighed 3.4 kg and 3.6 kg at term. She had a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks that she was told was normal, and her blood pressure has been normal throughout with no protein on urinalysis. The uterus is soft and non-tender, fetal parts are difficult to palpate through the fluid and the presentation is unstable. The scan today reports a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm with a single fetus, an estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile and a normally sited posterior placenta.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm, estimated fetal weight 60th centile, posterior placenta with no praevia, urinalysis no protein, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a detailed fetal anatomy review with repeat testing for gestational diabetes
Reassure her that mild excess fluid is common and repeat the scan in four weeks
Perform amnioreduction by needle drainage to relieve the maternal breathlessness
Prescribe oral indometacin to reduce fetal urine output and the fluid volume
Admit for induction of labour once antenatal corticosteroids have been given

subtopic_detail: Investigation sequencing after an unexplained late intrauterine fetal death
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 30-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 38 weeks and 1 day. She came in this morning because she had felt no movements since yesterday afternoon, and ultrasound has confirmed there is no fetal heart activity.

Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated, with normal growth on a 34 week scan and normal blood pressure throughout. She has had no abdominal pain, bleeding or fever. Her blood group is A positive. She is distressed but composed, and she and her partner have asked you what happens next and whether they will ever know why. Induction of labour has not yet been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms absent fetal cardiac activity, urinalysis no protein, full blood count and coagulation profile within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation plan?

options.text: Arrange an inherited thrombophilia screen and antiphospholipid antibodies today
Send placental tissue for histopathology after birth and take no maternal bloods
Send cord blood for karyotype after birth and defer all other investigations
Send maternal blood for a Kleihauer test now and offer autopsy with placental histopathology
Request maternal serology for the full congenital infection panel as the priority

subtopic_detail: Setting and adjuncts for repair of an anal sphincter injury after instrumental birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite immediately after a forceps birth of a 4.1 kg baby to a 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy. The second stage lasted two hours and a mediolateral episiotomy was performed.

Her epidural is still running and is providing good analgesia. On systematic examination with the woman in lithotomy and good lighting, the tear extends through the perineal body and you can see torn fibres of the external anal sphincter. On digital rectal examination the torn muscle involves rather more than half the thickness of the external sphincter, the internal sphincter is intact and the anal mucosa is intact. Estimated blood loss so far is 350 mL and the uterus is well contracted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tear through the perineal body with more than 50 per cent thickness of external anal sphincter torn, internal anal sphincter intact, anorectal mucosa intact, uterus contracted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the tear?

options.text: Repair in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration with absorbable suture
Repair in theatre under regional anaesthesia with antibiotic cover and postoperative laxatives
Repair in theatre by an experienced operator with antibiotics and postoperative laxatives
Repair the perineal body only and manage the sphincter tear conservatively with physiotherapy
Pack the perineum and plan a delayed secondary repair with a colorectal surgeon

subtopic_detail: Choosing the instrument for an assisted birth before 34 weeks gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 33 weeks and 4 days who is in spontaneous preterm labour. She has been fully dilated and pushing for 55 minutes and her epidural is working well.

The cardiotocograph has developed recurrent late decelerations over the last twelve minutes with reduced variability between them, and a fetal scalp lactate is not available at this hospital. She received a full course of antenatal corticosteroids two days ago and magnesium sulfate is running. On examination the head is direct occipitoanterior at station plus two centimetres below the ischial spines, with no caput and no moulding, and the bladder is empty. The consultant, the paediatric team and theatre have all been alerted and are present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph with recurrent late decelerations and reduced baseline variability, estimated fetal weight 2100 g, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mode of birth?

options.text: Assisted birth with forceps in the birth suite with the theatre team standing by
Assisted birth with a soft cup vacuum extractor applied at the flexion point
Vacuum extraction first and forceps afterwards if the vacuum attempt is unsuccessful
Emergency caesarean section under the working epidural without an instrumental attempt
Oxytocin infusion with continued maternal pushing and repeat assessment in thirty minutes

subtopic_detail: Treating a protozoal genital infection and its partner implications
stem:
You are the sexual health registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman with three weeks of vaginal discharge, soreness and stinging when she passes urine. She has one regular male partner of two years and no other partners.

On speculum examination there is a frothy yellow green discharge pooling in the posterior fornix and the ectocervix is studded with punctate red areas. The vaginal pH is 5.5. A self collected vaginal swab reports nucleic acid detected for Trichomonas vaginalis, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected and no candida seen. She is not pregnant, takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no drug allergies. Her partner has no symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Frothy yellow green discharge, punctate cervical erythema, vaginal pH 5.5, no adnexal or cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Trichomonas vaginalis nucleic acid detected, chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected, urine pregnancy test negative, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral metronidazole for her, with treatment of her partner at the same time
Intravaginal metronidazole gel nightly for five nights with review afterwards
Intravaginal clotrimazole pessaries for six nights with a topical antifungal cream
Single dose oral azithromycin for her and for her partner on the same day
Oral metronidazole for her, with partner treatment only if he becomes symptomatic

subtopic_detail: Managing provoked vestibular pain after repeated antifungal courses have failed
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman with fourteen months of burning pain at the vaginal entrance whenever she attempts intercourse or tries to insert a tampon. She has no pain at rest, and none when cycling or sitting through a work day.

She has taken four courses of oral fluconazole and used several antifungal creams, none of which changed the pain. She and her partner have stopped attempting sex and she is tearful describing the effect on their relationship. On examination the vulval skin looks entirely normal. Light touch with a cotton bud at the posterior vestibule reproduces her pain exactly, while the same touch on the labia majora and perineum is painless. The pelvic floor muscles are tender and she cannot relax them on request.

data_table.Examination: Vulval skin normal with no pallor, fissuring or architectural change, no discharge, cotton bud test positive at the posterior vestibule only, hypertonic tender pelvic floor musculature
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab with no candida or bacterial pathogen isolated, fungal culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further eight week course of weekly oral fluconazole and review
Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy alongside education and topical local anaesthetic
Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied nightly for three months
Refer for vestibulectomy with vaginal advancement flap at the earliest opportunity
Prescribe oral amitriptyline at night as sole therapy with dose escalation monthly

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a fluctuant vulval gland abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department for a 29-year-old woman with three days of worsening swelling and pain at the right side of the vaginal opening. She cannot sit down and has walked in leaning on her partner.

Examination shows a tense, tender, fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across at the posterior aspect of the right labium majus, distorting the introitus, with surrounding erythema limited to the swelling itself. She is afebrile with normal observations and there is no induration extending into the perineum or thigh, no crepitus and no area of dusky skin. She has had one similar but smaller episode two years ago that settled with antibiotics alone. She is not pregnant and has no medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling of the posterior right labium majus, localised erythema, no perineal induration, no crepitus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral di or flucloxacillin for seven days with analgesia and warm baths at home
Needle aspiration of the collection under local anaesthesia in the department
Incision and drainage with insertion of a balloon tipped catheter left in situ
Simple incision and drainage with a gauze wick changed daily by the practice nurse
Marsupialisation of the gland in theatre on the next available operating list

subtopic_detail: Structuring induction and maintenance therapy for repeated culture proven vaginal yeast infection
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34-year-old teacher who has had five episodes of vulval itch with a thick white discharge in the past twelve months. Each episode was confirmed on high vaginal swab, each cleared within days of a topical antifungal, and each returned within six to ten weeks.

She uses no soap on the vulva, wears cotton underwear and has not used antibiotics for two years. She has one regular partner who has no symptoms. Her most recent swab grew Candida albicans with sensitivity to azoles, and no bacterial pathogen or trichomonas was detected. She is not pregnant, takes no immunosuppressant medication, and her glycated haemoglobin and human immunodeficiency virus serology are both normal.

data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema with satellite lesions, thick adherent white discharge, vaginal pH 4.2
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab growing Candida albicans sensitive to azoles, glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Recommend oral lactobacillus probiotics daily with dietary sugar restriction
A single oral fluconazole dose taken at the onset of each future episode
Intravaginal clotrimazole pessaries used twice weekly for the next six months
Treat her partner with a topical antifungal at the same time as each episode
Oral fluconazole induction over one week then weekly maintenance for six months

subtopic_detail: Choosing between a history indicated suture and ultrasound surveillance in recurrent midtrimester loss
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the maternal fetal medicine clinic seeing a 31-year-old woman at 13 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had three previous pregnancies that ended at 19, 21 and 20 weeks, and no living children.

On each occasion she described pressure and a watery discharge over a day or two, and was found to be several centimetres dilated with bulging membranes before she had any contractions. There was no bleeding, no fever and no abdominal pain on any of the three occasions, and placental histopathology after the second loss showed no chorioamnionitis. Her current pregnancy is a singleton with normal first trimester screening and a nuchal translucency within normal limits. Today's transvaginal cervical length is 34 mm with no funnelling and a mid vaginal swab shows normal flora.

data_table.Examination: Uterus consistent with dates, cervix closed on speculum examination, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal cervical length 34 mm with no funnelling, mid vaginal swab normal flora, first trimester combined screening low risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her cervix in this pregnancy?

options.text: Serial cervical length scans from 16 weeks with a suture if the length falls below 25 mm
History indicated cervical cerclage placed now while the cervix is still long
Vaginal progesterone nightly from 16 weeks with no scans and no suture
Cervical pessary inserted at 16 weeks and removed at 36 weeks gestation
Reduced activity with pelvic rest and weekly review through the second trimester

subtopic_detail: Timing birth by peak bile acid concentration in cholestasis of pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 33 weeks and 2 days. For twelve days she has been unable to sleep because of itching, worst on her palms and the soles of her feet, and she has scratched the skin of her forearms until it bled.

There is no rash apart from linear excoriations. She has no right upper quadrant pain, headache or visual disturbance. Blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. Fetal growth is on the 45th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers and the cardiotocograph is normal. Viral hepatitis serology is negative and a liver ultrasound shows normal ducts and no gallstones.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 10), alanine aminotransferase 156 U/L (less than 30 in pregnancy), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (2-24), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Continue the pregnancy to 39 to 40 weeks with weekly bile acid measurement
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks gestation
Deliver today by caesarean section after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
Prescribe emollients with a sedating antihistamine at night and review at term
Commence oral dexamethasone for pruritus and continue routine antenatal care

subtopic_detail: Follow up interval for an incidental simple adnexal cyst in a premenopausal woman
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman referred after an ultrasound arranged for one episode of right sided abdominal pain that settled the same day and has not returned.

She has regular 29 day cycles with no bloating, early satiety or weight loss, and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Abdominal and pelvic examination is normal. The pelvic ultrasound was performed on day 7 of her cycle, and the findings for both ovaries and the uterus are recorded in her file.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no palpable mass, no ascites, cervix and uterus normal on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with a 6 cm unilocular anechoic right ovarian cyst, thin smooth wall, no solid areas or septations, no internal vascularity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Annual ultrasound surveillance while the cyst remains unchanged and asymptomatic
Measure serum CA125 and calculate a risk of malignancy index before deciding
Refer for laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy to obtain a histological diagnosis
Start the combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress and resolve the cyst
Repeat the ultrasound in six weeks and discharge her if the cyst has resolved

subtopic_detail: Acting on endometrial thickness in a woman with bleeding after the menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman who had two episodes of light red vaginal bleeding in the past three weeks. Her last menstrual period was four years ago and she has taken no hormone therapy.

She has a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with a small amount of blood at the external os and no visible lesion, and her cervical screening test six months ago detected no oncogenic human papillomavirus. Bimanual examination finds a mobile, normal sized, non-tender uterus with no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a regular endometrium measuring 9 mm with no focal lesion, normal ovaries and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with blood at the external os, mobile normal sized uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with endometrial thickness 9 mm and no focal lesion, cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the bleeding reflects atrophic change and review if it recurs
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months to see whether it thins
Measure serum CA125 and refer only if the result is above the reference range
Commence a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device to control the bleeding
Arrange endometrial sampling, proceeding to hysteroscopy if sampling is inadequate

subtopic_detail: Heavy bleeding on day twelve after a normal vaginal birth with an open cervical os and a tender uterus
stem: A woman who gave birth vaginally 12 days ago soaked four maternity pads in 2 hours and passed two golf-ball sized clots. Her lochia is offensive and her abdomen aches constantly. Bleeding has slowed and she is not dizzy.

data_table.Examination: Temperature 38.2 degrees C, pulse 104 /min; tender uterus; cervical os admits a fingertip
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L, white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 88 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine and discharge with advice to return
Genital tract and blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics and ultrasound
Straight to theatre for suction curettage without imaging
Oral amoxicillin alone with general practice review in two days
Transfuse two units of red cells and repeat the blood count

subtopic_detail: Fluctuant lump in a breastfeeding woman whose mastitis has not settled after two days of oral antibiotics
stem: A woman 5 weeks after her first birth was prescribed oral flucloxacillin 2 days ago for a red painful right breast. Her fever has settled but the pain is now sharply localised and she can feel a lump.

data_table.Examination: Fluctuant tender 4 cm mass in the right upper outer quadrant with overlying erythema, no skin breakdown
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound shows a 38 by 30 mm collection with internal debris

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Ultrasound guided needle aspiration, continuing antibiotics and feeding
Incision and drainage in theatre under general anaesthesia
Change to oral cefalexin and review her in three days
Stop feeding from that breast and suppress lactation with cabergoline
Mammography with core biopsy before any drainage procedure

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia at twenty eight weeks in a woman who cannot tolerate any oral iron preparation
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her routine bloods show a haemoglobin of 92 g/L with a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L.

She has tried three different oral iron preparations since her booking visit, including alternate day dosing, and each produced severe nausea and constipation that she could not sustain beyond a fortnight. She is tired and breathless climbing stairs but has no chest pain or palpitations. She is vegetarian, has had no bleeding in this pregnancy, and her previous birth involved a postpartum haemorrhage of 900 mL. Her mean cell volume is 76 fL and her C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Her blood group is O positive with a negative antibody screen and there is no history of transfusion reaction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), blood group O positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Prescribe a further oral iron preparation to be taken on alternate days with ascorbic acid
Arrange an intravenous iron infusion now and recheck her haemoglobin in about four weeks
Transfuse two units of packed red cells to correct the anaemia in advance of her birth
Start vitamin B12 and folate supplementation and repeat the full blood examination in six weeks
Investigate for a haemoglobinopathy with electrophoresis before committing her to any iron therapy

subtopic_detail: Household exposure to chickenpox at sixteen weeks in a woman with negative varicella serology
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by a 29-year-old woman who is 16 weeks pregnant. Her 4-year-old nephew stayed at her house the night before last and developed a vesicular rash yesterday morning, which his own doctor has diagnosed as chickenpox.

She played with him for several hours on both days. She has no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms today, and feels entirely well. She does not recall having chickenpox and was not vaccinated as a child. Her booking bloods, taken six weeks ago, include a varicella zoster immunoglobulin G that was reported as not detected. She has no immunosuppressive illness, takes no corticosteroids, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far. It is currently 30 hours since her last contact with the child.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No rash, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Booking varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not detected, full blood examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give her the varicella vaccine today and arrange a second dose in four weeks as planned
Reassure her that maternal antibody will protect the pregnancy and review her only if a rash appears
Arrange zoster immunoglobulin as soon as possible and advise her to report any rash immediately
Commence oral aciclovir immediately at treatment dose and continue it for the next seven days
Organise amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction testing to assess the risk to the fetus

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis three months after birth in a breastfeeding woman with a painless gland
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman three months after the birth of her second child. She reports palpitations, sweating and irritability for the past three weeks and has lost 4 kg despite eating well.

She is fully breastfeeding. Her thyroid is not enlarged, not nodular and not tender, and she has no eye signs, no pretibial change and no thyroid bruit. She had a similar episode after her first birth that settled without treatment, though she then felt sluggish and cold for several months. Her thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 34 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative and thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm per hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 per minute and regular, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm peripheries, thyroid not palpable and non-tender, no eye signs
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 34 pmol/L (10-20), thyroid receptor antibodies negative, thyroid peroxidase antibodies strongly positive, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12 mm per hour (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start carbimazole and titrate the dose against her thyroid function tests every four weeks
Prescribe propranolol for symptom control and recheck her thyroid function in four to six weeks
Refer her for radioactive iodine uptake scanning to establish the cause of her thyrotoxicosis
Begin levothyroxine now in anticipation of the hypothyroid phase that typically develops later
Commence prednisolone at an anti inflammatory dose and taper it over the following four weeks

subtopic_detail: Urinary leakage with coughing and exercise in a parous woman with a normal post void residual
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old woman who leaks urine when she coughs, sneezes or plays netball. It began after her third vaginal birth and has worsened over two years to the point where she wears a pad on training days.

She empties her bladder about six times a day and once at night, and does not leak on the way to the toilet or when she hears running water. She has no dysuria, no haematuria and no pelvic pain. Examination shows a well oestrogenised vagina, no prolapse beyond the hymen, and leakage of urine from the urethra when she coughs with a comfortably full bladder. Her bladder scan afterwards shows a post-void residual of 20 mL. Urine dipstick is negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood, and her body mass index is 31 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Leakage from the urethra on coughing with a full bladder, no prolapse beyond the hymen, well oestrogenised vaginal epithelium
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual 20 mL, urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood, bladder diary shows six voids per day and one at night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Prescribe an anticholinergic bladder relaxant and review her symptom diary in three months
Refer her for urodynamic studies before any conservative treatment is offered to her
Arrange supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for at least three months
Refer her to a gynaecologist for a midurethral sling procedure to correct the urethral support
Commence vaginal oestrogen cream three nights a week and reassess her leakage after two months

subtopic_detail: Actinomyces like organisms reported on cytology in an asymptomatic copper intrauterine device user
stem:
You are the general practitioner phoning a 34-year-old woman with the results of her cervical screening test. She has had a copper intrauterine device in place for four years and intends to keep it until it expires.

Her test detected oncogenic human papillomavirus of a type other than 16 or 18, and the reflex liquid based cytology reported no intraepithelial lesion or malignancy but noted actinomyces like organisms. She has no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge, and her periods are regular and unchanged in pattern. She has one regular partner and has never had pelvic infection. On examination her abdomen is soft and non-tender, the device threads are visible at the cervix, and there is no cervical excitation or adnexal tenderness.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass or tenderness, device threads visible
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus detected, not type 16 or 18; liquid based cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion with actinomyces like organisms noted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Remove the device now and send it for culture, then reinsert a new one after two weeks
Treat her with a two week course of oral amoxicillin and repeat her cytology afterwards
Arrange pelvic ultrasound and refer her to gynaecology for assessment of possible pelvic infection
Leave the device in place without antibiotics and repeat the screening test in twelve months
Refer her for immediate colposcopy because oncogenic human papillomavirus has been detected

subtopic_detail: Discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at twenty weeks
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 20 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy has noticed rapid abdominal enlargement and feels breathless lying flat.

data_table.Imaging: One sac deepest pocket 9.4 cm with a visible bladder; the other 1.4 cm with no bladder seen over 40 minutes; normal umbilical artery and ductus venosus Dopplers, no hydrops; weight discordance 14 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue fortnightly ultrasound and intervene only if Dopplers worsen
Serial amnioreduction from the larger sac to prolong the pregnancy
Antenatal corticosteroids and delivery by caesarean this week
Selective reduction of the smaller fetus by cord occlusion
Urgent fetal medicine referral for laser of the placental anastomoses

subtopic_detail: Abdominal distension and reduced urine output nine days after oocyte retrieval and fresh embryo transfer
stem: A 32-year-old woman had 32 oocytes retrieved 11 days ago and a fresh embryo transfer 9 days ago. Over 3 days her abdomen has swollen, she has gained 4 kg and is breathless lying down, passing little dark urine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 98/62 mmHg, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.49 (0.33-0.45), sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, albumin 26 g/L
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged ovaries with ascites above the umbilicus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide to shift the fluid, with urine output monitored
Discharge with oral rehydration advice and review in 48 hours
A dopamine agonist to reduce vascular permeability, review tomorrow
Admit for intravenous crystalloid and low molecular weight heparin
Laparoscopy to exclude torsion and drain the ascites under vision

subtopic_detail: Ruptured membranes at thirty four weeks in a woman known to carry group B streptococcus
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 34+2 weeks felt a gush of clear fluid 4 hours ago and continues to leak. Speculum confirms pooling with a closed cervix. A vaginal and rectal swab at 33 weeks grew Group B Streptococcus. She has no uterine tenderness and no contractions.

data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 4 mg/L, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Fetal: Cardiotocograph normal; cephalic, estimated weight 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management to 37 weeks with weekly swabs and monitoring
Oral erythromycin for 10 days with birth planned at 36 weeks
Corticosteroids and tocolysis, reassessing her in 48 hours
Caesarean section today, as labour is contraindicated at this gestation
Intravenous benzylpenicillin and induction of labour without delay

subtopic_detail: Collapse immediately after delivery of the placenta with a fundus that cannot be palpated abdominally
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite three minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at term. The midwife applied controlled cord traction and the placenta delivered, and the woman immediately became grey and clammy and says she feels a crushing pressure low in her pelvis.

Blood loss so far is estimated at 1200 mL and continues. On abdominal palpation you cannot feel a fundus at all, and there is a cup shaped depression where it should be. On vaginal examination a firm rounded mass fills the vagina and the placenta has separated from it completely. Two large bore cannulas are in place and crystalloid is running. Her pulse is 46 beats per minute with a blood pressure of 74/40 mmHg, which the midwife notes is out of proportion to the volume lost so far.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 46 per minute, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on 6 L per minute by mask, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No palpable uterine fundus abdominally with a cup shaped depression, firm rounded mass filling the vagina, placenta completely separated, ongoing bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing, group and hold sent, massive haemorrhage protocol activated

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Replace the uterus manually through the cervix straight away while resuscitation continues
Give intramuscular ergometrine and start an oxytocin infusion to control the ongoing bleeding
Apply bimanual uterine compression and continue it until the anaesthetic team can attend her
Give intravenous tranexamic acid and transfuse two units of red cells before examining her further
Transfer her to theatre for laparotomy so the uterus can be repositioned from within the abdomen

subtopic_detail: Scant periods with cyclical pain six months after surgical evacuation for retained products of conception
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who gave birth fourteen months ago. She had a 1500 mL postpartum haemorrhage and underwent suction evacuation of retained products at day nine, which was repeated a fortnight later for continued bleeding.

Her periods returned six months ago as a single day of brown staining and have since become one or two hours of light spotting each cycle. Every month, two days before the spotting, she gets deep central pelvic cramping that lasts about 36 hours and settles when the spotting starts. She stopped breastfeeding four months ago, has not resumed contraception and would like another pregnancy. Her pregnancy test is negative. Her follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, oestradiol, prolactin and thyroid stimulating hormone are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, normal vulva and vagina, cervix appears normal, uterus anteverted, normal size, non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (3-10 follicular), luteinising hormone 5.1 IU/L (2-10 follicular), oestradiol 320 pmol/L (100-400 follicular), prolactin 240 mIU/L (100-500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that lactational suppression explains the pattern and review her again in six months
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill for three months to establish a regular bleeding pattern
Perform a progestogen withdrawal test and diagnose premature ovarian insufficiency if she does not bleed
Refer her for hysteroscopy so the cavity can be inspected and any adhesions divided at the same time
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to characterise the uterus before any intervention

subtopic_detail: Markedly increased nuchal translucency at twelve weeks with a structurally normal appearing fetus
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 38-year-old woman who is 12 weeks and four days into her first pregnancy. She had a combined first trimester screening test three days ago.
