The nuchal translucency measured 4.6 mm with a crown rump length of 63 mm, and the fetus appeared structurally normal with a visible nasal bone and normal ductus venosus flow. Her biochemistry gave a combined risk of 1 in 15 for trisomy 21. She and her partner say they want as much information as possible as early as possible, and would consider termination for a serious abnormality. She has no family history of genetic disease and her booking bloods, including her blood group, were unremarkable. She is well and the pregnancy is a spontaneous conception.

data_table.Imaging: Nuchal translucency 4.6 mm at a crown rump length of 63 mm, nasal bone present, normal ductus venosus a wave, no structural abnormality visible, single live fetus
data_table.Investigations: Combined first trimester screening risk 1 in 15 for trisomy 21, blood group A positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about further testing?

options.text: Arrange non-invasive prenatal testing of cell free DNA and proceed further only if it is high risk
Repeat the nuchal translucency measurement in two weeks and decide on testing from that result
Defer all further testing until the detailed morphology scan at twenty weeks demonstrates the anatomy
Book amniocentesis at fifteen weeks as the safest way to obtain a definitive genetic result for her
Offer chorionic villus sampling now with chromosomal microarray testing of the sample obtained

subtopic_detail: Itch of the palms and soles without a rash at 34 weeks with a raised serum bile acid level
stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks has 12 days of itch, worst overnight, on her palms and soles, with excoriations but no primary rash. Blood pressure is 112/68 mmHg with no proteinuria.

data_table.Investigations: Bile acids 42 micromol/L (less than 19), ALT 96 U/L (less than 35), platelets 244 x10^9/L, hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Liver ultrasound normal; fetus on the 40th centile with a normal cardiotocograph

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the rest of the pregnancy?

options.text: Repeat bile acids weekly and plan birth at 38 to 39 weeks
Caesarean section within 48 hours given the stillbirth risk
Weekly cardiotocography, continuing the pregnancy to 41 weeks
Betamethasone now and induction of labour at 36 weeks
Topical emollients alone, with review in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Six months of monthly abdominal pain and now urinary retention in a fourteen year old who has never bled, with normal breast and pubic hair development
stem: A 14-year-old girl has 12 hours of severe lower abdominal pain and has not passed urine since last night. For 6 months she has had cramping pain for three or four days each month. She has never menstruated.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair; tender suprapubic mass with a palpable bladder; bluish membrane bulging at the introitus
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; bladder scan 620 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Incise the membrane in the emergency department under local anaesthetic
Request a karyotype and hormone profile before any surgical treatment
Refer for urgent hymenotomy in theatre under general anaesthetic
Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging before any surgical treatment
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress further bleeding

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth at 38 weeks for a woman on insulin whose estimated fetal weight sits just below the threshold that would prompt discussion of caesarean
stem: A 32-year-old woman at 38+1 weeks has gestational diabetes on insulin since 30 weeks, with all readings at target. Her first baby was born vaginally at 39 weeks weighing 3620 g. The cervix is 2 cm long, soft and 1 cm dilated.

data_table.Imaging: Estimated fetal weight 4350 g on the 98th centile, normal liquor and Dopplers, cephalic

lead_in: What would you first recommend about timing and mode of birth?

options.text: Elective caesarean section this week because of the estimated weight
Await spontaneous labour and reassess her at 40 weeks gestation
Repeat the growth scan in two weeks and decide the timing then
Induction of labour this week after discussing the options
Stop her insulin now and plan an induction at 41 weeks

subtopic_detail: A three day history of a painful swelling at the vaginal opening in a woman who cannot sit down
stem: A 28-year-old woman has 3 days of increasing pain and swelling at the right side of the vaginal opening and can no longer sit comfortably. She has no discharge, urinary symptoms or fever.

data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant tender 4 cm swelling at the posterior right introitus, no surrounding cellulitis, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 12 mg/L, temperature 36.9 degrees C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin for seven days with review in one week
Wide bore needle aspiration with the fluid sent for culture
Warm baths and simple analgesia, reviewing in 48 hours
Incision and drainage with a Word catheter for four to six weeks
Excision of the gland on the next gynaecology theatre list

subtopic_detail: A single ulcerated area that has not healed on potent topical steroid while the surrounding vulval itch is well controlled
stem: A 64-year-old woman with biopsy proven lichen sclerosus has one sore spot on the right for 10 weeks while the itch elsewhere has settled. She has applied clobetasol nightly there for 6 weeks without improvement.

data_table.Examination: Pale atrophic skin with loss of the labia minora; 12 mm ulcer on the right labium majus with a rolled, indurated edge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the topical corticosteroid to twice daily and review in 6 weeks
Take an urgent biopsy of the ulcer and refer her to a specialist unit
Start topical tacrolimus for 6 weeks and reassess the ulcer then
Swab for herpes simplex and start empirical oral valaciclovir
Prescribe a topical antifungal cream and review in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Two years of cramping pain confined to the first two days of each period in a sixteen year old missing school
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16-year-old girl who has come with her mother about painful periods. Her periods started at twelve and became regular at fourteen, arriving every 28 to 30 days and lasting five days.

For the past two years she has had cramping lower abdominal pain that begins a few hours before the bleeding starts, is worst on the first day, and has settled by the end of the second day. It is associated with nausea and loose stools on the first day, and she has missed one or two days of school in most months this year. She has no pain at any other time in the cycle, no pain with bowel movements or urination outside her period, and she is not sexually active. Abdominal examination is normal with no masses and no tenderness today, and she is on day nineteen of her cycle. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g when the pain starts with little effect.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen with no palpable mass, normal external genitalia, no pelvic examination performed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and ferritin within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start regular ibuprofen beginning as the pain starts each cycle
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound before starting any medical treatment
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a break
Refer her for diagnostic laparoscopy to look for endometriosis now
Prescribe codeine with paracetamol to be taken on the worst days

subtopic_detail: An intensely itchy blistering eruption beginning around the umbilicus at 32 weeks with normal liver biochemistry
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks has a 2-week intensely itchy rash that began around the umbilicus and spread to both thighs. Over 4 days tense blisters up to a centimetre have appeared and burst.

data_table.Examination: Urticarial plaques with tense bullae periumbilically and on the thighs; umbilicus involved, striae spared
data_table.Investigations: Bile acids and transaminases normal; eosinophils 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her this is benign and prescribe a topical steroid
Measure serum bile acids and plan birth at 37 weeks
Prescribe an oral antihistamine with emollients, review in 2 weeks
Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin
Induction of labour this week to bring the rash to an end

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of vomiting at nine weeks with a 3 per cent weight loss in a woman still tolerating some oral fluid
stem: A 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks has vomited four or five times a day for 3 weeks despite dry crackers, small meals and ginger. She keeps down about a litre of fluid daily and has lost 2 kg.

data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 1+, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, TSH 0.09 mIU/L with normal free thyroxine
data_table.Ultrasound: Single intrauterine pregnancy, no molar features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous rehydration and intravenous antiemetics today
Start oral ondansetron 4 mg as required and review in one week
Start oral doxylamine with pyridoxine and review in one week
Start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and taper over a fortnight
Start carbimazole for the suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone

subtopic_detail: Severe nipple pain at the moment of attachment on day twelve with a wedge shaped nipple after feeds
stem: A 29-year-old woman 12 days after her first birth has sharp pain at the instant the baby latches, easing once the milk flows and gone by the end of the feed. There is no burning between feeds.

data_table.Examination: Linear fissure at the base of each nipple; the nipple emerges wedge-shaped with a white crease
data_table.Infant: Birth weight regained, mouth clear with no plaques

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Observe a full feed and correct attachment with lactation support
Prescribe topical miconazole for her and oral gel for the baby
Prescribe oral fluconazole for her and review her in one week
Advise nipple shields for every feed and review her in two weeks
Prescribe topical mupirocin to the cracks and continue feeding

subtopic_detail: Worsening wheeze at 28 weeks in a woman who stopped her inhaled preventer early in pregnancy, speaking in short phrases
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 28 weeks has 2 days of worsening wheeze after a head cold. She stopped her budesonide with formoterol preventer at 8 weeks and has used salbutamol alone, most recently three-hourly. She is speaking in short phrases and using accessory muscles.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, RR 28 /min, SpO2 93% on room air
data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 210 L/min against a personal best of 470 L/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol alone, avoiding systemic corticosteroid in pregnancy
Intravenous magnesium sulfate as the first treatment for her wheeze
Oxygen with repeated salbutamol and a systemic corticosteroid
Urgent delivery of the baby to relieve her respiratory distress
Nebulised adrenaline and observation over the next four hours

subtopic_detail: A first unaccompanied antenatal visit at 26 weeks with grip pattern bruising and a request that nothing be written down
stem: A 24-year-old woman at 26 weeks attends antenatal clinic alone for the first time. She has bruises on both upper arms and says her partner held her against a wall two nights ago, the fourth such episode this year. She asks you not to document it.

data_table.Examination: Bruises of differing ages on both upper arms
data_table.Social: Two-year-old at home, unhurt; partner checks her phone and controls her money

lead_in: What would you do first?

options.text: Assess her immediate safety and offer a family violence service referral
Contact the police so they can act on the assault she describes
Notify child protection because a two-year-old lives in the home
Advise her to leave today and arrange emergency accommodation
Arrange couples counselling with a relationship service for them both

subtopic_detail: Four months of bleeding after intercourse with a smooth lesion protruding from the external os and a recent negative screening test
stem: A 34-year-old woman has 4 months of light bleeding after intercourse. Her periods are unchanged with no intermenstrual bleeding. Her cervical screening test 14 months ago was negative for human papillomavirus.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated 12 mm lesion on a narrow stalk through the external os, bleeding lightly on contact; rest of the cervix normal
data_table.Investigations: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea tests negative; pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat her cervical screening test today and manage on the result
Refer for colposcopy and take no action at this appointment
Stop the combined oral contraceptive pill and review in 3 months
Remove the lesion in clinic and send it for histology
Refer for hysteroscopy and endometrial sampling under anaesthetic

subtopic_detail: Non-immune rubella serology identified on booking bloods
stem:
You are reviewing a 29-year-old woman at 12 weeks in her first pregnancy to discuss her booking bloods. Her rubella IgG is reported as non-immune, although her childhood record documents two doses of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.

She feels well, has had no rash or fever, and has had no known contact with anyone with a rash illness. She works in an accounting office with no contact with young children. Her hepatitis B surface antigen, syphilis and HIV serology are negative, she is varicella immune, and her blood group is O positive. She asks whether she can simply have the vaccine now to protect the pregnancy.

data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG non-immune; varicella IgG immune; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; syphilis and HIV serology negative; blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give the vaccine now, since the risk from a live vaccine in pregnancy is only theoretical
Give the vaccine now and advise her to avoid pregnancy for the next 28 days
Defer vaccination and give it after birth before she leaves the maternity unit
Give normal human immunoglobulin now to provide passive protection during pregnancy
Repeat the antibody test at 28 weeks and vaccinate only if she remains non-immune

subtopic_detail: Vaccination advice at a routine second trimester antenatal visit
stem:
You are reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy at a routine antenatal visit. She received an influenza vaccine at 12 weeks in this pregnancy and has no allergies.

During her first pregnancy three years ago she was given a whooping cough vaccine at 30 weeks, and she asks whether she needs it again so soon. Her 3-year-old is fully immunised on schedule. She has had no contact with anyone with a prolonged cough and feels well, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal growth on examination.

data_table.Medications: Pregnancy multivitamin with iodine; influenza vaccine given at 12 weeks this pregnancy; diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine given at 30 weeks of her previous pregnancy three years ago

lead_in: What should you advise about whooping cough vaccination?

options.text: Give a diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis vaccine during this pregnancy now
Defer vaccination until after the birth and vaccinate her and household contacts then
Advise that no further dose is needed because she was vaccinated three years ago
Defer the dose until 36 weeks so that her antibody levels peak closer to the birth
Check her pertussis serology and vaccinate only if her antibody titres are found low

subtopic_detail: Fever and a discharging abdominal wound six days after caesarean section
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman who presents six days after an emergency caesarean performed at full dilatation. She reports two days of increasing pain at the wound with fever and a discharge that has stained her dressing.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she had gestational diabetes managed with insulin. On examination the lower transverse wound has erythema extending 4 cm beyond the incision line with surrounding induration, and serous fluid discharges from the lateral third when gentle pressure is applied. The uterus is non-tender, lochia is not offensive, and there is no calf tenderness or leg swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.3 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Open and drain the infected wound segment and commence intravenous antibiotics
Prescribe oral cefalexin and arrange community nurse review of the wound in 48 hours
Arrange urgent CT abdomen and pelvis before any antimicrobial treatment is commenced
Commence intravenous antibiotics for endometritis and observe the wound expectantly
Refer for immediate return to theatre for full wound resuture under general anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Maternal exposure to a childhood exanthem and surveillance for fetal anaemia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 33-year-old childcare worker at 15 weeks in her second pregnancy. Ten days ago several children in her room developed a bright red facial rash followed by a lace-like rash on their limbs, and one was diagnosed by a general practitioner.

She has had mild joint aches in both hands for three days but no rash and no fever. Her booking bloods showed rubella immunity and negative syphilis, hepatitis B and HIV serology. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated. Examination reveals no rash, no lymphadenopathy and a uterus consistent with dates. Urgent serology now returns parvovirus B19 IgM positive with IgG negative.

data_table.Investigations: Parvovirus B19 IgM positive, IgG negative; rubella IgG immune; full blood count within normal limits; ultrasound today shows a single live fetus with normal anatomy, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer termination of pregnancy given the high risk of severe congenital malformation
Reassure her that the normal scan today excludes any risk to the fetus from this infection
Commence maternal intravenous immunoglobulin to prevent transplacental viral transmission
Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction to confirm fetal infection
Arrange serial ultrasound with middle cerebral artery Doppler for the next 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Febrile illness in the second trimester after high risk food exposure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 27-year-old woman at 24 weeks who presents with three days of fever, aching muscles, headache and loose stools. She attended a family gathering five days ago where she ate soft cheese, prepacked sliced ham and a rockmelon fruit platter.

She reports normal fetal movements and no abdominal pain, no vaginal bleeding and no fluid loss. There is no dysuria and no frequency. On examination her chest is clear, there is no renal angle tenderness and the uterus is soft and non-tender. Urinalysis shows no nitrites, no leucocytes and no protein. A midstream urine has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 106/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 152/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (6.0-16.0 in pregnancy), C-reactive protein 64 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures taken; cardiotocography not indicated at this gestation and fetal heart auscultated as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for presumed urinary tract infection and review in 48 hours
Prescribe oral paracetamol and oral fluids and review if symptoms persist beyond a week
Take blood cultures and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin empirically
Send stool for culture and withhold antibiotics until an organism has been identified
Arrange amniocentesis for culture to establish whether intrauterine infection has occurred

subtopic_detail: Interpreting maternal serology after an abnormal second trimester ultrasound
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman at 22 weeks whose morphology scan reports fetal ventriculomegaly with periventricular echogenicity, an echogenic bowel and an abdominal circumference below the third centile. She has a 2-year-old in childcare.

She recalls a week of sore throat and tiredness around 12 weeks that she attributed to a virus. She has had no rash and no known contact with anyone with a rash illness. Her booking serology showed rubella immunity, and syphilis, hepatitis B and HIV were negative. Serology now shows cytomegalovirus IgM positive with IgG positive and low IgG avidity.

data_table.Investigations: Cytomegalovirus IgM positive, IgG positive, IgG avidity low; toxoplasma IgM negative; parvovirus B19 IgG positive with IgM negative; full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What does the serology result indicate and what should follow?

options.text: Past infection before conception, so the scan findings need an alternative explanation
A false positive IgM result, so serology should simply be repeated in four weeks
Recent primary maternal infection, and amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction
Recent primary maternal infection, and immediate delivery to allow neonatal antiviral therapy
Reactivation of latent maternal infection, which carries no meaningful risk to the fetus

subtopic_detail: Antenatal planning for a woman with type 3 female genital cutting
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy. She was born in Somalia, arrived in Australia four years ago, and underwent genital cutting as a young child in her country of birth.

Through a professional interpreter she describes taking several minutes to pass urine and having had three urinary infections in the past year. She has never had a vaginal examination and is frightened about giving birth. With her consent, examination shows a horizontal band of scar tissue across the vaginal opening with a residual aperture of approximately 1 cm, and no ulceration or discharge. Her uterus is consistent with dates and the pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

data_table.Examination: Horizontal scar band across the introitus with a residual aperture of about 1 cm; no ulceration, no discharge, no cyst; uterus consistent with 22 weeks

options.text: Arrange elective caesarean at 39 weeks to avoid perineal complications entirely
Defer any action antenatally and perform deinfibulation during the second stage
Offer antenatal deinfibulation performed by a clinician experienced in the procedure
Notify police, since her circumstances require mandatory reporting of an offence
Plan a midline episiotomy at birth without prior examination or discussion with her

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain in the third trimester with a non-diagnostic ultrasound
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 28-year-old woman at 27 weeks who has had 18 hours of abdominal pain that began around the umbilicus and has settled into the right side of her abdomen, higher than she expected. She has vomited twice and has eaten nothing since yesterday.

She reports normal fetal movements, no vaginal bleeding, no fluid loss and no contractions. There is no dysuria, frequency or loin pain. On examination she is tender in the right flank and right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding, and the uterus is soft and non-tender between palpations. Urinalysis shows no nitrites, no leucocytes and no blood, and ultrasound reports the appendix not visualised, no renal tract dilatation and normal fetal biometry.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 104/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (6.0-16.0 in pregnancy), neutrophils 12.6 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), lipase within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to define the cause of her abdominal pain
Arrange MRI of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast and involve the surgical team
Commence intravenous antibiotics for pyelonephritis and reassess her again in 24 hours
Repeat the ultrasound in 12 hours and manage her pain with regular simple analgesia
Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without further imaging being performed first

subtopic_detail: Offensive discharge and bleeding in a woman using a vaginal support device
stem:
An 81-year-old woman is brought to your clinic by her daughter with six weeks of blood stained, offensive vaginal discharge. She has had a ring pessary in place for uterovaginal prolapse and has not attended for review in almost three years after her usual clinic appointments lapsed.

She has no pain, no fever and no urinary symptoms, and is otherwise well and independent. On speculum examination the pessary is in situ and the vaginal walls are thin and pale, with a 2 cm area of granulation and superficial ulceration at the posterior fornix where the device sits. The cervix appears healthy. There is no mass palpable abdominally and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Examination: Ring pessary in situ, no offensive necrotic tissue beyond the ulcerated area, uterus not descended below the introitus with the pessary removed, no adnexal masses palpable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Leave the pessary in place, prescribe an antifungal pessary and review in six weeks
Refer for urgent vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair as definitive prolapse treatment
Remove the pessary, commence topical vaginal oestrogen, and biopsy any non-healing lesion
Replace the pessary with a larger size to reduce movement and prescribe oral antibiotics
Arrange transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness before any local treatment

subtopic_detail: Painful vulval and vaginal erosions with scarring in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 61-year-old woman attends your clinic with 14 months of vulval soreness and burning that is worse on urination and makes intercourse impossible. She has tried two courses of antifungal cream and a barrier ointment without benefit.

She also reports painful gums that bleed when brushing and a rough patch inside her cheek. On examination there is loss of the labia minora with early adhesion of the introitus, and glazed red erosions with a fine white lacy border at the introitus and lower vagina. The clitoral hood is not fused and there are no white parchment-like plaques on the perineum or perianal skin. A vulval swab shows no candida and no bacterial pathogens.

data_table.Examination: Glazed erythematous erosions at the introitus and lower vagina with a reticulate white border; loss of labia minora; buccal mucosa shows a white lacy pattern; no perianal involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe an extended course of oral fluconazole for resistant vulvovaginal candidiasis
Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen alone and review the symptoms after three months
Refer for surgical division of the introital adhesions before any medical treatment starts
Prescribe an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid and arrange biopsy with long term review
Prescribe topical lidocaine gel and refer to a pelvic pain service for vulvodynia management

subtopic_detail: Interpreting an abnormal thyroid stimulating hormone in early pregnancy
stem:
You review a 32-year-old woman at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy who had thyroid function tested by her general practitioner because of fatigue. She has no goitre, no cold intolerance, no constipation and no dry skin, and her weight is stable.

She has no personal or family history of thyroid disease and has never had neck irradiation. She takes a pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine. On examination her pulse is regular, there is no tremor, no lid lag and no palpable thyroid enlargement. She is anxious about the result and asks whether her baby will be affected.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 5.8 mIU/L (pregnancy specific upper limit for the first trimester 4.0), free thyroxine 13.1 pmol/L (10.0-20.0), thyroid peroxidase antibody positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence levothyroxine now and repeat thyroid function testing in four weeks
Repeat the thyroid function test in the second trimester without commencing any treatment
Reassure her that the result is normal for pregnancy and requires no further action
Arrange thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide uptake scanning to define the underlying cause
Increase her dietary iodine intake and recheck thyroid function after eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Antiseizure medication review in a woman planning pregnancy
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures attends your clinic to discuss becoming pregnant in the next year. She has been seizure free for four years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having previously failed a trial of levetiracetam because of intolerable irritability.

She drives to work and describes her independence as very important to her. She takes no other medicines and does not smoke or drink. She has read online that her medicine is dangerous in pregnancy and has already stopped taking it three days ago without telling anyone. She has had no seizures since stopping and feels well.

data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, ceased three days ago by the patient; no folate supplement; no other regular medicines

lead_in: What is the most important immediate action?

options.text: Advise her to restart her medicine today and arrange urgent neurology review for a planned switch
Support her decision to remain off treatment given four years of seizure freedom
Commence high dose folic acid and advise her to conceive as soon as possible while off treatment
Substitute levetiracetam at full dose today given her plan to conceive within the year
Arrange serum valproate concentration measurement before deciding on any change to therapy

subtopic_detail: Perineal assessment immediately after an assisted vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar who has just performed a forceps birth for a prolonged second stage in a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy. The baby weighed 4.1 kg and a mediolateral episiotomy was performed. Blood loss is 350 mL and the uterus is well contracted.

You are inspecting the perineum before repair with adequate regional analgesia and good lighting. The episiotomy extends towards the anal margin. On systematic examination with a lubricated gloved finger in the rectum and a thumb in the vagina, you can feel a defect in the external anal sphincter involving approximately half its thickness, with the internal sphincter appearing intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mediolateral episiotomy extending to the anal margin; partial thickness external anal sphincter defect; internal anal sphincter intact; anal mucosa intact

lead_in: How should this injury be classified and managed?

options.text: Second degree tear, repaired in the birth room using a continuous absorbable suture technique
Third degree tear subcategory a, repaired in the birth room with a standard perineal technique
Fourth degree tear, repaired in theatre with anal mucosal repair before sphincter reconstruction
Third degree tear subcategory b, repaired in theatre by an appropriately trained operator
Third degree tear subcategory c, managed conservatively with a delayed secondary repair at three months

subtopic_detail: overdue routine cervical screening in a woman who declines a speculum examination after past trauma
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 32-year-old woman attends for a repeat prescription and mentions she has never had a cervical screening test. She is now seven years past the age at which screening should have started.

She has no abnormal bleeding, no bleeding after intercourse, no unusual discharge and no pelvic pain. She has had two normal vaginal births and no gynaecological surgery. She tells you that she experienced sexual assault in her twenties and that the thought of a speculum examination is the reason she has avoided screening, and she becomes tearful describing this. She is not pregnant, uses a hormonal implant for contraception, and is otherwise well with a normal examination of the abdomen. She asks whether there is any way to be screened that does not involve an internal examination.

data_table.History: Never screened, seven years overdue, two normal vaginal births, hormonal implant in situ
data_table.Symptoms: No abnormal or postcoital bleeding, no discharge, no pelvic pain
data_table.Barriers: Declines speculum examination following past sexual assault

lead_in: What should you offer her?

options.text: A self-collected vaginal swab for human papillomavirus testing taken today in the practice
Referral to a gynaecologist for screening under general anaesthesia at a day surgery unit
A blood test for human papillomavirus antibodies as an alternative to any genital sampling
Deferral of screening with review in twelve months once she has completed trauma counselling
A liquid based cervical cytology sample collected by a female clinician using a small speculum

subtopic_detail: request for emergency contraception three days after unprotected sex with a high body mass index and no ongoing method
stem:
You are the doctor in a walk-in sexual health clinic. A 24-year-old woman attends asking for the morning after pill. Unprotected intercourse occurred 72 hours ago and again 20 hours ago.

Her last menstrual period began 12 days ago and her cycles are regular at 28 days. Her body mass index is 38 kg/m2 and she weighs 104 kg. She has no contraception at present, having stopped the combined pill two years ago, and tells you she does not want to become pregnant and would like something long term so that she is not in this position again. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, no abnormal bleeding, and a negative urine pregnancy test today. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea swabs have been taken. She has no known allergies and takes no regular medications, including no enzyme inducing drugs.

data_table.History: Unprotected intercourse 72 hours and 20 hours ago, day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, weight 104 kg, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, sexually transmitted infection swabs taken today

lead_in: What is the most effective option to offer her?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally now, with a double dose given because of her body weight
Insertion of a copper intrauterine device at this visit with swab results followed up
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally now, followed by an etonogestrel implant inserted today
A hormonal intrauterine device inserted today, which also treats heavy menstrual bleeding
Reassurance that pregnancy is unlikely, with a pregnancy test repeated in three weeks

subtopic_detail: counselling about skeletal effects for an adolescent who has used a three monthly injectable for two years
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 17-year-old woman who has used three monthly depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injections for two years. She is amenorrhoeic on it, is delighted with the method, and asks to continue.

She has intellectual disability and, with her mother, describes how difficult daily tablets were before the injections. Her weight is stable, she eats a varied diet, spends time outdoors most days and plays in a netball team. She has no fractures, no chronic illness, takes no corticosteroids or anticonvulsants, and has never had an eating disorder. Her mother has read online that the injection weakens bones permanently and asks whether it must be stopped at the two year mark. There is no family history of osteoporosis or early fracture, and her mother is 50 with no fracture history.

data_table.History: Two years of continuous three monthly injections, amenorrhoeic, no fractures
data_table.Risk factors: No corticosteroids or anticonvulsants, no eating disorder, weight bearing sport most weeks, stable weight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She should stop at two years because the skeletal loss becomes irreversible after that point
She should have a bone density scan now, with the result deciding whether to continue
She may continue it, with the benefits and alternatives reviewed at each repeat injection
She should switch to a combined oral contraceptive to protect bone with added oestrogen
She should start a bisphosphonate alongside the injection to prevent further loss of bone

subtopic_detail: heavy regular periods with a normal pelvis in a woman who wants to conceive within a few months
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 34-year-old woman describes periods that soak through a pad every hour on her two heaviest days and pass clots the size of a twenty cent coin, so that she works from home on those days.

Her cycles come every 28 days and last six days, and she has no bleeding between periods and none after intercourse. She has one child and she and her partner plan to start trying for a second pregnancy in about two months, so she does not want anything that prevents conception. Pelvic ultrasound performed last week is reported as a normal uterus with a regular endometrium 6 mm thick, no fibroid and normal ovaries. Cervical screening is up to date and negative. She has no bruising, no family history of bleeding disorder, and no symptoms of thyroid disease.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), ferritin 14 micrograms/L (15-200), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), coagulation screen within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound with a normal uterus, endometrium 6 mm, no fibroid, normal ovaries
data_table.Plans: Intends to conceive in approximately two months

lead_in: Which treatment should you recommend first?

options.text: A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device inserted at the next available appointment
A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress menstruation entirely
Endometrial ablation performed as a day case once she has completed her family
Tranexamic acid taken during menstruation, with oral iron to replete her stores
Referral for hysteroscopy and endometrial sampling before any medical therapy is started

subtopic_detail: maternal seroconversion to a herpesvirus in the first trimester detected on stored booking serum
stem:
You are the registrar in a maternal fetal medicine clinic. A 29-year-old woman at 15 weeks in her second pregnancy is referred after a febrile illness with sore throat and fatigue at 12 weeks that was attributed to a viral infection. Her first child attends childcare.

Serology taken at that time showed immunoglobulin M positive with low avidity immunoglobulin G, while her stored booking serum from 8 weeks was negative for immunoglobulin G, confirming seroconversion during pregnancy. Heterophile antibody and toxoplasma serology are negative. She has no rash and no lymphadenopathy now, and her liver function tests have returned to normal. A detailed ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with normal biometry, normal brain anatomy, no echogenic bowel, no ventriculomegaly and normal amniotic fluid. She is anxious and wants to know what happens next.

data_table.Serology: Immunoglobulin M positive with low avidity immunoglobulin G at 12 weeks, booking serum at 8 weeks immunoglobulin G negative, heterophile and toxoplasma serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound at 15 weeks structurally normal with normal biometry, no ventriculomegaly, no echogenic bowel, normal amniotic fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Repeat maternal serology in four weeks to confirm the seroconversion before acting further
Plan amniocentesis for viral nucleic acid testing after 21 weeks and at least six weeks post infection
Reassure her that the normal scan excludes fetal infection and return to routine care
Start maternal valaciclovir and arrange follow up ultrasound examinations every four weeks
Offer chorionic villus sampling this week so that a result is available before 20 weeks

subtopic_detail: monthly abdominal pain with urinary retention in an adolescent who has never menstruated despite full breast development
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department. A 14-year-old girl presents unable to pass urine for 10 hours, with lower abdominal pain. A bladder scan shows 780 mL of retained urine and a catheter has drained it with immediate relief.

She has never had a period. Her mother says her breasts started developing about three years ago and she has had pubic and axillary hair for two years. For the past six months she has had cramping lower abdominal pain lasting three to four days, arriving at roughly monthly intervals and worsening each time. On abdominal examination there is a smooth suprapubic mass palpable 4 cm above the pubic symphysis, which remains after the bladder has been emptied. She is otherwise well, her height is on the 60th centile, and she has no galactorrhoea, no hirsutism, no headaches and no visual symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Breast and pubic hair development complete for age, smooth suprapubic mass persisting after bladder drainage, no hirsutism
data_table.History: Primary amenorrhoea with six months of cyclical monthly pain, 10 hours of urinary retention relieved by catheterisation
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, urinalysis with no nitrites or leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone and prolactin and arrange endocrine outpatient review
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the cyclical pain and review in three months
Inspect the introitus and arrange pelvic ultrasound to define the level of the obstruction
Request a karyotype for suspected complete androgen insensitivity presenting as amenorrhoea
Arrange an indwelling catheter for a week and repeat the trial of void in the outpatient clinic

subtopic_detail: choice of contraception before discharge on day two for a fully breastfeeding woman with a raised body mass index
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward. A 33-year-old woman is due for discharge on day two after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her third child. She is fully breastfeeding and tells you she does not want another pregnancy soon and would prefer to leave hospital with contraception organised.

Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and she had gestational diabetes managed with metformin, which has been stopped. She smoked until she found out she was pregnant and has not resumed. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no migraine, and her blood pressure has been normal throughout. She says that with two toddlers at home she is certain she will forget daily tablets, and that she has never used a device before and does not want anything inserted into the uterus today.

data_table.History: Day two postpartum, fully breastfeeding, gestational diabetes on metformin now ceased, ex-smoker
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, uterus well contracted, lochia normal
data_table.Preferences: Wants contraception before discharge, expects poor tablet adherence, declines intrauterine insertion today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraception to provide before discharge?

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive pill started today with the first dose given on the ward
Reliance on full breastfeeding with amenorrhoea as contraception for the first six months
A progestogen-only pill dispensed on discharge with the first tablet taken on day 21
An etonogestrel implant inserted in the ward before she goes home today
Condoms until the six week check, when longer acting options can be discussed properly

subtopic_detail: threads no longer felt after an intrauterine device insertion with a negative pregnancy test and no expulsion witnessed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman who had a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device inserted eight months ago. She could feel the threads at first but has not been able to find them for the past two months, and you cannot see them at the cervical os on speculum examination.

Insertion was described in the notes as more difficult than usual, with the sound passing to 9 cm and the patient reporting sharp pain at that point. Her periods have been very light throughout and she has no pelvic pain, no fever, no abnormal discharge and no dyspareunia. She has never seen the device pass and has not noticed it in the toilet or on a pad. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. She has been sexually active without other contraception, and she would like to keep using this method if it is still in place.

data_table.Examination: No threads visible at the cervical os, uterus non-tender, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.History: Difficult insertion eight months ago with sharp pain as the sound passed to 9 cm, threads felt initially then lost
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What should you do next?

options.text: Reassure her that the threads have simply retracted and review at her next cervical screening test
Attempt blind removal with thread retrieval forceps and insert a new device at the same visit
Arrange pelvic ultrasound, advise additional contraception, and image the abdomen if it is not seen
Refer directly for laparoscopy on the basis of the difficult insertion and the lost threads
Take endocervical swabs and treat empirically for pelvic infection before any imaging is arranged

subtopic_detail: perineal trauma extending into the external anal sphincter identified immediately after an assisted birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 27-year-old woman has just had a forceps birth of a 4100 g baby in the occipitoposterior position after a prolonged second stage, under an epidural that is still working well.

You perform a systematic perineal and rectal examination immediately after birth. There is a midline tear extending through the perineal body, and on rectal examination you can feel a defect involving about half the thickness of the external anal sphincter, with the internal sphincter and the rectal mucosa intact. Bleeding is moderate and the uterus is well contracted after active management of the third stage. The woman is comfortable, her observations are normal, and the baby is on her chest feeding. The midwife asks whether you will repair the tear in the room.

data_table.Examination: Midline perineal tear through the perineal body with a partial thickness defect of the external anal sphincter, internal sphincter and rectal mucosa intact
data_table.Birth details: Forceps birth, occipitoposterior position, birth weight 4100 g, prolonged second stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this perineal injury?

options.text: Repair in theatre with regional anaesthesia, a single dose of intravenous antibiotic and laxatives after
Repair in the birth room using the working epidural, with oral antibiotics started afterwards
Repair only the perineal body now and refer for delayed sphincter repair at six weeks postpartum
Leave the tear to heal by secondary intention with pelvic floor physiotherapy from day two
Arrange endoanal ultrasound before repair to define the extent of the sphincter disruption

subtopic_detail: bleeding after intercourse with a red ring around the os in a pill user whose screening is current and negative
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 25-year-old woman who has noticed light bleeding after intercourse on about half a dozen occasions in the past four months, described as a smear of blood rather than a flow.

She has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for three years with no missed pills, and her withdrawal bleeds are regular and light. She has no pelvic pain, no dyspareunia, no abnormal discharge and no intermenstrual bleeding at other times. On speculum examination the cervix has a symmetrical red velvety area extending circumferentially around the external os with a smooth border, and it bleeds slightly when touched with a swab. There is no ulceration, no irregular mass and no friable exophytic lesion. Her human papillomavirus screening test three months ago was negative for oncogenic types, and nucleic acid tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea taken today are both negative.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical circumferential red velvety area around the external os with a smooth border, contact bleeding on swabbing, no ulceration or irregular mass
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus screening negative for oncogenic types three months ago, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative
data_table.History: Combined oral contraceptive pill for three years, regular light withdrawal bleeds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently for colposcopy and directed biopsy of the abnormal looking cervical area
Explain the finding, review in three months, and investigate further if bleeding persists
Treat the cervix with cryotherapy or diathermy ablation at this visit to stop the bleeding
Repeat the human papillomavirus screening test now given the abnormal cervical appearance
Stop the combined oral contraceptive pill and change to a copper intrauterine device instead

subtopic_detail: screening for diabetes at 26 weeks in a woman who has had sleeve gastrectomy and gets symptoms after sugary drinks
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 25 weeks attends to arrange diabetes screening. She had a sleeve gastrectomy 3 years ago with 40 kg of sustained weight loss. Sugary drinks leave her sweaty, shaky and lightheaded 20 minutes later, and she fainted once after a milkshake.

data_table.Investigations: Booking glycated haemoglobin 5.2 percent (less than 6.0); fetus on the 50th centile

lead_in: How should she be screened for diabetes in this pregnancy?

options.text: The standard 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks
Repeat the glycated haemoglobin at 26 weeks and treat above 5.9 percent
A week of capillary glucose monitoring fasting and after meals
No screening, as her booking test was normal after weight loss
A fasting venous glucose alone, with no further test below 5.1 mmol/L

subtopic_detail: suprapubic pain relieved by voiding with repeatedly sterile urine after multiple antibiotic courses
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman referred with two years of bladder symptoms. She passes urine about 14 times during the day and three times at night, and describes constant suprapubic pressure that builds as the bladder fills and eases for a while after she voids.

She has had seven courses of antibiotics in the past year for presumed urinary infection, with temporary improvement she attributes to the accompanying fluid intake. Every midstream sample sent in that time has been reported as no growth, including two taken while she was symptomatic and off antibiotics. She has no haematuria, no weight loss, no fevers and no flank pain, and she has never smoked. A bladder diary shows small voided volumes of 100 to 150 mL with no leakage and no urgency incontinence episodes. Renal tract ultrasound with a post-void residual of 20 mL is normal, and urine cytology is negative.

data_table.Symptom pattern: Suprapubic pain worsening with bladder filling and relieved by voiding, frequency 14 times daily and three times nightly
data_table.Investigations: Repeated midstream cultures with no growth including two while symptomatic off antibiotics, urine cytology negative
data_table.Imaging: Renal tract ultrasound normal with post-void residual 20 mL, bladder diary showing voided volumes 100 to 150 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe low dose nitrofurantoin nightly for six months as prophylaxis against recurrent infection
Start solifenacin and review the response to antimuscarinic therapy in eight weeks
Arrange urgent cystoscopy and computed tomography urography to exclude bladder malignancy
Begin bladder retraining and dietary trigger avoidance with low dose amitriptyline at night
Refer for intravesical botulinum toxin injection into the detrusor muscle under cystoscopy

subtopic_detail: National cervical screening after LSIL cytology with negative HPV
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 35-year-old woman in your clinic. She is asymptomatic, in a stable heterosexual relationship for the last four years, and has three previous normal five-yearly cervical screening tests. She has never had genital warts, no abnormal bleeding, no post-coital bleeding, and no immunosuppression. She has never been pregnant.

Six weeks ago she attended for her routine self-collected cervical screening test as part of a workplace wellbeing program. The pathology laboratory reports the sample as high-risk human papillomavirus not detected, and a reflex liquid-based cytology performed on the same specimen reports low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) equivalent.

data_table.Screening result: HPV oncogenic types 16, 18, and other high-risk types NOT detected; reflex cytology LSIL
data_table.Prior results: Three consecutive negative five-yearly cervical screening tests, last two years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step according to Australia's cervical screening pathway?

options.text: Refer for immediate colposcopy because reflex cytology reports LSIL and any squamous lesion requires visualisation of the transformation zone
Repeat the cervical screening test in twelve months to check for HPV persistence and follow up cytology at the same visit
Return to routine five-yearly screening because the oncogenic HPV result is negative and there is no cytology-relevant risk without HPV infection
Request a repeat clinician-collected liquid-based cytology in eight weeks to confirm the LSIL finding before deciding on further action
Arrange endocervical curettage in the outpatient clinic to exclude a glandular lesion missed on a self-collected sample

subtopic_detail: Lactational breast abscess management with ongoing breastfeeding
stem: A 29-year-old woman 4 weeks postpartum has a tender red left breast that has not settled after 3 days of oral flucloxacillin. She remains febrile and wants to keep breastfeeding.

data_table.Examination: Discrete 3.5 cm fluctuant lump in the upper outer quadrant, temperature 38.3 degrees C
data_table.Ultrasound: 3.5 x 2.8 cm hypoechoic collection at 3 cm depth, areola spared

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue flucloxacillin, add oral metronidazole and review in 72 hours
Ultrasound guided needle aspiration, culture the pus and keep breastfeeding
Incision and drainage in theatre, with formula feeding until the wound heals
Stop feeding on that side, give cabergoline and continue flucloxacillin
Urgent core biopsy to exclude inflammatory carcinoma before any drainage

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for Group B streptococcus with previous affected sibling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman at 36 plus 3 weeks in the antenatal clinic. Her first baby, now three years old, had culture-confirmed Group B streptococcal early-onset sepsis at 20 hours of life and made a full recovery after IV benzylpenicillin. In her current pregnancy the routine 36 week rectovaginal screening swab reports Group B streptococcus not detected.

She has no known drug allergies, no significant medical history, and no prior preterm birth. Her BMI is 24 kg/m^2. She is planning a vaginal birth in a public tertiary hospital with continuous CTG monitoring available.

data_table.Antenatal screening: 36-week rectovaginal Group B streptococcus swab: NOT detected; urine culture from booking negative
data_table.Obstetric history: First baby with culture-confirmed early-onset GBS sepsis at 20 hours; treated to recovery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic plan?

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every four hours until birth, commenced in labour or at membrane rupture whichever is earlier during this admission
No intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is required because the current 36-week rectovaginal swab is negative and screening supersedes prior obstetric history
Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times a day from 37 weeks continued until the onset of labour to eradicate any low-level Group B streptococcal genital colonisation
IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg every eight hours from admission in labour, given the severity of the Group B streptococcal disease that occurred in her previous baby
Recommend elective caesarean at 39 weeks to bypass the birth canal and avoid the need for any intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis during her labour

subtopic_detail: Investigation pathway after three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman in the outpatient clinic. She and her partner have had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages over the last two years at 8, 6 and 9 weeks; all were confirmed with a positive urine pregnancy test and each was managed expectantly with confirmed complete miscarriage on transvaginal ultrasound.

She has regular 28 day menstrual cycles and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease. Her BMI is 26 kg/m^2, she does not smoke or drink alcohol and takes no medications. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her partner is fit and well.

She saw a naturopath privately and had a karyotype on the tissue from the most recent loss which reports a euploid 46 XY specimen.

data_table.Examination: Non-tender abdomen; normal external genitalia; uterus anteverted and mobile on bimanual
data_table.Prior investigations: Product of conception karyotype from third loss: 46 XY euploid

lead_in: Which set of investigations is most appropriate as first-line workup?

options.text: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing and detailed semen analysis as first-line, deferring maternal blood work until the paternal contribution has been clarified
Inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C and S, antithrombin, homocysteine and MTHFR polymorphism screen only
TORCH serology, cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, and toxoplasma IgG and IgM as the initial workup before any structural investigation
Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis with bacterial and mycoplasma culture and empirical treatment with a two-week course of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
Antiphospholipid antibody screen on two occasions twelve weeks apart, thyroid function, parental karyotypes, and pelvic imaging with three-dimensional ultrasound or hysterosalpingography

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia detected at second trimester scan
stem: A 33-year-old primigravida at 32+4 weeks was rescanned after a 20-week report of a low-lying velamentous cord insertion. She has no bleeding, contractions or ruptured membranes, and lives 45 minutes from the tertiary hospital.

data_table.Ultrasound: Velamentous cord insertion with a fetal vessel crossing the internal os; placental edge 3.6 cm from the os; estimated fetal weight 55th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit now for steroids and planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks
Outpatient care with weekly cardiotocography and vaginal birth at term
Cervical cerclage at 33 weeks, then spontaneous vaginal birth at term
Induction of labour at 37 weeks, with caesarean only if bleeding occurs
Elective caesarean at 39 weeks after a second course of steroids

subtopic_detail: Post-caesarean pharmacological VTE prophylaxis in obesity
stem: A 34-year-old woman is 6 hours after an emergency in-labour caesarean at 39+2 weeks. Her booking body mass index was 41 kg/m^2 and she weighs 118 kg. She had insulin-treated gestational diabetes. Blood loss was 1300 mL and she is no longer bleeding. There is no history of venous thromboembolism.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological thromboprophylaxis?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily for 6 weeks instead of low molecular weight heparin
Oral rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for 6 weeks postpartum while breastfeeding
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for 10 days, with compression stockings
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily for 6 weeks postpartum
Weight-adjusted enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum after two prior caesareans
stem: A 36-year-old woman at 28+3 weeks in her third pregnancy has had two previous caesareans. She has no bleeding or contractions and lives 20 minutes from the tertiary centre.

data_table.Ultrasound: Anterior placenta covering the internal os, multiple lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear space, myometrium 1 mm, bridging bladder vessels

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Outpatient care, rescan at 34 weeks and elective caesarean at 38+6 weeks
MRI, steroids, and multidisciplinary caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks
Bilateral uterine artery embolisation now, aiming for vaginal birth at 37 weeks
Admit at 30 weeks for surveillance, aiming for vaginal birth at term
Emergency caesarean today with immediate hysterectomy at 28 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta with concurrent atony despite pharmacological uterotonics
stem: A 31-year-old woman gave birth vaginally 40 minutes ago. The placenta is undelivered despite oxytocin, cord traction and an infusion. Blood loss is 1600 mL, 900 mL in the last 15 minutes.

data_table.Bedside: Uterus boggy, firms briefly to massage; placenta palpable in mid-cavity; no tear
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly and a Bakri balloon, reassessing at 30 minutes
Activate massive transfusion and move to theatre for manual removal under anaesthesia
Umbilical vein oxytocin 30 units in 30 mL saline before manual removal
Bedside manual removal with nitrous oxide analgesia, transfusing when cells arrive
Uterine artery embolisation by interventional radiology, with vasopressors meanwhile

subtopic_detail: PPH first uterotonic escalation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite three minutes after a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39 weeks. The mother is a 30-year-old para 2 who laboured for eight hours; active management of the third stage was performed with 10 units intramuscular oxytocin at anterior shoulder delivery, and the placenta was delivered complete at four minutes. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72; there has been no antenatal hypertension.

The midwife reports estimated blood loss of 900 mL in the last two minutes, ongoing brisk trickle from the vaginal introitus, and a uterus that is soft to palpation above the umbilicus.

On your rapid review the mother is pale, alert, with brisk fresh vaginal bleeding and no perineal trauma visible on inspection. There is no calf swelling and no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Soft boggy uterus at umbilicus, brisk fresh vaginal bleeding, placenta appears complete on tray inspection, no perineal or vaginal wall trauma
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-160), venous access 16 gauge x 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 units and continue bimanual uterine compression by the treating team
Administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram, a synthetic prostaglandin F2 alpha, as next step
Administer misoprostol 800 microgram rectally as the immediate next uterotonic escalation step now
Give IV oxytocin 5 units by slow injection then infusion of 40 units over 4 hours plus ergometrine 250 microgram
Proceed to theatre for examination under anaesthesia before adding any further uterotonic escalation

subtopic_detail: Contraception choice with heavy menstrual bleeding and migraine with aura
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman in a mid-morning appointment for contraception review and heavy periods. She is nulliparous, in a stable relationship, and wants effective contraception without pregnancy for at least three years. Her cycles are regular at 28 days with seven days of heavy flow soaking through pads at two hourly intervals for the first three days; ferritin is 12 microgram/L. She has migraine with aura roughly monthly since her mid-teens; her body mass index is 24; she does not smoke.

On direct enquiry she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no breast or cervical cancer history, and no unexplained vaginal bleeding.

Cervical screening is up to date and normal; pelvic examination is unremarkable with a normal-size uterus and no adnexal mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 24, normal thyroid, non-tender abdomen, normal-size mobile anteverted uterus, no adnexal mass, cervix healthy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160), ferritin 12 microgram/L (30-200), TSH 1.4 mIU/L, urine hCG negative, recent HPV screen negative

lead_in: Which contraceptive option would you first recommend?

options.text: Progestogen-only pill norethisterone 350 microgram daily plus tranexamic acid during menstrual days
Combined oral contraceptive pill with ethinylestradiol 30 microgram plus levonorgestrel 150 microgram daily
Copper intrauterine device with 10-year duration and no menstrual loss reduction benefit at all
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks with bone-density monitoring
Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device 52 mg with 5-year duration and menstrual loss reduction

subtopic_detail: Effect of streptococcal carriage on fetal monitoring in labour
stem: A 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is in spontaneous labour at 40 weeks and has started her intravenous antibiotic. She has had a low risk pregnancy and wants minimal intervention.

data_table.Swab: Vagino-rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Labour: Cervix 5 cm, afebrile, clear liquor, intermittent auscultation normal so far

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to fetal monitoring?

options.text: Continue intermittent auscultation at the intervals already being used
Change to continuous cardiotocography for the remainder of her labour
Change to continuous cardiotocography for an hour after each antibiotic dose
Apply a fetal scalp electrode so the trace is not lost during the infusion
Continue intermittent auscultation but take a fetal blood sample hourly

subtopic_detail: Antepartum haemorrhage with fetal exsanguination pattern
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 32-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks and 3 days. She reports a sudden gush of vaginal fluid at home 20 minutes ago that appeared blood-stained, followed by cessation of fetal movements. She was well until the event. Her routine anomaly scan noted a low-lying placenta with a bilobed morphology and a single-vessel cord; a follow-up scan at 32 weeks reported the placenta had migrated away from the internal os.

She is haemodynamically stable and denies pain. Speculum examination shows a small pool of blood-stained liquor in the vaginal vault and a closed cervix with no active bleeding.

Cardiotocography is being applied as you arrive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Fetal: CTG baseline 88 /min, reduced variability, sinusoidal pattern
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin (maternal) 132 g/L, Kleihauer-Betke result pending, coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Trial of labour with continuous CTG monitoring given the maternal haemodynamic stability and painless bleed
Category 1 emergency caesarean section with paediatric team briefed for neonatal resuscitation and transfusion
Arrange urgent bedside ultrasound to localise the placenta before deciding on mode of delivery in birth suite
Give intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg for fetal lung maturity and admit for observation before delivery
Perform emergency artificial rupture of membranes to accelerate delivery vaginally in the birth suite now

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia with severe features and magnesium sulfate indication
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks and 5 days admitted from clinic for further assessment of hypertension. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 and she was previously well; there is no personal or family history of hypertension. Today at clinic her blood pressure was 168/108 on two readings 15 minutes apart. She reports a frontal headache since yesterday morning and mild epigastric discomfort described as heartburn.

On examination her tendon reflexes are brisk with two beats of ankle clonus. There is mild pitting pedal oedema. Fetal cardiotocography shows a reassuring baseline of 138/min with moderate variability and accelerations.

Proteinuria on dipstick is 3+; a random protein-to-creatinine ratio is 82 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Fetal: CTG baseline 138 /min, moderate variability, accelerations, no decelerations
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160), platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 148 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.41 mmol/L, urine protein-to-creatinine 82 mg/mmol, LDH 620 U/L (<250), coagulation within normal limits, blood film without schistocytes

lead_in: In addition to antihypertensive control and planning delivery, what is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydralazine 5 mg boluses every 15 minutes for blood pressure control, no magnesium
Commence intravenous diazepam 5 mg for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and reassess in one hour
Commence magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion for at least 24 hours
Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg and defer any further intervention pending steroid completion
Give aspirin 150 mg orally to reduce placental thromboxane production and delay progression of pre-eclampsia

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome - moderate outpatient vs admission
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman referred by her fertility unit five days after transvaginal oocyte retrieval. She had 21 oocytes retrieved and her human chorionic gonadotropin trigger was a full agonist replacement rather than recombinant hCG, and she has not yet had embryo transfer. She reports abdominal distension, mild dyspnoea when lying flat, and reduced urine output.

On examination her abdomen is distended, non-tender, with shifting dullness but no guarding. Her weight is up 3.5 kg from oocyte retrieval baseline. Chest expansion is symmetrical with dullness at the right base.

Her body mass index is 22 and she is otherwise well. Bedside ultrasound shows large multi-follicular ovaries (right 12 cm, left 11 cm) and moderate ascites; a small right pleural effusion is noted on chest X-ray.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, no guarding, dullness right lung base
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 46% (36-46), white cells 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), coagulation within normal limits, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient monitoring, oral fluid intake targets and next-day fertility unit review appointment
Perform urgent bilateral ovarian cystectomy to reduce ovarian volume and third-space losses in the acute phase
Give a 500 mL 0.45% saline bolus and start furosemide 40 mg intravenously to correct oedema and third-spacing
Admit for IV crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin, daily haematocrit, and paracentesis if respiratory decline
Give a single intramuscular dose of dexamethasone 8 mg to reduce vascular permeability and third-space losses

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with postpartum cardiac arrest and DIC
stem:
A 38-year-old woman, para 3, gave birth vaginally at 40 weeks 12 minutes ago after a 2-hour second stage. The placenta delivered complete at 7 minutes after routine IM oxytocin. Straight after the birth she said she felt breathless and 'panicky', coughed twice, became agitated and then stopped responding.

The midwife has started CPR at 30:2 and IV access is in place. You arrive with the resuscitation team.

data_table.Vital signs: No palpable central pulse, agonal breathing, SpO2 unrecordable, GCS 3
data_table.Examination: Soft, boggy uterus; torrential fresh vaginal bleeding; oozing from cannula sites; no perineal or vaginal trauma seen
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care haemoglobin 74 g/L (115-160), fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400), INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2)

lead_in: What is the single best pattern of immediate management?

options.text: Give IV alteplase as a bolus during CPR, then continue chest compressions for 60 minutes
Give a 500 mL crystalloid bolus and IM ergometrine, deferring blood products for 20 minutes
Move her to theatre now for a B-Lynch suture, continuing chest compressions during transfer
Give recombinant factor VIIa first, then start red cell transfusion once the INR has improved
Continue ALS, activate massive transfusion, and give tranexamic acid and cryoprecipitate

subtopic_detail: Uterine rupture during trial of labour after caesarean
stem:
A 34-year-old woman, para 1, is in labour at 40 weeks and 4 days, planning a vaginal birth after a lower segment caesarean for breech at term. Her membranes ruptured spontaneously with clear liquor and an oxytocin infusion was started 4 hours ago. One hour ago her cervix was 5 cm dilated, the vertex was at station 0 and she was contracting every 3 minutes.

The midwife calls you because her contractions stopped 3 minutes ago and she now has a constant burning pain across her lower abdomen, 'different from the contractions'. The fetal heart rate fell from 138 to 72 bpm 90 seconds ago and has not recovered. The theatre on the birth unit is free and the anaesthetist is on the floor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Presenting part no longer palpable on vaginal examination; fetal parts easily felt in the upper abdomen; small amount of fresh vaginal bleeding

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management?

options.text: Stop the oxytocin, give terbutaline 250 micrograms SC, and call a category 1 caesarean
Give IM ergometrine 250 micrograms and reassess uterine tone and bleeding in 10 minutes
Stop the oxytocin, call a category 1 caesarean, and site large-bore IV access with crossmatch
Stop the oxytocin, turn her left lateral, give a fluid bolus, and reassess the CTG in 10 minutes
Stop the oxytocin, give a fluid bolus, and book a category 2 caesarean within 60 minutes

subtopic_detail: PPH active management uterotonic choice
stem: A 32-year-old woman with untreated antenatal blood pressures around 145/95 mmHg delivered a 3.6 kg baby 10 minutes ago. Blood loss is 900 mL with a soft uterus above the umbilicus, a complete placenta and no laceration. Oxytocin 10 units was given and an infusion is running.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram with fundal massage
Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram with fundal massage
Bimanual compression alone, reassessing in 15 minutes
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g as the only further drug
An intrauterine balloon with no further uterotonic given

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate in severe pre-eclampsia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 28-year-old G1P0 at 34+2 weeks referred by her GP for elevated blood pressure and a severe frontal headache that started this morning. She has had two episodes of blurred vision and mild right upper quadrant discomfort since arrival.

Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 with normal booking bloods. Home readings over the past week have run 138-148/88-96. She is on no regular medications and reports no allergies.

On admission her blood pressure is 168/108 mmHg confirmed on repeat reading with a size appropriate cuff. Urinalysis shows 3+ proteinuria with a spot protein creatinine ratio of 65 mg/mmol (<30). CTG is reassuring at 145 bpm baseline with normal variability. She is neurologically alert with brisk reflexes and no clonus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 168/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC, fetal HR 145 /min
data_table.Examination: Alert, brisk reflexes without clonus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness, no peripheral oedema documented
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90), ALT 152 U/L (<45), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.14-0.34), LDH 380 U/L (<250)

lead_in: Alongside intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control, what is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, plus antenatal betamethasone
