Intravenous phenytoin loading 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis with oral maintenance postnatally
Nifedipine 10 mg orally as sole antihypertensive and admit for observation without seizure prophylaxis
Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia without corticosteroids or magnesium loading dose
Diazepam 10 mg intravenous now and reassess her neurological state and reflexes in one hour

subtopic_detail: GDM initial dietary trial before pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G1P0 at 27+3 weeks in the antenatal diabetes clinic. Her booking BMI was 31 kg/m2 and her mother was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at 45. She was screened at 26 weeks with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test after skipping first trimester HbA1c.

OGTT results: fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), one hour 11.0 mmol/L (<10.0), two hour 8.9 mmol/L (<8.5). She meets ADIPS criteria for gestational diabetes.

She reports no polydipsia, polyuria or infections. She is asymptomatic with no vision changes. She has been offered diabetes educator and dietitian input which she can attend within one week.

Today's dating scan showed appropriate for gestational age fetus with no polyhydramnios. Blood pressure and proteinuria are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC, fetal HR 148 /min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, symphyseal fundal height 27 cm, fetal movements reported normal
data_table.Investigations: As above; HbA1c today 5.6% (<5.7 non-pregnant), urea and creatinine normal, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in four weeks to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
Start metformin 500 mg twice daily now and titrate up to 2 g daily over the next two weeks
Start subcutaneous long-acting insulin at 0.2 units/kg at bedtime now with morning glucose review
Refer to diabetes educator and dietitian and start four times daily home glucose monitoring with review
Plan a category 1 induction of labour at 39 weeks now without additional glucose monitoring in the interim

subtopic_detail: Progestogen only pill in breastfeeding
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman for her six week postnatal check after an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery of a healthy term baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and plans to continue for at least six months. She wants to resume contraception before she and her partner become sexually active again.

She had one previous pregnancy that ended in a first trimester miscarriage. She has no history of migraine, venous thromboembolism, hypertension, cardiac or liver disease. Her BMI is 26 kg/m2 and blood pressure today is 118/74. She smokes five cigarettes daily and has cut down from twenty during the pregnancy.

She does not want an intrauterine device at this stage due to needle phobia and wants a method she can start today. She has not resumed periods.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Well healed episiotomy, uterus involuted, no pelvic tenderness, no varicose veins
data_table.Investigations: Nil today; postnatal bloods normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to prescribe today?

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted today after signed consent and post procedure observation
Combined oral contraceptive pill starting today with a three month review to reassess breastfeeding
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular given today with review in 12 weeks
Advise lactational amenorrhoea method alone until she has fully weaned her infant off breastfeeding
Progestogen only pill starting today with no additional precautions if fully breastfeeding and amenorrhoeic

subtopic_detail: Recurrent miscarriage antiphospholipid workup
stem:
You are the O and G registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman in the early pregnancy clinic six weeks after her third consecutive first trimester miscarriage. Her first pregnancy at 24 ended in a miscarriage at 8 weeks with a normal karyotype on products of conception. Her second at 26 miscarried at 10 weeks with a similar karyotype result. The most recent miscarriage at 12 weeks was managed medically with no complications.

She reports one episode of provoked deep vein thrombosis after a long haul flight two years ago that was treated with three months of rivaroxaban and has not recurred. She smokes ten cigarettes daily.

She is not currently pregnant and her partner has fathered another child in a previous relationship. Recent parental karyotypes were normal. A three dimensional pelvic ultrasound showed a normal uterine cavity with no septum. Thyroid function and prolactin are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, cardiovascular examination normal, no lower limb swelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide future pregnancy care?

options.text: Empirical low molecular weight heparin from a positive pregnancy test without further diagnostic workup
Hysteroscopy with septum resection to exclude uterine cavity abnormality missed on ultrasound
Antiphospholipid antibody screen: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 GP1 IgG and IgM
Send further parental karyotypes and array comparative genomic hybridisation on parental blood samples
Advise assisted reproductive technology with preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy screening

subtopic_detail: ICP delivery timing by bile acid tier
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 35+4 weeks has 3 weeks of severe itch, worse at night and on the palms and soles, with only scratch marks. Her first pregnancy had cholestasis and she was induced at 37 weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Fasting bile acids 108 micromol/L (was 62 last week), ALT 168 U/L, GGT 92 U/L, INR 1.0
data_table.Fetal: Normal growth, liquor and Dopplers; cardiotocograph reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Expectant management to spontaneous labour or 40 weeks with weekly bloods
Expedited birth at 36 weeks by induction with continuous monitoring
Category 1 caesarean this evening under general anaesthesia
Induction at 39+0 weeks with weekly outpatient bile acid monitoring
Stop the ursodeoxycholic acid and repeat bile acids in one week

subtopic_detail: Ectopic methotrexate criteria
stem: A 27-year-old woman whose last period was 7 weeks ago has 2 days of mild left iliac fossa pain and dark brown spotting. She is stable, scores her pain 3 out of 10, lives 20 minutes away and has reliable transport.

data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus, 2.4 cm left adnexal mass with no fetal pole or cardiac activity, no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 1820 IU/L; full blood count, liver and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Dilatation and curettage to establish the pregnancy location
Laparoscopic salpingectomy on this admission under anaesthesia
Laparoscopic salpingostomy on this admission with the tube preserved
Expectant management with weekly outpatient beta hCG only
Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with day 4 and 7 beta hCG

subtopic_detail: MCDA twin pregnancy - TTTS surveillance and delivery
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 26+3 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy attends for fortnightly ultrasound. Growth and liquor were concordant two weeks ago. She has no contractions and cervical length is 32 mm.

data_table.Twin A: 25th centile, maximum vertical pocket 1.4 cm, bladder not seen over 30 minutes, absent umbilical artery end diastolic flow
data_table.Twin B: 55th centile, maximum vertical pocket 9.6 cm, distended bladder, normal Dopplers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Selective reduction of twin A by bipolar cord occlusion now
Amnioreduction alone with a further scan in one week to restage
Betamethasone and delivery by caesarean within the next 48 hours
Urgent referral for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the anastomoses
Weekly biometry and Doppler surveillance without intervention

subtopic_detail: Vaginal birth after caesarean eligibility criteria per RANZCOG
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 36 weeks with an uncomplicated cephalic singleton plans a vaginal birth after one lower segment caesarean for breech, with a documented low transverse incision. Her district hospital has an on-site obstetric registrar, continuous cardiotocography, theatre on 30 minute recall, and anaesthetics on site within 15 minutes overnight.

data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight 55th centile, placenta anterior and clear of the scar

lead_in: Which feature makes planned vaginal birth here inappropriate?

options.text: The previous caesarean was for breech with a low transverse scar
The interval since the previous caesarean is 3 years
She is 36 weeks with a cephalic singleton of normal growth
Theatre and anaesthetics are on 30 minute recall, not immediate
The anterior placenta does not overlie the previous scar

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic choice in a woman with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 29-year-old primigravida in early labour at 39 weeks gestation. She had a vaginal group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks that was positive. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy (immediate anaphylaxis with tongue swelling and hypotension after an intramuscular procaine penicillin dose as a teenager). Her group B streptococcus isolate has been sensitivity tested and is reported as susceptible to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin (inducible resistance detected on D test), and sensitivity to vancomycin not requested by the laboratory.

She is contracting every 5 minutes with intact membranes. The birth suite midwife asks for the antibiotic order to give now. There is no other allergy and no other medical comorbidity. She has had no doses of prophylaxis yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, intact membranes, cephalic, fetal heart 138 /min
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab positive; sensitivities susceptible to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin with D test inducible resistance, no vancomycin sensitivity reported

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, no allergy modification needed
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery via a peripheral cannula in this labour
Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours until delivery via a peripheral cannula throughout this labour period
Oral erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours starting now and continued until delivery of the infant in this labour
Intravenous vancomycin 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours over at least 60 minutes until delivery, per AU guidance

subtopic_detail: Moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome outpatient vs inpatient management
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman in the emergency department 6 days after a fresh embryo transfer following a gonadotrophin cycle. She has abdominal distension, nausea, some vomiting and reduced urine output over the last day. She has no chest pain and no leg swelling. She has had two large volume fluids over the past 24 hours. Her pain is manageable with paracetamol.

Her weight is 4 kg above baseline. She is tolerating oral fluids in small amounts between vomits. Her most recent transabdominal ultrasound shows bilateral ovaries measuring 9 cm each, moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, no pleural effusion visible. Her home is 30 minutes from the tertiary hospital and she lives with her partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with generalised tenderness, no peritonism, bowel sounds present, mild dyspnoea when supine
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.44 L/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L, white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, beta hCG 210 IU/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management plan now?

options.text: Discharge with oral fluid guide, daily weight, daily urine output diary and same next day gynaecology review
Admit for intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 200 mL/hour and diagnostic paracentesis of the pouch of Douglas fluid
Admit for intravenous 25 percent albumin infusion and dopamine renal dose for prevention of oliguric renal injury
Admit for empirical broad spectrum antibiotics for possible ovarian abscess complicating this stimulation cycle
Admit for immediate laparoscopy to detorse and possibly resect the enlarged ovaries prior to further deterioration

subtopic_detail: Second line uterotonic choice with hypertensive contraindication
stem: A 34-year-old woman with gestational hypertension on labetalol has just delivered a 3.9 kg baby. Blood loss is 850 mL and rising with a boggy uterus and a complete placenta. An oxytocin infusion is running and bimanual compression is in progress. She has no asthma.
lead_in: Which second line uterotonic is most appropriate now?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram with metoclopramide cover
Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram, repeated at 15 minutes
Rectal misoprostol 800 microgram alone as the next agent
Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 units and observe 15 minutes
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate 200 microgram to relax the uterus

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia identification and delivery timing
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks had a 30-week transvaginal scan showing a bilobed placenta clear of the internal os, with unprotected fetal vessels crossing the os on colour Doppler. She has no bleeding, lives 40 minutes away, and has had no corticosteroids.

data_table.Fetal: Growth on the 40th centile, no contractions, no bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Serial growth scans and planned vaginal birth at 40 weeks
Caesarean this week at 32 weeks, with steroids given intrapartum
Admit at 32 to 34 weeks for steroids, with caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks
Outpatient care until 39 weeks, then caesarean if not labouring
Weekly cardiotocography and rescan, delivering when vessels move

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate toxicity clinical assessment vs level
stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia had a magnesium sulfate 4 g load 3 hours ago and is on 1 g per hour after a seizure. She is drowsier than 2 hours ago, with 25 mL of urine in the last hour.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, absent patellar and biceps reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L; magnesium level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the magnesium infusion to 2 g per hour empirically
Continue the current rate pending the magnesium level, review hourly
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to clear magnesium by diuresis
Stop magnesium, give calcium gluconate 1 g and support ventilation
Intravenous diazepam 5 mg with magnesium continued at a lower rate

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiorespiratory collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem: A 38-year-old woman collapsed in the second stage immediately after her membranes ruptured, with hypoxaemia and hypotension. Perimortem caesarean was performed at 5 minutes and circulation restored on noradrenaline. The uterus is boggy with dark non-clotting bleeding. Red cells, plasma and tranexamic acid are running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, BP 88/48 mmHg on noradrenaline, SpO2 92%
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 62 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.0), INR 2.8, pH 7.10

lead_in: Which single further intervention is most likely to reduce mortality?

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram per kg intravenous bolus
Continuous cell salvage from the surgical field with re-infusion
Intravenous ergometrine 500 microgram to reverse the uterine atony
Intravenous heparin 5000 unit bolus for the intravascular coagulation
Cryoprecipitate 10 units to fibrinogen above 2 g/L, with platelets

subtopic_detail: Elective delivery timing and mode in asymptomatic placenta praevia at term
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 34 weeks has a persistent complete anterior placenta praevia confirmed at 32 weeks, with no bleeding. She has had two uncomplicated vaginal births. Magnetic resonance imaging shows no features of an adherent placenta.

data_table.Investigations: Cervix 3.4 cm and closed, fetal biometry 50th centile, haemoglobin 118 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean at 36+0 weeks with betamethasone and cell salvage
Elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks without antenatal betamethasone
Elective caesarean at 39+0 weeks, inducing labour if she labours first
Trial of vaginal birth from 39+0 weeks given her two previous births
Elective caesarean at 34+0 weeks with betamethasone and magnesium sulfate

subtopic_detail: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia management in a postmenopausal woman keen to avoid surgery
stem: A 62-year-old woman has 6 months of postmenopausal bleeding. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m^2 and she takes metformin. She has completed her family and asks about non-surgical options.

data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 14 mm; hysteroscopic biopsy shows atypical hyperplasia with no invasive component; magnetic resonance imaging normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Oral medroxyprogesterone 20 mg daily with 3 monthly hysteroscopy
A 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device for at least 12 months
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Six monthly ultrasound, rebiopsy if thickness exceeds 5 mm
Endometrial ablation with a second generation device

subtopic_detail: Immediate manoeuvres for umbilical cord prolapse at full dilation in a term singleton
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 39 weeks has been in the second stage for 20 minutes with the head at station +1. After a gush of liquor a loop of pulsating cord is visible in the vagina. The epidural is working and theatre has been alerted.

data_table.Cardiotocograph: Profound deceleration to 60 /min lasting more than 2 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Push the cord back above the presenting part and prepare for caesarean
Elevate the presenting part and adopt knee to chest, planning assisted birth
Wrap the cord in warm saline gauze and arrange intrapartum ultrasound
Ask her to push with contractions in the left lateral position
Fill the bladder with 500 mL saline as the only immediate manoeuvre

subtopic_detail: Discriminating asymptomatic uterine dehiscence from uterine rupture at trial of labour after caesarean
stem: A 32-year-old woman with one previous lower segment caesarean is 8 hours into a trial of labour at 40 weeks. She is 8 cm dilated at station 0 with an effective epidural, and reports mild suprapubic discomfort between contractions.

data_table.Examination: Uterine tone normal between contractions, no abnormal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal; ultrasound shows lower segment 2 mm with continuous serosa, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean for suspected uterine rupture, with massive transfusion
Transvaginal manual palpation of the scar under general anaesthetic
Terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously and continue the trial of labour
Increase the oxytocin infusion to shorten the time the scar is stressed
Continue labour with continuous cardiotocography and senior obstetric review

subtopic_detail: Maternal cardiac arrest at 30 weeks requiring perimortem caesarean
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks on magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia has collapsed and is pulseless with electrical activity. Compressions, ventilation, left uterine displacement and adrenaline 1 mg have been given. She has been in arrest 2 minutes. Theatre is 5 floors away.

data_table.Bedside: Uterus at the umbilicus; magnesium level 2.4 mmol/L earlier today (2.0-3.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Transport urgently to theatre for caesarean once the team has scrubbed
Insert a supraglottic airway and continue resuscitation for 5 minutes
Give a further 1 mg adrenaline and resuscitate for another 10 minutes
Stop the magnesium and give calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent
Perimortem caesarean at the bedside, aiming to deliver by 4 minutes

subtopic_detail: Placenta percreta with bladder invasion identified antenatally requires multidisciplinary planning
stem: A 37-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her fourth pregnancy has had three caesareans. Magnetic resonance imaging at 28 weeks shows anterior placenta praevia with loss of the retroplacental clear space, disruption of the bladder wall interface and placental bulging into the bladder. She has had no bleeding and no antenatal steroids.

data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 108 g/L, group O positive, antibody screen negative

lead_in: Which peri-operative plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Caesarean at 37+0 weeks locally, removing the placenta manually
Caesarean at 39+0 weeks with placental removal and no hysterectomy
Induction at 39+0 weeks with uterine artery embolisation as needed
Caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks with steroids, cell salvage and hysterectomy
Caesarean at 32+0 weeks with immediate hysterectomy, without steroids

subtopic_detail: Severe preeclampsia with severe features at 27 weeks: expectant vs immediate delivery
stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 27+3 weeks has severe pre-eclampsia. Blood pressure remains 168/112 mmHg despite labetalol 200 mg eight-hourly and nifedipine 40 mg twelve-hourly. She has no headache, visual symptoms, epigastric pain or oliguria. Magnesium sulfate and the first betamethasone dose are given.

data_table.Investigations: Protein:creatinine 340 mg/mmol, platelets 148 x10^9/L, normal transaminases, creatinine 78 micromol/L
data_table.Fetal: Estimated weight 10th centile, end diastolic flow present, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Emergency caesarean within 30 minutes, as severe disease always demands delivery
Change to oral methyldopa and manage her with weekly outpatient review
Inpatient expectant management, completing steroids and delivering by 34 weeks
Induction of labour after prostaglandin ripening within the next 48 hours
Add aspirin 150 mg daily and discharge for weekly outpatient review

subtopic_detail: High grade squamous vulval intraepithelial neoplasia treatment selection
stem: A 42-year-old woman has a persistent itchy 2 cm hyperpigmented plaque on the right labium minus with mild thickening. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day, has never been vaccinated against human papillomavirus, and wishes to preserve vulval anatomy.

data_table.Biopsy: Vulval high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, usual type, human papillomavirus 16 positive, no invasion
data_table.Examination: No ulceration, no palpable inguinal nodes, vagina and cervix normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Wide local excision with a 5 mm negative peripheral margin
Reassurance with clinical review at 12 months and no treatment
Simple total vulvectomy to remove all infected epithelium
External beam radiotherapy 45 Gy in 25 fractions to the vulva
Topical imiquimod 5 percent three times weekly for 16 weeks

subtopic_detail: Third line uterotonic choice for atonic postpartum haemorrhage after first line failure
stem: A 32-year-old woman with essential hypertension well controlled on amlodipine delivered a 3900 g baby. Ten minutes after the placenta, blood loss is 1200 mL with a poorly contracted uterus and a complete placenta. An oxytocin bolus and infusion have been given. She has no asthma.

data_table.Genital tract: No cervical or vaginal laceration identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation now, before any further uterotonic
Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram before any ergot agent
Rectal misoprostol 800 microgram alone, with no ergot agent
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes first
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram with tranexamic acid 1 g

subtopic_detail: Immediate antihypertensive choice for severe range blood pressure in pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 26-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks presents with a 2 day history of headache and epigastric pain. Her booking blood pressure was 108/64 mmHg. Today her blood pressure has been 166/112, 172/108 and 168/110 mmHg over the past 30 minutes on repeated automated cuff. Urinary protein creatinine ratio is 78 mg/mmol.

She has brisk reflexes but no clonus and no visual disturbance. Fetal cardiotocograph is reassuring. Bloods show platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (below 35), creatinine 78 micromol/L. She is on no regular medication and has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 168/110 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Reflexes: Brisk, no clonus, no visual disturbance
data_table.Laboratory: Platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (below 35), creatinine 78 micromol/L, urinary protein creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive management?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and start magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading, then a 1 g/hour infusion for seizure prophylaxis at this stage
Oral atenolol 50 mg once and observe for one hour to confirm response before adding any parenteral agent or magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure below 90 mmHg and hold magnesium sulfate until an eclamptic seizure occurs
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg immediately for rapid onset and repeat every 15 minutes as needed to bring blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg within one hour
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to reduce vascular volume and lower blood pressure and defer magnesium sulfate to prevent worsening of the pre-eclamptic profile

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum antibiotic decision in labour without antenatal group B streptococcus screening result
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 39+2 weeks is in spontaneous active labour at 5 cm with intact membranes. She missed her 36 week appointment and has no Group B Streptococcus swab result. She has no penicillin allergy, is afebrile, and the liquor is clear when the membranes rupture.

data_table.Screening: No swab result; no prior colonisation, no previous affected baby, no bacteriuria this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic plan?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics, as she is at term, afebrile and has clear liquor
Oral amoxicillin 1 g now and six-hourly through labour
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g, then 1.8 g four-hourly until birth
Send a rectovaginal swab now and treat only if it is positive
A single intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g dose at admission

subtopic_detail: Selecting a reversible contraceptive in a woman with migraine with aura and heavy menstrual bleeding
stem: A 29-year-old nulliparous woman has migraine with visual aura twice a month and heavy periods, soaking a pad every 2 hours for the first 3 days. Pelvic ultrasound 4 months ago was normal. She wants reliable contraception and lighter periods.

data_table.Background: Non-smoker, body mass index 24, BP 116/72 mmHg, no thromboembolism history

lead_in: Which contraceptive is most appropriate to recommend first?

options.text: Desogestrel 75 microgram daily with tranexamic acid for heavy days
A combined pill of ethinylestradiol 30 microgram taken continuously
A combined transdermal patch changed weekly, 3 weeks in every 4
A 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device lasting 5 to 8 years
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg every 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dosing after a sensitising event in a rhesus negative woman at 20 weeks
stem: A 25-year-old woman at 20+4 weeks who is O RhD negative fell from her bicycle onto her right side. She has right lower quadrant bruising and mild discomfort, with no bleeding and no contractions. She has had no anti-D this pregnancy.

data_table.Ultrasound: Normally grown fetus, normally sited placenta, no retroplacental collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D management now?

options.text: Anti-D 625 IU intravenously now, for faster onset than intramuscular
Anti-D 1500 IU intramuscularly now as the routine 28 week dose
Send a Kleihauer test and withhold anti-D until it is positive
No dose today; give the routine anti-D at her 28 week visit
Anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly now, with a Kleihauer test to guide more

subtopic_detail: First response to overt umbilical cord prolapse at full dilatation in a hospital birth suite
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 39+5 weeks in the second stage has a gush of clear liquor, after which a pulsating cord is felt below the presenting part. She is fully dilated with the vertex at station 0. Theatre is 4 minutes away.

data_table.Cardiotocograph: Fetal heart rate 78 /min for 2 minutes with reduced variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and prepare for assisted vaginal birth
Encourage active pushing with oxytocin augmentation as the head is at the spines
Replace the cord in the uterus and continue expectant monitoring
Transfer for category 1 caesarean without any manual elevation
Fill the bladder with 500 mL saline to elevate the presenting part

subtopic_detail: Choice between medical and surgical management of an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy
stem: A 26-year-old woman whose last period was 7 weeks ago has 3 days of mild right iliac fossa pain and light spotting. She is stable, has no shoulder tip pain, lives 10 minutes away and has reliable transport.

data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus, right adnexal mass 2.4 cm, no cardiac activity, no free fluid
data_table.Laboratory: Beta hCG 3200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L, no renal or hepatic disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy today because the beta hCG exceeds 3000 IU/L
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate with day 4 and day 7 beta hCG
Expectant management with weekly beta hCG and no intervention
A single dose of vaginal misoprostol 800 microgram, hCG at 48 hours
Laparoscopic salpingostomy today to preserve her future fertility

subtopic_detail: First hour management of maternal sepsis from pyelonephritis at 22 weeks with an equivocal lactate
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 22+2 weeks has 24 hours of fever, right loin pain and rigors, with vomiting and dizziness on standing. She has right renal angle tenderness and no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 24 /min, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 2.4 mmol/L, white cell count 18 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L
data_table.Urine: Leucocytes and nitrites on dipstick; no obstruction on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Betamethasone for fetal lung maturation, with antibiotics started afterwards
Oral cefalexin, avoiding gentamicin because of the fetal ototoxicity risk
Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g, with fluid resuscitation withheld for 4 hours
Blood cultures, intravenous gentamicin and ampicillin within 1 hour, and fluid
Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem as empirical carbapenem cover

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis loading and maintenance in a woman with severe pre-eclampsia at 34 plus 3 weeks
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 34+3 weeks has severe pre-eclampsia with headache and epigastric pain. Intravenous labetalol has been started and betamethasone organised; renal function is preserved.

data_table.Bloods: Platelets 118 x10^9/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L, ALT 88 U/L (5-45)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Intramuscular 5 g into each buttock, then 5 g four-hourly thereafter
Withhold magnesium and give diazepam only if a seizure occurs
Intravenous 2 g over 5 minutes, then 2 g hourly to serum level
Intravenous 4 g over 20 minutes, then 1 g hourly for 24 hours postpartum
Intravenous 6 g bolus, then 2 to 3 g hourly titrated to blood pressure

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis timing and interval for a Group B Streptococcus positive woman in early labour at 39 weeks
stem: A 29-year-old parous woman at 39+2 weeks is in early labour, 3 cm dilated, with membranes ruptured 90 minutes ago. Her 36-week vaginal and rectal swab grew Group B Streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Observations: Temperature 36.8 degrees C, HR 88 /min, BP 118/72 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Single intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g with no further doses during labour
Withhold antibiotics unless fever develops or membranes rupture beyond 18 hours
Oral amoxicillin 1 g eight-hourly, first dose before transfer to birth suite
Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg eight-hourly for the duration of labour
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g, then 1.8 g four-hourly until birth

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis dosing and timing in an unsensitised RhD negative primigravida
stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at 27+5 weeks is RhD negative with no red cell antibodies at booking. She has had no bleeding, trauma or invasive procedures. Cell free fetal DNA RhD typing is not funded in her state.

data_table.Booking bloods: Group O RhD negative, no red cell antibodies, haemoglobin 122 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D regimen?

options.text: Anti-D 625 IU intramuscularly today and a second dose at 34 weeks
A single 1500 IU intramuscular dose today, with none until after birth
Defer anti-D to 34 weeks and give a single 625 IU dose then
Defer until cell free fetal DNA confirms an RhD positive fetus
Repeat the antibody screen in 2 weeks before giving any anti-D

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacological therapy for uterine atony postpartum haemorrhage of 800 mL at 10 minutes after normal vaginal delivery
stem: A 34-year-old parous woman gave birth vaginally 10 minutes ago after a third stage managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU. Blood loss is 800 mL and continuing. The uterus is soft, the placenta complete, with no genital tract laceration.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram, repeated every 15 minutes as needed
Intravenous oxytocin infusion 40 IU with uterine massage, ergometrine next
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g alone, reassessing bleeding at 30 minutes
Sublingual misoprostol 800 microgram, reassessing bleeding at 20 minutes
Intrauterine balloon tamponade before any further uterotonic therapy

subtopic_detail: Expectant management timing decision in confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 33 plus 2 weeks without chorioamnionitis
stem: A 29-year-old parous woman at 33+2 weeks has confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 6 hours ago with clear liquor. She is not contracting, the cardiotocograph is reactive, and the first betamethasone dose was given 4 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 36.8 degrees C, HR 84 /min, BP 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Bloods: C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (below 5), white cell count 9.6 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induce labour today, as expectancy beyond 32 weeks adds no fetal benefit
Caesarean section tonight, once the second corticosteroid dose is given
Admit for expectant management with erythromycin and delivery at 37 weeks
Magnesium sulfate 4 g then 1 g hourly now for fetal neuroprotection
Atosiban tocolysis for 48 hours to complete the corticosteroid course

subtopic_detail: Suspected complete hydatidiform mole with markedly elevated beta hCG, hyperemesis and classic ultrasound features at 9 weeks
stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 9+2 weeks has severe hyperemesis, brown discharge for 3 days and passed a grape-like fragment yesterday. The uterus is larger than dates.

data_table.Ultrasound: Enlarged uterus, no fetal parts, echogenic mass with multiple small anechoic spaces, bilateral 5 cm theca lutein cysts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 today for a non-viable pregnancy
Outpatient dilatation and sharp curettage in 2 weeks, with later review
Intravenous oxytocin infusion to expel the tissue, with no surgical evacuation
Admit for suction curettage with histopathology and registry hCG surveillance
Urgent total abdominal hysterectomy today as the definitive management

subtopic_detail: Antenatal referral and delivery planning for a woman with three prior caesarean sections and a low anterior placenta at 32 weeks with placenta accreta spectrum features on ultrasound
stem: A 36-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her fourth pregnancy has had three previous caesarean sections. She has had no bleeding or contractions and lives 45 minutes from the tertiary centre.

data_table.Ultrasound: Anterior placenta over the internal os, lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, bridging bladder vessels

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue general practitioner shared care, rescan at 36 weeks and deliver locally
Admit today for an elective lower segment caesarean section at 32 weeks
Amniocentesis at 34 weeks for fetal lung maturity before planning delivery
Refer for classical caesarean and hysterectomy at 39 weeks by the on-call team
Refer to a tertiary multidisciplinary team for caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36+6 weeks

subtopic_detail: Recognition and immediate management of amniotic fluid embolism presenting as intrapartum collapse with disseminated intravascular coagulation
stem: A 33-year-old woman collapsed immediately after a normal vaginal birth at 40 weeks with sudden dyspnoea. Circulation returned after 3 minutes of resuscitation and she is intubated on adrenaline. Blood oozes from venepuncture sites, with no retained placenta or tear.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 /min, BP 78/42 mmHg, SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0, pH 7.14
data_table.Coagulation: Haemoglobin 82 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (2.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Massive transfusion protocol with fibrinogen concentrate 4 g and balanced components
Intravenous heparin bolus and infusion before any blood component transfusion
Recombinant factor VIIa before replacing fibrinogen or correcting the acidosis
Tranexamic acid 4 g alone, with blood components deferred 30 minutes
Atropine, ondansetron and ketorolac alone, with blood components deferred

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic choice in a woman with chronic hypertension
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 32-year-old G3P2 woman is 15 minutes into her third stage after a normal vaginal birth of a 3.8 kg baby at 40+1 weeks. She has essential hypertension on labetalol and asthma controlled on budesonide/formoterol.

She has soaked two large obstetric pads and continues to bleed briskly from the vagina. Vital signs are pulse 128, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Estimated blood loss is 1200 mL. The placenta was delivered intact and complete. On bimanual examination the fundus is soft and above the umbilicus, and there is no laceration visible on inspection.

She has already received oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly with delivery of the anterior shoulder and an intravenous infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1000 mL of Hartmann's solution is running. The senior midwife asks which second-line uterotonic to give next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Uterine fundus soft and above the umbilicus, placenta intact, no visible laceration
data_table.Medications: Labetalol for hypertension, budesonide/formoterol for asthma; oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery plus oxytocin 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann's IV infusion

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate second-line uterotonic?

options.text: Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular, may repeat every 15 minutes to 8 doses maximum
Ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscular, may repeat every 2 hours to 5 doses maximum
Misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum single dose combined with bimanual compression
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes with no additional uterotonic given
Additional oxytocin 10 units intravenous bolus over 1 minute without changing the infusion

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 38-year-old primigravida is admitted at 34+2 weeks gestation with new blood pressure of 172/108 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart, and 3+ proteinuria on dipstick. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg and her pregnancy has otherwise been unremarkable. She reports a right upper quadrant heaviness and one episode of visual flickering this morning.

On examination her reflexes are brisk with no clonus and her fundi show no papilloedema. Vital signs are pulse 92, blood pressure 168/104 mmHg after 15 minutes rest, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148. Blood results show haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 78 U/L (5-45), AST 84 U/L (5-45), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), urine protein:creatinine ratio 250 mg/mmol (<30).

Intravenous labetalol is being drawn up. CTG is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 168/104 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, FHR 148
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 78 U/L (5-45), AST 84 U/L (5-45), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.44 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), urine PCR 250 mg/mmol (<30)

lead_in: In addition to intravenous labetalol, what is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/h infusion
Phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous over 30 minutes as seizure prophylaxis
Diazepam 10 mg intravenous over 1 minute for seizure prophylaxis and sedation
Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular alone with delayed antihypertensive therapy
Immediate emergency caesarean section before further stabilisation of blood pressure

subtopic_detail: OGTT threshold interpretation at 26 weeks
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar. A 34-year-old G2P1 woman at 26+3 weeks gestation attends for review of her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Her previous baby weighed 4.4 kg at 39 weeks and was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery; she had no formal diabetes testing in that pregnancy. She has a BMI of 33 and her mother has type 2 diabetes.

Her 75 g OGTT results are fasting 4.9 mmol/L (fasting under 5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (1 hour under 10.0), 2 hour 8.4 mmol/L (2 hour under 8.5). Her booking HbA1c was 5.4 percent (under 5.7 percent), booking bloods otherwise normal. Her blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg and urinalysis shows no glycosuria and no proteinuria. Fetal growth on symphysis-fundal height measurement is on the 75th percentile.

She asks whether the results are normal, and what happens next.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): Fasting 4.9 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hour 8.4 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Examination: BP 118/72 mmHg, no glycosuria, no proteinuria, SFH on 75th centile

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Order fasting insulin and HbA1c today to distinguish gestational from pre-existing diabetes
Reassure her the test is normal and continue routine antenatal care visits
Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks at 30 weeks because only one value is abnormal
Start metformin 500 mg orally twice daily now without further monitoring or education
Diagnose gestational diabetes and refer to the antenatal diabetes clinic for education

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic in a woman with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 6+4 weeks has 3 days of left iliac fossa ache and light spotting. She had a right salpingectomy 2 years ago for a ruptured ectopic and is trying to conceive.

data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; 22 mm left adnexal mass with yolk sac, no cardiac activity
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 3200 IU/L today, 3150 IU/L 48 hours ago

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate with day 4 and day 7 hCG follow-up
Laparoscopy with the intention of left salpingectomy of the affected tube
Laparoscopy with the intention of salpingostomy on the affected tube
Repeat the beta hCG in 48 hours and observe with no intervention
Suction curettage first to confirm the pregnancy is not intrauterine

subtopic_detail: Threatened preterm labour at 30 weeks with contraindications to nifedipine
stem: A 26-year-old woman at 30+1 weeks has 4 hours of painful contractions every 4 minutes. Her placenta covers the internal os by 32 mm and her last baby was born at 34 weeks. There is no bleeding and the cardiotocograph is reactive. Betamethasone and magnesium sulfate have been given.

data_table.Examination: Cervical length 12 mm on transvaginal ultrasound, fetal fibronectin positive, no bleeding

lead_in: Which tocolytic is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous atosiban by loading dose then infusion for 48 hours
Oral nifedipine 20 mg then 10 to 20 mg six-hourly for 48 hours
Intravenous salbutamol titrated to contraction frequency
Rectal indometacin 100 mg then 25 mg six-hourly for 48 hours
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g as the primary tocolytic

subtopic_detail: Late onset FGR delivery timing with abnormal umbilical Doppler
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 36+4 weeks has been under surveillance since a 32 week scan showed an estimated weight on the 5th centile with normal Dopplers. Blood pressure is normal with no proteinuria.

data_table.Ultrasound: Estimated weight 3rd centile, abdominal circumference below the 1st centile, umbilical artery pulsatility index 97th centile, cerebroplacental ratio below 1.0

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management step?

options.text: Twice weekly cardiotocography as an outpatient and repeat Doppler in 7 days
Induction of labour after a course of betamethasone started today
Elective caesarean without a trial of labour for the small fetus
Admit for daily cardiotocography and defer delivery until 39 weeks
Start aspirin 150 mg daily and continue to 39 weeks with weekly scans

subtopic_detail: Severe OHSS after IVF requiring paracentesis versus admission
stem: A 33-year-old woman is 9 days after retrieval of 32 oocytes with an hCG trigger and fresh embryo transfer. She has 4 days of abdominal distension, breathlessness and reduced urine output.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 92% on air
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 51% (36-46), sodium 128 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L, albumin 24 g/L
data_table.Ultrasound: Bilateral 12 cm ovaries with ascites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate laparotomy and bilateral oophorectomy to remove the enlarged ovaries
Outpatient monitoring with high protein oral fluids and daily blood tests
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to increase urine output and reduce the ascites
Admit for intravenous crystalloid, albumin and ultrasound guided paracentesis
Repeat the beta hCG in 48 hours before any further intervention

subtopic_detail: Second twin non-cephalic presentation management
stem: A 28-year-old woman with a dichorionic twin pregnancy at 38+1 weeks delivered a cephalic first twin 16 minutes ago. The second twin is transverse with the back down, membranes intact, estimated weight 2.6 kg. She is fully dilated with no presenting part palpable and no cord felt.

data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 155 /min with recurrent variable decelerations to 90 /min
data_table.Setting: Epidural working, theatre 3 minutes away, consultant present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for the second twin?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean under general anaesthesia
External cephalic version with intravenous salbutamol tocolysis
Internal podalic version and breech extraction under epidural top-up
Rupture the membranes to let the presenting part descend, then oxytocin
Await spontaneous rotation for 30 minutes if the trace stays reassuring

subtopic_detail: Mode of delivery counselling after prior third or fourth degree perineal tear
stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks had a 4a perineal tear repaired in theatre by a consultant at her first birth 2 years ago. She asks about mode of delivery this time.

data_table.Symptoms: Flatus incontinence 2 to 3 times a month, no faecal incontinence
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound: healed 60 degree sphincter defect; manometry resting 42 mmHg, squeeze 96 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice on mode of delivery?

options.text: Support planned vaginal birth after discussing the recurrent tear risk
Recommend elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as the default
Recommend vaginal birth with prophylactic mediolateral episiotomy always
Recommend induction at 38 weeks to limit fetal size and tear risk
Defer the decision until labour, when fetal size can be confirmed

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis by 75 g OGTT
stem:
You are the antenatal shared care GP. A 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 27 weeks gestation returns for a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test result. She is well.

Her BMI at booking was 29 kg/m2 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. She has no polyuria or polydipsia and fetal movements are normal. Fetal biometry at 28 weeks last week was on the 60th centile with a normal umbilical artery Doppler.

The pathology report shows fasting plasma glucose 5.2 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L, and 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L. Her ferritin, thyroid function, and urinalysis at this visit were within normal limits.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): Fasting 5.2 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Booking: Nulliparous, 31 y, BMI 29 kg/m2, family history type 2 diabetes
data_table.Fetal growth: Biometry 60th centile at 28 weeks; UA Doppler within normal limits
data_table.Other labs: Ferritin, thyroid function, urinalysis within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Reassure the woman that the results are within normal limits for the trimester and continue routine antenatal care
Repeat the OGTT in 4 weeks because only the 1 hour and 2 hour values met threshold and the fasting result was borderline
Commence metformin 500 mg orally with breakfast immediately without a dietary trial or self monitoring interval
Order HbA1c and only diagnose GDM if the result is 5.7% or greater as a confirmatory test in addition to the OGTT
Diagnose gestational diabetes and refer to the joint diabetes antenatal clinic for education and self monitoring

subtopic_detail: Second line uterotonic when hypertensive
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar. A 34-year-old primipara has had a spontaneous vaginal birth 15 minutes ago at 40 weeks after augmentation for prolonged first stage. Estimated blood loss so far is 900 mL and continues to trickle.

Her booking blood pressure was 128/82. She developed gestational hypertension at 36 weeks and has been on labetalol 200 mg twice daily. Blood pressure in early labour was 152/98 and again 156/102 in second stage. She has no known allergies.

On examination the uterus feels boggy. The placenta appears complete on inspection. The perineum is intact. Intramuscular oxytocin 10 units was given with the anterior shoulder and a 40 unit oxytocin infusion in 1 L Hartmann is now running at 250 mL/hour. Uterine massage continues.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 156/98, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Uterine tone: Boggy on abdominal palpation despite massage
data_table.Uterotonics given: IM oxytocin 10 units at anterior shoulder; oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann infusion at 250 mL/hour
data_table.Blood pressure trend: Gestational hypertension on labetalol 200 mg BD; BP 152/98 then 156/102 in second stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to add?

options.text: Carboprost (15 methyl PGF2 alpha) 250 microgram intramuscular, up to 8 doses at 15 minute intervals
Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular immediately as a second line uterotonic
Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual as the second line uterotonic after oxytocin infusion
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes and stop further uterotonics
Insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon before any further pharmacological escalation

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 6+3 weeks has 2 days of left iliac fossa discomfort and light spotting. She is stable, with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no rebound. She lives nearby with reliable transport and can attend follow-up.

data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus, 22 mm left tubal mass, no cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy today, as any tubal ectopic needs surgery
Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with beta hCG surveillance to day 7
Serial beta hCG every 48 hours with expectant management for 2 weeks
Oral mifepristone followed by vaginal misoprostol 800 microgram
Laparoscopic salpingostomy to preserve tubal patency for future fertility

subtopic_detail: NCSP result triage
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a Cervical Screening Test result for a 32-year-old woman. She had a self collected vaginal swab through the general practice 5 days ago and this is her first screening test.

She is well, has a regular sexual partner of 3 years, and uses combined oral contraceptive pills. Her last cervical screening prior to today was never; she was overseas during the transition from Pap smear to the NCSP renewed program. She has no dyspareunia and no post coital bleeding.

The report reads: HPV detected, other high risk type (not 16 or 18). Because the sample is self collected there is no liquid based cytology reported on this sample.

data_table.History: 32 y, first ever cervical screen; no post coital or intermenstrual bleeding
data_table.Sample: Self collected vaginal swab; no cytology reported on self collected sample
data_table.Result: HPV detected, non 16/18 high risk type

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step under the National Cervical Screening Program?

options.text: Repeat the self collected HPV test in 12 months without cytology and manage on the future HPV result
Refer directly to colposcopy today because any HPV positive self collected sample requires colposcopy
Recall for a clinician collected cervical sample for reflex liquid based cytology and act on that cytology result
Recall for a clinician collected sample to repeat HPV testing rather than proceed to cytology triage this cycle
Reassure the woman that non 16 or 18 HPV clears spontaneously and rescreen at the routine 5 year interval

subtopic_detail: MgSO4 loading in severe pre-eclampsia
stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks on labetalol 200 mg twice daily has a persistent frontal headache and one settled episode of blurred vision. Reflexes are brisk, with no clonus and no epigastric tenderness.

data_table.Investigations: Urine protein 3+, platelets 145 x10^9/L, normal liver and renal function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg with reassessment every 5 minutes
Increase labetalol to 400 mg three times daily and reassess in an hour
Betamethasone 11.4 mg and defer other intervention for 24 hours
Magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g hourly, with antihypertensive
Caesarean within 30 minutes without magnesium or blood pressure control

subtopic_detail: Obstetric cholestasis surveillance
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 34+4 weeks has 10 days of generalised itch, worse on the palms and soles at night, with no rash or jaundice. Her first pregnancy had cholestasis at 35 weeks and she was induced at 37 weeks.

data_table.Liver panel: ALT 118 U/L (5-40), GGT 92 U/L, bilirubin 12 micromol/L, fasting bile acids 62 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal pregnancy skin change and use emollients
Ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily with expectancy beyond 40 weeks
Oral vitamin K and chlorphenamine, repeating the bloods in 2 weeks
Category 1 caesarean today because bile acids exceed 40 micromol/L
Ursodeoxycholic acid, weekly bile acids and planned birth by 36 weeks

subtopic_detail: Placenta praevia bleed at 32 weeks
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 32+1 weeks with two previous caesareans has painless bright red bleeding that soaked a pad, with 250 mL further loss over 30 minutes. Scans at 20 and 28 weeks showed the placenta covering the internal os. She is group O RhD negative.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, presenting part high, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg, cross-match, anti-D 625 IU and prepare for caesarean
Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix and the bleeding source
Artificial rupture of the membranes to compress the placental edge
Discharge with antenatal clinic follow-up in 48 hours once bleeding slows
Tranexamic acid 1 g, deferring betamethasone until the bleeding settles

subtopic_detail: Breech delivery route counselling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal day unit. A 32-year-old primigravida at 36+5 weeks has a persistent frank breech presentation on ultrasound today after an unsuccessful external cephalic version 2 hours ago.

Estimated fetal weight is 3.2 kg with an amniotic fluid index of 12 cm and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. She has no cephalopelvic disproportion on examination and no hyperextension of the fetal neck. She has had no antepartum complications.

She asks about mode of birth. She has read that vaginal breech birth can be attempted at experienced units and wants an honest discussion. Her partner is supportive of either option. The senior obstetrician has agreed to be available.

data_table.Fetal parameters: Frank breech; EFW 3.2 kg; AFI 12 cm; UA Doppler within normal limits; no neck hyperextension
data_table.Maternal: 36+5 weeks; primigravida; no obstetric complications; adequate maternal pelvis on examination
data_table.Care: Senior obstetric team on call; woman wants an evidence-based discussion

lead_in: What information best reflects the evidence base to guide her decision?

options.text: Planned vaginal breech birth has equivalent or lower perinatal morbidity than caesarean section in selected primigravidae
Planned caesarean has a lower composite of perinatal mortality and serious morbidity than planned vaginal breech
Planned caesarean increases the risk of neonatal intracranial haemorrhage relative to a planned vaginal breech birth
A trial of vaginal breech is only reasonable if a second attempt at external cephalic version fails at 39 weeks under regional anaesthesia
Estimated fetal weight above 3 kg alone contraindicates any attempt at planned vaginal breech birth at term

subtopic_detail: Severe cyclical irritability with full remission after menstruation in a woman seeking treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who says that for about a week before each period she becomes so irritable and tearful that she has twice considered resigning from her job. She describes feeling entirely herself again within two days of her period starting.

She has had this pattern for three years and it has worsened since stopping the combined oral contraceptive pill eighteen months ago. Her cycles are regular at 29 days. She sleeps and functions normally in the fortnight after menstruation, denies any low mood or anxiety at those times, and has never had a period of persistent low mood lasting more than two weeks. She uses condoms, does not smoke, and her thyroid function and full blood count taken by a colleague last month were normal. She has kept no record of her symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask her to complete a daily symptom rating record across two consecutive menstrual cycles
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at low dose taken continuously and review in six weeks
Measure serum oestradiol and progesterone in the luteal phase to confirm a hormonal imbalance
Refer for consideration of a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy
Refer for psychological therapy addressing the workplace stressors that appear to precipitate symptoms

subtopic_detail: Inability to tolerate vaginal penetration with involuntary muscle guarding on attempted examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman who has never been able to have penetrative intercourse with her partner of two years. She says that whenever penetration is attempted her body tightens up and she feels she is being torn, and she has begun avoiding intimacy altogether.

She has never used tampons for the same reason. She describes her relationship as loving and reports no history of sexual assault or coercion. She has regular periods without pain and no vaginal discharge, itching or postcoital bleeding. On attempting examination she withdraws and her thighs adduct before you make contact with the introitus, and you are able to inspect the vulva only briefly. The visible vulval skin is normal with no fissuring, no pallor and no architectural change.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval skin with no fissures, pallor or architectural change, involuntary pelvic floor and thigh adductor contraction on approach to the introitus, internal examination not tolerated

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Prescription of vaginal oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks to improve introital tissue elasticity
Referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded desensitisation and pelvic floor down training
Prescription of topical lidocaine gel applied to the introitus for twenty minutes before intercourse
Examination under general anaesthesia to exclude an obstructing vaginal septum or other anomaly
Referral for botulinum toxin injection into the levator ani muscles under sedation as definitive therapy

subtopic_detail: Smooth cervical lesion found at screening in a woman reporting bleeding after intercourse
stem:
You are the general practice registrar performing a routine cervical screening test on a 41-year-old woman who mentions that she has bled a few times after intercourse over the past three months.

On speculum examination there is a smooth, bright red, pedunculated lesion about 12 mm long protruding from the cervical os on a narrow stalk. The surrounding ectocervix looks healthy with no ulceration, no friable irregular tissue and no induration on palpation. Her previous screening test two years ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Her periods are regular and she has no intermenstrual bleeding, no pelvic pain and no abnormal discharge. Her result returns today as negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated bright red cervical lesion 12 mm on a narrow stalk arising from the os, healthy surrounding ectocervix, no ulceration or induration, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not tender
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, previous test two years ago also negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to gynaecological oncology given that postcoital bleeding with a cervical lesion is present
Prescribe a course of doxycycline and metronidazole for presumed cervicitis and review in four weeks
Remove the lesion in clinic by twisting the stalk and send the tissue for histological examination
Reassure her that a negative screening test excludes significant pathology and repeat testing in five years
Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling before any attempt is made at removal

subtopic_detail: Device stem palpable at the external os on routine check after insertion
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman six weeks after insertion of a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device. She reports cramping and irregular bleeding since insertion and says her partner can feel something hard during intercourse.

She has been using no other method of contraception since insertion and had unprotected intercourse four days ago. Her last menstrual period began nine days ago. On speculum examination the threads are visible but the firm white stem of the device is protruding about 1 cm through the external os. The uterus is anteverted, normal in size and non-tender, with no cervical excitation and no adnexal tenderness. She is afebrile and there is no offensive discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Device stem visible protruding approximately 1 cm through the external os with threads present, uterus anteverted and non-tender, no cervical excitation, no adnexal mass or tenderness, no offensive discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange transvaginal ultrasound to confirm the device position before deciding on any intervention
Reassure her that irregular bleeding settles by six months and review the device position in three months
Take endocervical swabs and treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease before removing the device
Remove the device now, provide emergency contraception cover and arrange a replacement insertion
Reposition the device upwards into the uterine fundus using an instrument under direct vision

subtopic_detail: Couple asking when to stop other contraception after male surgical sterilisation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman and her 41-year-old partner for a joint appointment about contraception. He had a vasectomy eleven weeks ago and they want to know whether she can now have her hormonal implant removed.

He reports that the wound healed without incident and that he has ejaculated well over thirty times since the procedure. He has not yet provided any semen sample, saying the clinic gave him a form but he did not get around to it. They have three children and are certain their family is complete. She has tolerated the implant well and is keen to stop it as soon as it is safe to do so. Neither has any other medical history.

data_table.Examination: Well healed scrotal incisions, no haematoma, no tenderness, testes normal to palpation
data_table.Investigations: No post procedure semen analysis performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Advise that the implant can be removed now because more than twenty ejaculations have occurred
Advise that the implant can be removed once sixteen weeks have elapsed from the date of the procedure
Arrange scrotal ultrasound to confirm that the vas has been successfully divided on both sides
Remove the implant and advise condom use for a further three months as a precautionary measure
Continue the implant until a semen sample confirms clearance, and arrange that analysis now

subtopic_detail: Cyclical lower abdominal pain with absent menarche and normal secondary sexual development
stem:
You are the paediatric and adolescent gynaecology registrar seeing a 14-year-old girl brought by her mother because she has never had a period and has had monthly lower abdominal pain for six months.

The pain lasts three to four days each month and is now severe enough that she has missed school on several occasions. Her mother says her daughter has recently started complaining of difficulty passing urine on the worst days. Breast development began at eleven and both breast and pubic hair development are at the adult stage. She is on the 60th centile for height, has no headaches or visual symptoms, and has a normal sense of smell. Abdominal examination reveals a smooth suprapubic mass rising to just below the umbilicus, and she is not sexually active.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, height on the 60th centile, smooth non-tender suprapubic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus, external genitalia otherwise not yet inspected
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Inspect the external genitalia with the parent present and arrange pelvic ultrasound the same day
Measure follicle stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and oestradiol before performing any examination
Request a karyotype and serum testosterone to investigate a disorder of sexual development in this girl
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the cycle and relieve the monthly pain she describes
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis as the initial imaging test to define the anatomy

subtopic_detail: Vaginal bulge in an older woman with significant comorbidity declining an operation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 78-year-old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a lump she can feel at the vaginal entrance by the end of each day. It has been present for a year and now interferes with her gardening.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring home oxygen at night, and her cardiologist has documented an ejection fraction of 35 percent. She has been told she is a poor anaesthetic candidate and says clearly that she does not want an operation. On examination there is descent of the anterior vaginal wall to 1 cm beyond the hymen on straining, with a well oestrogenised appearance following six weeks of topical oestrogen prescribed by her general practitioner. She empties her bladder completely and has no incontinence, no bleeding and no ulceration of the vaginal skin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descent to 1 cm beyond the hymen on Valsalva, vaginal epithelium well oestrogenised, no ulceration, post-void residual volume 30 mL
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual 30 mL on bladder scan, urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Referral for colpocleisis as an obliterative procedure carrying lower operative risk than reconstruction
Fitting of a vaginal support pessary with a planned review to check fit and vaginal skin condition
Referral for anterior colporrhaphy under regional anaesthesia to minimise the perioperative risk involved
A supervised pelvic floor muscle training program alone as definitive management of the bulge symptom
Continuation of topical vaginal oestrogen alone with review of her symptoms again in six months' time

subtopic_detail: Rapidly progressive coarse hair growth with clitoral change in a woman in her thirties
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman with coarse dark hair on her chin, upper lip and lower abdomen. She says the change began about eight months ago and has accelerated, and that she now shaves daily when previously she needed nothing.

Her periods were regular every 28 days until six months ago and she has had none for the past three months. She has noticed her voice sounding deeper on recordings and that her hairline has receded at the temples. She takes no medications, no supplements and no androgenic preparations, and there is no family history of excess hair growth. Her body mass index is 23 kg per square metre and there are no violaceous striae, no proximal weakness and no facial rounding. On examination the clitoris measures 9 mm in transverse diameter.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coarse terminal hair on chin, upper lip and lower abdomen, temporal hairline recession, clitoral transverse diameter 9 mm, body mass index 23 kg per square metre, no striae or proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 340 mIU/L (less than 500)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for laser hair reduction and reassure her that this pattern is a common familial variation
Measure early morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone alone to investigate for non classical adrenal hyperplasia
Measure total testosterone with dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and arrange pelvic and adrenal imaging
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill with an antiandrogenic progestogen and review after six months
Arrange an overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the first investigation of the androgen excess

subtopic_detail: Three first trimester losses with a uterine cavity abnormality seen on two dimensional imaging
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman referred after three consecutive first trimester miscarriages, each at around nine weeks with fetal heart activity previously seen.

Her partner is the same for all three pregnancies and she has no living children. Her cycles are regular, she has never had pelvic infection or uterine instrumentation apart from one suction curettage, and her body mass index is 24 kg per square metre. Two dimensional transvaginal ultrasound reports a possible partition within the uterine cavity, and the sonographer notes that the external uterine contour could not be clearly assessed on that view. Antiphospholipid antibodies measured twelve weeks apart are negative, both parental karyotypes are normal, and her thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin are within the reference range.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulva, vagina and cervix, uterus anteverted and normal in size, no adnexal masses, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant negative, anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart, parental karyotypes normal, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.1 percent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Hysterosalpingography to outline the uterine cavity and to confirm that both fallopian tubes are patent
Endometrial biopsy with culture to investigate chronic endometritis as a contributor to the losses
Products of conception karyotyping arranged prospectively should a further pregnancy loss occur
Three dimensional transvaginal ultrasound to define the cavity outline together with the fundal contour
Diagnostic hysteroscopy under general anaesthesia to inspect and record the appearance of the cavity

subtopic_detail: Bone protection choice in a woman with ovarian failure well before the usual age
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman who stopped menstruating eighteen months ago and has had hot flushes and vaginal dryness since. Follicle stimulating hormone measured twice more than four weeks apart was elevated on both occasions with a low oestradiol.

Her bone density scan shows a lumbar spine Z score of minus 2.3. She has never had a fragility fracture, does not smoke, drinks minimal alcohol and walks daily. She has completed her family and uses condoms. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no history of venous thrombosis, and her blood pressure and lipids are normal. She has read online that hormone therapy causes breast cancer and asks whether she should take a bone medication instead.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 62 IU/L then 58 IU/L more than four weeks apart (follicular phase 3-10), oestradiol 42 pmol/L (follicular phase 90-400), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 74 nmol/L (greater than 50), lumbar spine Z score minus 2.3

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her bone health?

options.text: Weekly oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and repeat densitometry in two years
Six monthly subcutaneous denosumab with calcium and vitamin D and monitoring of bone turnover markers
Calcium and vitamin D supplementation with a resistance exercise program and repeat scanning in five years
A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress symptoms and to maintain bone density
Systemic oestrogen with a progestogen for endometrial protection, continued until the average age of menopause

subtopic_detail: Milky nipple discharge with a modestly raised hormone level in a woman on antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman referred with milky discharge from both nipples for four months and periods that have become infrequent, with the last one nine weeks ago.

She has schizophrenia treated with risperidone 4 mg daily for the past year with good symptom control, and takes no other medication. She has no headache, no visual field disturbance and no galactorrhoea on only one side. Her thyroid function is normal and a pregnancy test is negative. Her prolactin measured on a single unstressed morning sample is 2100 mIU/L. She tells you that her mental state has been the most stable it has ever been and that she is fearful of any change to her treatment.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, breasts otherwise normal with no mass, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features
