data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2100 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), urine pregnancy test negative, urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss a change of antipsychotic with her treating psychiatrist and review her prolactin afterwards
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa before making any change to her medication
Start cabergoline at low dose and titrate according to prolactin response with monthly measurements
Request macroprolactin measurement on the existing sample to identify a biologically inactive complex
Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore withdrawal bleeding and protect her bone density

subtopic_detail: Scant or absent menstruation with cyclical pain following instrumentation of the uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman whose periods have become barely a smear on a pad since she had a suction curettage for retained products of conception seven months ago, complicated by endometritis treated with antibiotics.

Before that pregnancy her periods were heavy and lasted five days. She now has cramping lower abdominal pain each month at the time she expects to bleed, but almost nothing appears. She has been trying to conceive for four months without success. A pregnancy test is negative, her follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol are consistent with normal ovarian function, prolactin and thyroid function are normal, and transvaginal ultrasound reports a thin irregular endometrial echo with some bright linear areas within the cavity.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulva, vagina and cervix, uterus anteverted and normal in size, mild suprapubic tenderness, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (follicular phase 3-10), oestradiol 310 pmol/L (follicular phase 90-400), prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), transvaginal ultrasound showing a thin irregular endometrial echo with bright linear intracavity areas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation given four months of trying to conceive without success
Refer for hysteroscopy with a view to adhesiolysis and a strategy to prevent adhesions reforming
Prescribe a three month course of cyclical oestrogen and progestogen and reassess her bleeding pattern
Arrange repeat pelvic ultrasound in the luteal phase to reassess the thickness of the endometrium
Commence a further course of doxycycline and metronidazole to treat persisting chronic endometritis

subtopic_detail: Diffusely enlarged tender uterus with heavy painful bleeding in a woman wanting to conceive
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman with periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful over four years, now soaking through protection hourly on the worst two days. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for eight months.

She describes deep pelvic pressure and pain that begins several days before bleeding starts and continues throughout. On bimanual examination the uterus is diffusely enlarged to about the size of a ten week pregnancy, globular, softer than expected and tender to palpation, with no separate palpable lump and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports asymmetrical myometrial thickening with the posterior wall measuring twice the anterior wall, small myometrial cysts and indistinct borders between the endometrium and the myometrium, and no discrete mass with a surrounding rim.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Globular tender uterus enlarged to approximately ten week size, no discrete mass, no rectovaginal nodularity, cervix normal, adnexae free
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200), transvaginal ultrasound showing asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts and an indistinct endometrial myometrial junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange endometrial ablation to destroy the endometrium and to reduce the volume of menstrual loss
Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months with add back hormone therapy
Treat the iron deficiency and offer a non hormonal option for bleeding and pain while she conceives
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device as the most effective treatment for her bleeding and pain
Refer for uterine artery embolisation to reduce the uterine volume and to control the heavy bleeding

subtopic_detail: Burning pain reproduced by light touch at the vestibule with normal vulval skin
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman with two years of burning pain at the vaginal entrance whenever anything touches it, including tampons, tight jeans and intercourse. She says the pain begins the instant there is contact and lasts for hours afterwards.

She has been treated with four courses of topical and oral antifungals over the past year, each prescribed for presumed thrush, without any benefit. She has no discharge, no itch and no odour. On examination the vulval skin is entirely normal with no erythema, no fissuring, no pallor, no loss of architecture and no lesions. Light contact with a cotton bud at the posterior vestibule reproduces her pain sharply and reproducibly, while the same touch on the labia majora and the inner thigh causes nothing. A high vaginal swab and culture taken last month were negative.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture and colour, no fissures, erosions or lesions, cotton bud testing sharply positive at the posterior vestibule and negative on labia majora and thigh, pelvic floor muscles tender and hypertonic on gentle digital assessment
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab with fungal culture negative, no other tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Perform a vulval punch biopsy of the vestibule to establish the histological diagnosis before treatment
Refer for vestibulectomy to excise the painful tissue as the definitive surgical treatment of her pain
Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment nightly for three months to settle vulval inflammation
Stop all antifungal treatment and refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy with psychosexual support alongside
Prescribe a six month course of weekly oral fluconazole for chronic recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis

subtopic_detail: Sudden severe unilateral pain in early pregnancy after ovarian stimulation with enlarged ovaries
stem: A 32-year-old woman at 6 weeks after embryo transfer woke 4 hours ago with sudden severe right-sided colicky pain and has vomited five times. Her ovaries were noted to be enlarged three days ago.

data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa guarding, distended abdomen, urine output 20 mL in 2 hours
data_table.Ultrasound: Viable intrauterine pregnancy; right ovary 82 mm with absent venous flow and preserved arterial flow; moderate ascites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid, analgesia and serial review, deferring surgery
Laparoscopy with right salpingo-oophorectomy, as a torted ovary is lost
Ultrasound guided paracentesis to relieve pressure and improve urine output
Urgent pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to confirm the diagnosis first
Resuscitate with intravenous fluid and laparoscopically detort the ovary

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dose for a sensitising event falling just beyond the twelve week threshold
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 13 weeks and 2 days. She reports fresh vaginal bleeding that soaked one pad over the past four hours, with no pain and no tissue passed.

Her booking bloods show blood group O RhD negative with a negative red cell antibody screen. A bedside ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity and a crown rump length consistent with dates, and no retroplacental clot. Her cervix is closed on speculum examination with a small amount of blood in the vault. She has had no previous pregnancy and has never received a blood transfusion.

data_table.Examination: Uterus non-tender, cervix closed, small volume fresh blood in the posterior fornix
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative, red cell antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), ultrasound showing a viable single intrauterine pregnancy at 13 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin now and rely on the routine prophylactic dose scheduled at twenty eight weeks
Give 250 international units of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within seventy two hours of the bleeding starting
Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin and repeat the red cell antibody screen in four weeks to look for sensitisation
Give 625 international units of anti-D immunoglobulin intramuscularly within seventy two hours of the bleeding starting
Perform a Kleihauer test first and give anti-D immunoglobulin only if a fetal bleed is quantified

subtopic_detail: Timing of glucose reassessment after insulin treated gestational diabetes once the baby is born
stem:
You are the obstetric resident doing a day two postnatal round on a 33-year-old woman who had a normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks and required isophane insulin at night from 31 weeks for fasting readings above target.

Her insulin was ceased after birth and her capillary glucose readings since delivery have all been between 4.4 and 6.1 mmol/L while eating normally. She is breastfeeding without difficulty and the baby's blood glucose screening was normal. She asks what happens next with her diabetes and whether she should stay on a monitor at home.

data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.4 to 6.1 mmol/L off insulin, booking body mass index 29 kg/m2, antenatal 75 g oral glucose tolerance test fasting 5.4 mmol/L and two hour 9.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for reassessing her glucose tolerance?

options.text: Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test before discharge from hospital, then ongoing testing every one to three years
Arrange a fasting venous glucose level at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
Continue home capillary glucose monitoring for six weeks and arrange further testing only if readings exceed target
Arrange a glycated haemoglobin level at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years
Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks after the birth, then ongoing testing every one to three years

subtopic_detail: Referral pathway when a self collected screening sample returns the higher risk oncogenic genotypes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing results for a 41-year-old woman who has never attended for cervical screening and who chose a self collected vaginal sample at her last visit. She has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain, and she has two children born vaginally.

Her sample returns positive for human papillomavirus type 16. The laboratory comment notes that liquid based cytology was not performed on this specimen. She is not pregnant, her last menstrual period was two weeks ago, and she has no immunosuppression and no history of a previous abnormal result.

data_table.Examination: Abdominal examination normal, no speculum examination performed at the screening visit
data_table.Investigations: Self collected vaginal sample positive for oncogenic human papillomavirus type 16, no cytology performed on the specimen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and refer for colposcopy if the same genotype persists
Refer her directly for colposcopy at this visit, without taking any further sample beforehand
Repeat the self collected sample now to confirm the genotype before making any referral for colposcopy
Take a clinician collected sample for cytology and refer for colposcopy only if it shows a high grade change
Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and rescreen in five years in line with the routine interval

subtopic_detail: Choice of latency antibiotic after membranes rupture in the early third trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 30 weeks and 1 day. She reports a sudden gush of clear fluid two hours ago followed by continuing dampness, and she has no contractions and no bleeding.

Speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix. Her temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius, the uterus is soft and non-tender, and cardiotocography shows a baseline of 145 beats per minute with normal variability and no decelerations. Her low vaginal swab from 28 weeks grew no group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy. The first dose of betamethasone has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Clear liquor pooling in the posterior fornix, cervix closed and uneffaced, uterus soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), low vaginal swab at 28 weeks negative for group B streptococcus

lead_in: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Oral erythromycin given for ten days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
Intravenous benzylpenicillin in labour only, with no antibiotic while she remains undelivered
No antibiotic now, with cultures repeated in forty eight hours and treatment if they are positive
Oral metronidazole given for seven days, with expectant management and daily surveillance
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for ten days, with expectant management and daily surveillance

subtopic_detail: Choosing emergency contraception at day five when body weight reduces oral efficacy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman who had unprotected intercourse five days ago, on day 11 of a regular 28 day cycle. She has taken no contraception for the past year and does not wish to be pregnant.

She weighs 96 kg with a body mass index of 34 kg/m2. She has no pelvic pain, no abnormal discharge and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, and a urine pregnancy test today is negative. She tells you she would like reliable ongoing contraception as well, and she is willing to consider any option including a procedure today.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus normal size and mobile
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, body mass index 34 kg/m2, last menstrual period eleven days ago

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine device today, with screening swabs taken at the same visit
Insertion of a copper intrauterine device today, with screening swabs taken at the same visit
A single oral dose of levonorgestrel today, with a contraceptive discussion at a follow up visit
No emergency contraception because five days have elapsed, with a pregnancy test arranged in three weeks
A single oral dose of ulipristal acetate today, with a contraceptive discussion at a follow up visit

subtopic_detail: Sudden urge with leakage on the way to the toilet and three voids a night in a woman of sixty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old retired teacher with twelve months of a sudden desperate need to pass urine, with leakage before she reaches the toilet about three times a week. She gets up three times a night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes, laughs or lifts her grandchildren, and she has no sensation of anything coming down. She had two vaginal births in her thirties. She drinks six cups of tea and two cans of diet cola a day and takes no diuretic. Her last period was eleven years ago and she uses no hormone therapy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, pale thin vaginal epithelium with loss of rugae, no descent of the anterior or posterior wall beyond the hymen on straining, no leak demonstrated on cough, voluntary pelvic floor contraction present but weak
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes, blood and glucose, post-void residual volume 30 mL on bladder scan, glycated haemoglobin 38 mmol/mol, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies before starting any treatment for these symptoms
Start oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and review her symptoms in three months
Refer for a midurethral sling procedure and review her six weeks afterwards
Start mirabegron 25 mg daily and review her symptoms in three months' time
Start bladder training with caffeine reduction and pelvic floor exercises

subtopic_detail: Coarse facial and chest hair developing gradually over two years with testosterone 3.2 at twenty four
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old retail manager who has been shaving her chin and upper lip daily for the past year and has noticed coarse dark hairs appearing between her breasts. The change has come on gradually over about two years.

Her periods come every forty to sixty days and have done so since she was sixteen. Her voice has not changed, she has no increase in muscle bulk and she has not noticed any change in her external genitalia or thinning at her temples. She is not trying to conceive, uses condoms, and has no personal or family history of migraine, thrombosis or breast cancer. She does not smoke.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, coarse terminal hair over the chin, upper lip, periareolar area and linea alba, no clitoromegaly, no temporal recession, no abdominal or pelvic mass, no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 3.2 nmol/L (0.3-1.8), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate within normal limits, early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits, prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), pelvic ultrasound shows multifollicular ovaries with normal volume and no adnexal mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for the hair growth?

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily and review her hair growth in six months
Start spironolactone 100 mg daily and review her hair growth in six months
Refer for computed tomography of the adrenal glands and pelvic ultrasound
Start a combined oral contraceptive and review the hair at six months
Start finasteride 5 mg daily and review her hair growth in six months' time

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic positive chlamydia nucleic acid test on routine antenatal screening at twelve weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at twelve weeks and two days. Her booking investigations included a self collected vaginal swab, which has returned positive for Chlamydia trachomatis on nucleic acid amplification testing.

She has no discharge, no pelvic pain, no bleeding and no urinary symptoms. Testing for gonorrhoea on the same swab was negative, and her syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B serology were all non-reactive. She has had one regular partner for eighteen months and reports no other partners in that time. She has no drug allergies and is taking only pregnancy multivitamins.

data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, abdomen non-tender, no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis B serology non-reactive, haemoglobin 122 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), midstream urine shows no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days with a test of cure in four weeks
Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose with a test of cure in four weeks
Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for seven days with no test of cure
Defer treatment until after delivery and repeat the swab in the third trimester
Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once with a test of cure in four weeks' time

subtopic_detail: Choosing the follow up test after mifepristone and misoprostol for an eight week intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27-year-old woman in her second pregnancy who has decided, after two discussions and a week to think about it, to end this pregnancy. She has one child and is clear and settled about her decision.

Her dating ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length corresponding to eight weeks and one day, with cardiac activity present. She has no abdominal pain and no bleeding. Her blood group is O negative with no preformed antibodies. She lives forty minutes from the regional hospital, has her own car, and a friend has agreed to stay with her overnight.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, uterus not palpable abdominally, no cervical excitation, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows a single intrauterine gestational sac with a crown rump length of 8 weeks 1 day and cardiac activity present, blood group O negative with negative antibody screen, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), chlamydia nucleic acid test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with anti-D immunoglobulin and a review in two weeks
Mifepristone then misoprostol, with a low sensitivity pregnancy test in two weeks
Misoprostol alone repeated as needed, with a serum hCG measurement in two weeks
Refer for surgical aspiration as her blood group makes medical treatment unsuitable
Mifepristone then misoprostol, with a routine pelvic ultrasound in two weeks' time

subtopic_detail: A globular tender uterus with myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone at forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old administrator with three children who describes three years of periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful. She passes clots the size of fifty cent pieces and changes a super tampon and a pad hourly on her two worst days.

The pain now begins two days before the bleeding starts and continues throughout, and she has deep pain with intercourse in the week before a period. Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. She has completed her family and does not want an operation if it can be avoided. On examination her uterus is uniformly enlarged to about ten weeks size, globular, mobile and tender, with no separate adnexal mass.

data_table.Examination: Uniformly enlarged globular uterus of about ten weeks size, mobile and tender on bimanual examination, no adnexal mass, no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas, cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globular uterus with asymmetrical anterior myometrial thickening, small myometrial cysts, an indistinct endometrial to myometrial junction and no discrete fibroid; endometrial thickness 6 mm; both ovaries normal; haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and review her bleeding in six months
Refer for total hysterectomy and review her in the clinic before the operation
Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist and review her in six months
Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system and review in six months
Start tranexamic acid during menses only and review her bleeding in six months

subtopic_detail: A lumbar spine T score of minus 2.6 in a woman whose periods stopped at the age of forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 47-year-old librarian whose periods stopped five years ago. Two follicle stimulating hormone measurements taken a month apart at the time were both in the postmenopausal range and a chromosomal and autoimmune screen found no cause.

She declined hormone therapy at the time because she did not like the idea of taking hormones, and she has taken nothing since. Her bone density scan has now been done and is reported below. She has never fractured a bone, does not smoke, drinks two standard drinks a week, and has about one serve of dairy food a day. Her coeliac serology, thyroid function, parathyroid hormone and calcium are all normal. She has no history of thrombosis, breast cancer, liver disease or migraine with aura.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 116/72 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, no kyphosis, height unchanged from her recorded height at age thirty, no proximal muscle weakness
data_table.Investigations: Bone mineral density T score minus 2.6 at the lumbar spine and minus 2.1 at the femoral neck, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 48 nmol/L (50-150), parathyroid hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for her bone density?

options.text: Start weekly alendronate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and exercise
Start denosumab six monthly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Start menopausal hormone therapy with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Start raloxifene daily with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
Advise weight bearing exercise and repeat her bone density in two years

subtopic_detail: Aftercare and future birth counselling on day one after theatre repair of a 3b anal sphincter injury
stem:
You are the obstetrics resident on the postnatal ward seeing a 29-year-old woman on the first day after the birth of her first baby. She had a forceps birth with a mediolateral episiotomy for a prolonged second stage, and the baby weighed 3.9 kg.

The consultant repaired a tear involving more than half the thickness of the external anal sphincter in theatre under regional anaesthesia. The urinary catheter has been removed and she is voiding normally with good volumes. She has no incontinence of flatus or faeces and her pain is controlled on regular paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory. She asks what happens now and whether she will have to have a caesarean next time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Perineal repair intact with mild bruising and no haematoma, no cellulitis or discharge, uterus well contracted at the umbilicus, lochia normal, voiding residual volume 40 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate postnatal plan?

options.text: Broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives, physiotherapy and review at three months
Broad spectrum antibiotics and laxatives, with review only if symptoms develop
Laxatives and physiotherapy, with a planned caesarean section for any next birth
Antibiotics and physiotherapy, with a constipating agent to protect the repair
Physiotherapy alone, with endoanal ultrasound and manometry before discharge

subtopic_detail: Fifteen hot flushes a day in a woman taking tamoxifen after receptor positive early breast cancer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 49-year-old graphic designer fourteen months into tamoxifen, prescribed after breast conserving surgery and radiotherapy for a grade 2 oestrogen receptor positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative early breast cancer.

She counts fifteen to twenty hot flushes a day and wakes four times most nights drenched. She is falling asleep at her desk, has taken three days off this month, and tells you she is close to stopping the tablets because she cannot go on like this for another four years. Her mood is not low and she is enjoying her work when she is rested. She is still having periods and takes no other medication. Her oncologist has written asking you to manage the symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Surgical scar well healed with no mass in either breast, no axillary lymphadenopathy, no chest wall nodules, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and liver function within normal limits, most recent mammogram and ultrasound reported as no evidence of recurrence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for her flushes?

options.text: Start transdermal oestradiol with micronised progesterone for symptom control
Start paroxetine 20 mg daily and review her flush frequency in four weeks
Stop the tamoxifen and switch to an aromatase inhibitor for the remaining years
Start a vaginal oestradiol pessary and review her flush frequency in four weeks
Start venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily and review her flush frequency in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Gestational ceiling for fetal neuroprotection when birth is expected within hours
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 31-year-old woman in her third pregnancy at 29 weeks and 4 days. She has been contracting every three minutes for two hours, her cervix is 6 cm dilated and the membranes are intact.

She received both doses of betamethasone eight days ago during an earlier admission for threatened preterm labour. The neonatal team has been called and the cot is confirmed. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, her reflexes are normal, her urine output has been 60 mL per hour, and her creatinine is within normal limits. Cardiotocography shows a normal trace. She has had no magnesium in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Cervix 6 cm dilated, membranes intact, vertex presenting at station minus 2, contractions every three minutes
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), patellar reflexes normal, urine output 60 mL per hour, cardiotocography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional treatment to start now?

options.text: A repeat course of intramuscular betamethasone as two doses given twenty four hours apart
Intravenous magnesium sulfate as a loading dose followed by an infusion until the birth
Intravenous magnesium sulfate withheld because the gestation has passed the threshold for neuroprotective benefit
Intravenous nifedipine tocolysis as a loading dose followed by maintenance until 34 weeks
Intravenous benzylpenicillin as a loading dose followed by four hourly doses until the birth

subtopic_detail: Duration of postnatal thromboprophylaxis after caesarean in a woman with a previous unprovoked clot
stem:
You are the obstetric resident writing discharge medications for a 36-year-old woman on day three after an emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. Her booking body mass index was 31 kg/m2.

She had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis in her left leg at the age of 28, treated with six months of anticoagulation, and she received prophylactic enoxaparin throughout this pregnancy. Thrombophilia screening after that event was negative. Her wound is clean, she is mobilising independently, her haemoglobin is 108 g/L and her platelet count is normal. She is breastfeeding and asks how long she needs to keep having injections.

data_table.Examination: Caesarean wound clean and dry, calves soft and non-tender, mobilising independently
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: How long should her postnatal thromboprophylaxis continue?

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin until discharge only, with graduated compression stockings continued at home
Six weeks of prophylactic enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
Six weeks of oral rivaroxaban from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
Six weeks of therapeutic dose enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
Ten days of prophylactic enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital

subtopic_detail: Operative plan when imaging suggests abnormal placental invasion over a previous scar
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternal fetal medicine clinic reviewing a 34-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal birth, and this pregnancy was conceived spontaneously.

Ultrasound reports an anterior placenta reaching the internal os, with multiple placental lacunae, loss of the clear zone between placenta and myometrium, and bridging vessels crossing into the bladder wall on colour Doppler. She has had two small painless antepartum bleeds that settled without intervention. She has no pain now, the fetal growth is on the 45th centile, and she has been counselled in detail about the range of intrapartum possibilities by the consultant.

data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, no vaginal bleeding today, fetus in cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound showing anterior placenta praevia with multiple lacunae, loss of the clear zone and bridging vessels to the bladder, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), fetal growth on the 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left in situ, the uterus closed and methotrexate given afterwards
Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with manual removal of the placenta and uterine artery embolisation if bleeding follows
Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left undisturbed and hysterectomy performed at the same operation
Magnetic resonance imaging now, with the mode and timing of birth deferred until that result is available
Planned caesarean at 39 weeks with the placenta left undisturbed and hysterectomy performed at the same operation

subtopic_detail: Delivery timing when serum bile acid concentration crosses the highest stillbirth risk band
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks and 3 days in her second pregnancy. For three weeks she has had intense itching of her palms and soles that keeps her awake, with no rash other than scratch marks.

Her total serum bile acids taken non fasting are 118 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase is 96 units/L, bilirubin is normal, and a liver ultrasound, hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen are all unremarkable. Fetal growth is on the 60th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers and a reassuring cardiotocograph. She has been taking ursodeoxycholic acid for two weeks with modest relief of itch. Her first pregnancy ended in a normal birth at term.

data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations on the forearms and shins, no primary rash, no jaundice, uterus soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 10), alanine aminotransferase 96 units/L (5-35), bilirubin 9 micromol/L (less than 20), viral hepatitis serology negative, autoimmune screen negative, umbilical artery Dopplers normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Increase the ursodeoxycholic acid dose and defer any decision about birth until the bile acids have been rechecked
Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after a course of corticosteroids, with continued inpatient fetal monitoring meanwhile
Repeat liver function tests and bile acids weekly and deliver only if alanine aminotransferase rises above 200 units/L
Deliver by caesarean section within twenty four hours because of the height of the bile acid concentration
Plan birth at 39 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography and growth scans every two weeks until then

subtopic_detail: Breathlessness three weeks after birth wrongly attributed to blood loss and deconditioning
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 38-year-old woman three weeks after the birth of twins by caesarean section. She describes six days of breathlessness climbing the stairs, waking at night needing to sit up, and ankle swelling that has not settled.

She lost 700 mL at operation and was told her blood count was low afterwards. Her haemoglobin today is 118 g/L, having been 104 g/L on day two. She has bilateral basal crackles, a raised jugular venous pressure and pitting oedema to mid shin, with calves that are soft and equal. Her chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and upper lobe venous diversion, and an electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic change. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout the pregnancy and today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure 6 cm above the sternal angle, bilateral basal crackles, pitting oedema to mid shin, calves soft and equal, caesarean wound healed
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), chest radiograph showing cardiomegaly and upper lobe venous diversion, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion with outpatient review, on the basis that her symptoms date from the operative blood loss
Oral amoxicillin with doxycycline and discharge, treating the findings as an atypical community-acquired pneumonia
Computed tomography pulmonary angiography with therapeutic enoxaparin started while awaiting the scan
Reassurance with graded exercise and a general practice review in two weeks, treating this as postnatal deconditioning
Urgent transthoracic echocardiography with intravenous furosemide and admission under a physician

subtopic_detail: A fourth culture confirmed episode of vulval itch and thick discharge within twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old physiotherapist with her fourth episode this year of intense vulval itch, burning on passing urine and thick white discharge. Each previous episode was confirmed on swab and settled within days of a single antifungal capsule, then returned six to eight weeks later.

She is not pregnant, has taken no antibiotics or corticosteroids, and has had the same partner for three years. Her glycated haemoglobin last month was 33 mmol/mol and a human immunodeficiency virus test six months ago was negative. Today's high vaginal swab has grown Candida albicans, reported as sensitive to fluconazole.

data_table.Examination: Erythema and oedema of the vulva with two shallow fissures in the interlabial folds, thick adherent white discharge, no ulceration, no lichenification, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab culture grew Candida albicans sensitive to fluconazole with no bacterial pathogen, vaginal pH 4.2, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid tests negative, glycated haemoglobin 33 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: A single fluconazole dose now and a further single dose at each recurrence
A single fluconazole dose now and the same treatment for her regular partner
Topical nystatin pessaries nightly for fourteen days and then as required
Oral nystatin to decolonise the bowel and a single fluconazole dose now
Induction fluconazole then weekly fluconazole for six months as maintenance

subtopic_detail: A dilated non-filling left tube on hysterosalpingogram in a couple accepted for in vitro fertilisation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 33-year-old woman and her partner after three years of trying to conceive with no pregnancy. She has never been pregnant.

Her cycles are regular at twenty nine days and a mid luteal progesterone confirms ovulation, her anti-Mullerian hormone is normal for her age, and her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions. She had a laparoscopic appendicectomy at nineteen and was treated for chlamydia at twenty two. Her hysterosalpingogram and a follow up ultrasound are reported below. The couple have been accepted for a funded cycle of in vitro fertilisation and would like to start with the next cycle.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, abdomen soft with a healed port site scar, uterus anteverted and mobile on bimanual examination, no adnexal tenderness, no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Hysterosalpingogram shows free fill and spill on the right, with the left tube dilated along its length and no spill of contrast; transvaginal ultrasound confirms a 3 cm fluid filled tubular left adnexal structure with incomplete septa; both ovaries normal with an antral follicle count of 14; mid luteal progesterone 38 nmol/L; chlamydia nucleic acid test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy before the first embryo transfer is performed
Proceed directly to embryo transfer and reassess the tube only if it fails
Aspirate the hydrosalpinx under ultrasound guidance at the time of oocyte collection
Prescribe doxycycline for fourteen days and repeat the imaging afterwards
Refer for laparoscopic tubal reconstructive surgery to restore its patency

subtopic_detail: A firm hyperkeratotic plaque persisting after three months of correctly applied ultrapotent corticosteroid
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64-year-old woman who has had vulval lichen sclerosus for five years, controlled on maintenance clobetasol propionate ointment with only occasional itch.

Four months ago she noticed a persistently sore spot on the left labium majus. You confirmed at the last visit that she applies the ointment daily to the affected area and she has used two 30 g tubes in three months, so quantity and technique are not the problem. The pale atrophic skin elsewhere on her vulva has improved over the same period and the itch has settled everywhere except this one area. She has had no bleeding and no discharge. Her cervical screening history is complete and negative and she has never smoked.

data_table.Examination: A 1.5 cm firm raised hyperkeratotic plaque with a central fissure on the left labium majus, unchanged since the last review, with surrounding pale atrophic skin and loss of the labia minora, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Swab of the fissure grew mixed skin flora with no Candida and no Staphylococcus aureus, glycated haemoglobin 36 mmol/mol, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the steroid to twice daily and review the area in eight weeks
Add a topical antifungal to the steroid and review the area in eight weeks
Start topical tacrolimus ointment and review the area in eight weeks' time
Take a punch biopsy of the plaque and review her with the histology report
Refer for laser vaporisation of the plaque and review her after treatment

subtopic_detail: An incidental 5 cm unilocular ovarian cyst with a normal tumour marker eight years after the last period
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman referred after a computed tomography scan performed for renal colic showed a right ovarian cyst. Her last menstrual period was eight years ago and she has had no bleeding since.

She has no abdominal pain, no bloating, no early satiety and no change in bowel or urinary habit, and her weight is stable. No relative has had ovarian, breast, bowel or endometrial cancer. A dedicated transvaginal ultrasound has now been performed and is reported below, and her tumour marker has been measured.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no palpable mass and no shifting dullness, no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, normal vulva and cervix on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a right ovarian cyst of 5.2 cm that is unilocular and anechoic with a thin smooth wall, no solid component, no papillary projections, no internal septations and no internal vascularity on Doppler; left ovary normal; no free fluid in the pelvis; CA125 18 kIU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for laparotomy and staging
Arrange laparoscopic oophorectomy at the local hospital within six weeks
Repeat the ultrasound and the tumour marker in four to six months' time
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any other decision
Discharge her with no further imaging as the tumour marker is normal

subtopic_detail: A request for permanent contraception from a woman of twenty six who has never been pregnant
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old electrician who asks to be referred for an operation to permanently prevent pregnancy. She has been with the same partner for four years, has never been pregnant, and says she has known since her teens that she does not want children.

She has taken the combined pill for eight years, forgets it two or three times a month and has troublesome breakthrough bleeding, and has twice used emergency contraception in the past year. She has seen two other general practitioners about this and was told each time that she would change her mind, which she found humiliating. She has no medical contraindication to any contraceptive method, her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke. Her partner supports whatever she decides.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, abdomen soft with no mass, no clinical evidence of anaemia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), urine pregnancy test negative, cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus twelve months ago

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer her directly for laparoscopic tubal occlusion without further discussion
Recommend a contraceptive implant or intrauterine device as the first option
Decline the request and advise her to return when she is over thirty five
Recommend that her partner have a vasectomy instead of any procedure for her
Recommend the progestogen only pill and review her bleeding in three months

subtopic_detail: Planning birth when unprotected fetal vessels are seen crossing the membranes below the presenting part
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her first pregnancy, conceived after in vitro fertilisation. Her morphology scan reported a bilobed placenta and a repeat transvaginal scan today has been arranged because of that finding.

The scan shows fetal vessels running through the membranes across the internal os, 1 cm below the presenting part, confirmed as fetal in origin on colour and pulsed wave Doppler. She has had no bleeding and no contractions, the membranes are intact, fetal growth is on the 55th centile and the cardiotocograph is normal. She lives forty minutes from the hospital and has been counselled about the range of birth options by the consultant.

data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, no vaginal bleeding, cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing fetal vessels crossing the internal os within the membranes, bilobed placenta, fetal growth on the 55th centile, cardiotocography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Admit from about 32 weeks, give corticosteroids, and perform emergency caesarean only if bleeding or labour occurs
Manage as an outpatient, give corticosteroids at 36 weeks, and plan caesarean section at 39 weeks before labour
Manage as an outpatient, plan induction of labour at 38 weeks, and perform amniotomy under direct vision in theatre
Admit from about 32 weeks, give corticosteroids, and plan caesarean section at 34 to 36 weeks before labour
Repeat the transvaginal scan at 36 weeks, and decide on the mode of birth only if the vessels still overlie the os

subtopic_detail: Sudden fetal bradycardia with rising station during trial of labour after a previous caesarean
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 40 weeks in a trial of labour after one caesarean has an epidural and an oxytocin infusion. Forty minutes ago she was 8 cm dilated at station 0. She now feels suddenly unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 92/54 mmHg, fetal heart rate 80 /min for 4 minutes
data_table.Examination: Presenting part risen to station minus 2, fresh bleeding, uterus soft between contractions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Stop the oxytocin, give a tocolytic and reassess over 10 minutes
Fetal scalp lactate sampling to establish whether there is acidosis
Attempt an instrumental birth in the room at 8 cm dilatation
Immediate laparotomy, with the neonatal team and haemorrhage protocol
Fluid bolus, left lateral position and repeat examination in 5 minutes

subtopic_detail: Discordant liquor volumes in a shared placenta twin pregnancy at the mid second trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a maternal fetal medicine clinic reviewing a 26-year-old woman at 20 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, confirmed by a single placental mass and a T sign at 11 weeks.

Today's scan shows the deepest vertical pocket in the first sac at 1 cm with the bladder not visible, and in the second sac at 9 cm with a distended bladder. The second twin has absent end diastolic flow in the umbilical artery and a normal ductus venosus a wave. Estimated weights are discordant by 18 percent. Both twins have normal anatomy and both have cardiac activity. Her cervix measures 34 mm and she has no contractions.

data_table.Examination: Uterus larger than dates, soft and non-tender, cervix closed on ultrasound at 34 mm
data_table.Investigations: Monochorionic diamniotic twins at 20 weeks, deepest vertical pocket 1 cm in twin one with bladder not visualised and 9 cm in twin two with distended bladder, absent end diastolic flow in twin two umbilical artery, estimated weight discordance 18 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange fortnightly growth scans with umbilical artery Dopplers and intervene if the discordance exceeds 25 percent
Perform serial amnioreduction from the polyhydramniotic sac and repeat the scan at weekly intervals
Administer maternal corticosteroids and plan delivery of both twins within the next forty eight hours
Perform selective reduction of the smaller twin by cord occlusion to protect the larger twin from injury
Refer for fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses at a specialist fetal therapy centre

subtopic_detail: Tense ascites and haemoconcentration in the luteal phase after an assisted reproduction cycle
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar admitting a 31-year-old woman nine days after oocyte retrieval and five days after a fresh embryo transfer. She has marked abdominal distension, breathlessness when lying flat, and has passed only 300 mL of urine in the past twelve hours.

Her pulse is 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Her abdomen is tensely distended with shifting dullness, and her calves are soft. Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries measuring 11 cm bilaterally with gross ascites, and no ovarian torsion on Doppler. Her haematocrit is 0.52, white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, sodium 129 mmol/L and albumin 26 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tensely distended abdomen with shifting dullness, reduced air entry at both bases, calves soft and equal
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.52 (0.36-0.46), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), ultrasound showing 11 cm ovaries with gross ascites and normal Doppler flow

lead_in: Which combination of measures is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous crystalloid, fluid restriction to one litre daily and hypertonic saline for the low sodium level
Intravenous crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin and laparoscopic ovarian cyst aspiration under general anaesthesia
Intravenous crystalloid, broad spectrum antibiotics and computed tomography of the abdomen for the raised white cell count
Intravenous furosemide, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis for the tense ascites
Intravenous crystalloid, prophylactic enoxaparin and ultrasound guided paracentesis for the tense ascites

subtopic_detail: Breakthrough convulsions in the second trimester when the plasma drug concentration has fallen
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 22 weeks with focal epilepsy has had two generalised convulsions in a fortnight after 3 years seizure free on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily. Every dose has been taken, confirmed by her dispensing history. She has no fever, headache or hypertension.

data_table.Investigations: Plasma lamotrigine 40 percent below the preconception value; sodium, calcium, glucose and full blood count normal
data_table.Fetal: Normal growth and morphology with a reassuring cardiotocograph

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by repeated concentrations
Admit for magnesium sulfate and expedite delivery for eclampsia
Switch her to levetiracetam over the coming weeks
Continue the dose and add intermittent clobazam for clusters
Reduce the dose to limit fetal exposure and avoid triggers

subtopic_detail: Counselling about mode of birth when anal sphincter symptoms persist after a previous severe tear
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth was a forceps delivery with a repaired tear extending through both parts of the anal sphincter.

Since then she has had urgency of the bowels most days and has lost control of wind and, on three occasions in the past year, of loose stool. Endoanal ultrasound shows a persistent defect across a quarter of the sphincter circumference and anorectal manometry shows reduced resting and squeeze pressures. She has had pelvic floor physiotherapy for six months with limited benefit. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile and the current estimated fetal weight is appropriate for gestation.

data_table.Examination: Perineal scar with a thinned perineal body, reduced voluntary anal squeeze on digital examination
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound showing a persistent defect over 25 percent of the sphincter circumference, anorectal manometry showing reduced resting and squeeze pressures, fetal growth on the 50th centile

lead_in: What would you first recommend about the mode of birth?

options.text: Elective caesarean section, booked at 39 weeks after discussion of the risks of abdominal birth
Vaginal birth with an elective mediolateral episiotomy, planned at 39 weeks after discussion of the risks
Vaginal birth avoiding instrumental delivery, planned at 39 weeks after discussion of the risks of each route
Secondary sphincter repair during this pregnancy, followed by vaginal birth planned at 39 weeks
Further pelvic floor physiotherapy with biofeedback, and a decision about the mode of birth deferred to 37 weeks

subtopic_detail: Severe period pain in a teenager with a normal pelvic ultrasound and school absence
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16-year-old girl brought by her mother because of period pain that has kept her home from school for two or three days every month for the past eighteen months. She describes cramping that starts a day before bleeding and continues for three days, and pain with opening her bowels during her period.

She has tried paracetamol and has not used a regular anti inflammatory. She is not sexually active. A transabdominal pelvic ultrasound arranged by another doctor was reported as normal with no endometrioma and no adenomyosis. Her periods are regular at 29 days, her haemoglobin and ferritin are normal, and her growth and development are normal. Her mother asks whether she needs an operation to find out what is wrong.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, mild suprapubic tenderness, no masses, no internal examination performed
data_table.Investigations: Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound normal, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), ferritin 46 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: A trial of regular non-steroidal anti inflammatory medication with continuous hormonal treatment, reviewed in three months
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to look for deep infiltrating disease before starting any treatment
Referral for diagnostic laparoscopy to establish the diagnosis histologically before any treatment is started
A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back therapy, arranged through a gynaecology clinic
Reassurance that this is primary dysmenorrhoea with paracetamol as needed and review if her symptoms worsen

subtopic_detail: Bleeding after the menopause in a woman taking an oestrogen receptor modulator for breast cancer
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 61-year-old woman who has had two episodes of vaginal bleeding in the past month. Her last menstrual period was nine years ago and she has taken tamoxifen for four years after surgery and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer.

Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 9 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and several small cystic spaces, and a normal ovarian appearance. She takes no other hormonal treatment, has never used menopausal hormone therapy, and her cervical screening has been up to date and negative. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she has no hypertension or diabetes.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulva and vagina, cervix appears healthy, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing endometrial thickness 9 mm with cystic change, normal ovaries, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155), cervical screening negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Blind endometrial sampling with a suction device in the clinic, accepting the result if it shows benign endometrium
Reassurance and repeat ultrasound in three months, as the thickness is above the 4 mm threshold used generally
Cease the tamoxifen and observe whether the bleeding settles over the following three months before investigating
Hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy, arranged regardless of the measured endometrial thickness
Reassurance and repeat ultrasound in three months, as the thickness is below the 10 mm threshold for this drug

subtopic_detail: Endometrial thickness threshold triggering tissue sampling in postmenopausal bleeding
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman who reports two episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past six weeks, each lasting a day. Her last menstrual period was seven years ago and she has never used menopausal hormone therapy.

Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and a small amount of old blood in the vault, and her cervical screening test from last year was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a regular endometrial echo measuring 9 mm with no focal lesion and normal ovaries.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, healthy cervix with no visible lesion, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows regular endometrial thickness 9 mm, no focal lesion, both ovaries normal, human papillomavirus screening negative last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her and arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in three months' time
Commence a trial of cyclical oral progestogen and review the bleeding pattern in three months
Repeat the cervical screening test with reflex cytology and review the result in a month
Arrange hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy under the care of a gynaecologist
Request serum CA125 and refer only if the result is above the laboratory reference range

subtopic_detail: Follow-up requirement for an incidental simple ovarian cyst found in a premenopausal woman
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 27-year-old woman who had an abdominal ultrasound last week for intermittent right-sided discomfort that has since settled completely. She has regular 29-day cycles, no intermenstrual bleeding and no change in bowel or bladder habit.

Her abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable mass, and a bimanual examination is unremarkable. She has no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. The ultrasound describes a 42 mm unilocular anechoic right ovarian cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid areas, no internal septations and no vascularity on Doppler, with a normal left ovary and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no palpable mass, bimanual examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Right ovary contains a 42 mm unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid component, no septation, no Doppler flow; left ovary normal; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecologist for consideration of laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy this year
Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the formation of further cysts
Arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to confirm that the cyst has resolved
Request serum CA125 and calculate a risk of malignancy index before deciding on referral
Reassure her that no further imaging or gynaecology referral is required at this stage

subtopic_detail: Oral iron dosing schedule for a low ferritin identified in the second trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. She feels well, with no bleeding and normal fetal movements, and reports mild tiredness that she attributes to chasing a toddler.

She is vegetarian and her first child was born 14 months ago. Her booking bloods at 11 weeks were normal. Repeat bloods this week show haemoglobin 106 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 79 fL (80-100) and ferritin 12 micrograms/L (15-200), with normal C-reactive protein and a normal white cell count and platelet count.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, fetal heart rate 148/min on Doppler, no pallor of the conjunctivae, no koilonychia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 79 fL (80-100), ferritin 12 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (<5), white cell count and platelet count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose given as a single infusion in the day procedure unit
Dietary advice on iron rich foods alone with repeat full blood count at 28 weeks gestation
Oral elemental iron taken on alternate days on an empty stomach with vitamin C
Oral elemental iron taken three times daily with meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Serum folate and vitamin B12 assay with treatment deferred until those results return

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding when the uterine cavity is structurally normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who describes flooding through a super tampon and a pad every hour on her two heaviest days, with clots the size of a twenty cent coin and two days off work each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days.

She has completed her family and would prefer not to become pregnant, though she is not seeking permanent contraception. Pelvic examination is normal with a normal sized mobile uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterus with an endometrium of 6 mm, no fibroid and no polyp. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L (115-155) with ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-200), and thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Normal sized mobile uterus, no adnexal mass, cervix healthy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows normal uterus, endometrium 6 mm, no fibroid or polyp; haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155); ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-200); thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: Which treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory therapy started on the first day of each period
Oral norethisterone taken from day five to day twenty six of each menstrual cycle
Referral for endometrial ablation after counselling about future pregnancy implications
Insertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system at her next convenient visit
Oral tranexamic acid taken during the heaviest days of each menstrual period only

subtopic_detail: Colposcopy pathway after human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 on a self collected screening sample
stem:
You are the general practitioner contacting a 41-year-old woman with her cervical screening result. She chose self collection because she had found previous speculum examinations distressing, and this was her first screening test in eleven years.

She has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain, and she is not pregnant. Her only previous screening results were normal cytology on two occasions in her twenties. The laboratory reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, type 16, with a note that reflex cytology could not be performed on the self collected specimen.

data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test on a self collected vaginal sample: oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, type 16; reflex liquid based cytology not performed on this specimen type

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months to see whether the infection clears
Refer directly for colposcopy without arranging any further sampling beforehand
Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and repeat screening in twelve months' time
Repeat the self collected sample now to confirm the result before making any referral
Arrange a clinician collected sample for liquid based cytology and refer if it is abnormal

subtopic_detail: Where to operate on a complex adnexal mass with a high risk of malignancy index after menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar assessing a 64-year-old woman referred with four months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. She went through menopause at 51 and has never used hormone therapy.

Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and a firm irregular mass palpable in the right iliac fossa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 92 mm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections and marked internal vascularity, together with moderate ascites. Serum CA125 is 640 kU/L (<35). A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows omental thickening but no parenchymal liver or lung lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, firm irregular right iliac fossa mass, no palpable supraclavicular nodes
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 92 mm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections and marked vascularity, moderate ascites; CA125 640 kU/L (<35); computed tomography shows omental thickening without liver or lung metastases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to further characterise the adnexal mass
Arrange therapeutic paracentesis with cytology and review her again once the result returns
Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for multidisciplinary assessment and surgery
Repeat the CA125 in six weeks and refer if the value has risen above the current level
Arrange laparoscopic oophorectomy on the local gynaecology list within the next two weeks

subtopic_detail: Reading a raised CA125 against a suspected endometrioma before menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with a raised tumour marker and a request for urgent oncology assessment. She has had severe period pain since her teens, deep pain with intercourse and pain on opening her bowels during menstruation.

She has been trying to conceive for 18 months. Her appetite and weight are stable and there is no bloating or early satiety. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 46 mm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level internal echoes, no solid papillary projection and no internal vascularity, with the ovary tethered to the uterus on probe pressure. Serum CA125 is 118 kU/L (<35).

data_table.Examination: Tender nodularity palpable in the posterior fornix, fixed retroverted uterus, right adnexal tenderness, no ascites, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 46 mm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level internal echoes, no solid component, no internal vascularity, reduced ovarian mobility; CA125 118 kU/L (<35); full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: The finding requires tissue; arrange ultrasound guided cyst aspiration with fluid cytology
The marker is raised by benign disease; plan fertility focused gynaecology management
The marker is non-diagnostic; arrange serial measurement every six weeks for six months
The marker indicates likely malignancy; refer urgently to a gynaecological oncology centre
The finding needs suppression; start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months

subtopic_detail: Tumour based mismatch repair testing after endometrial carcinoma diagnosed before age fifty
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 46-year-old woman two weeks after a total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, reported as grade 1 with less than half myometrial invasion and no lymphovascular space invasion.

She is recovering well with no complications. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2, she has had three pregnancies and she has never had diabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome. Her father had bowel cancer at 52 and a paternal aunt had a uterine cancer in her forties. She asks whether her two daughters need to do anything.

data_table.Examination: Abdominal wounds healing well, no collection, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Histology: grade 1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma, myometrial invasion less than 50%, no lymphovascular space invasion, margins clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the family history is on the paternal side and carries no risk to daughters
Request mismatch repair immunohistochemistry on the hysterectomy tumour specimen
Request germline gene panel testing on a blood sample from her before any tumour testing
Arrange adjuvant vaginal vault brachytherapy and defer any genetic discussion until after it
Arrange colonoscopy for her and for both daughters within the next twelve month period

subtopic_detail: Switching from oral to intravenous iron in the third trimester after gastrointestinal intolerance
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal clinic reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She was started on oral iron at 22 weeks but stopped after ten days because of severe constipation and epigastric pain, and a second preparation caused the same problem.

She reports increasing breathlessness climbing stairs and has a placenta that was reported as low lying at her morphology scan, with a repeat scan booked for 34 weeks. Her bloods today show haemoglobin 86 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100) and ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-200), with normal C-reactive protein, normal B12 and folate, and a normal haemoglobin electrophoresis performed at booking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 C, fetal heart rate 145/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, cephalic presentation, pale conjunctivae, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 86 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), B12 and folate within normal limits, haemoglobin electrophoresis normal at booking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Recombinant human erythropoietin given subcutaneously with oral iron supplementation
A third oral iron preparation taken with food to improve gastrointestinal tolerability
Transfusion of two units of packed red cells arranged as an elective admission this week
Repeat the full blood count and ferritin in four weeks before committing to any treatment
Intravenous iron infusion arranged in the day unit within the coming week

subtopic_detail: Operative approach to a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity in a woman wanting pregnancy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 36-year-old woman with two years of progressively heavier periods and two early miscarriages. She has been trying to conceive for a third pregnancy for the past year.

She has already completed a six month trial of tranexamic acid with only partial benefit and declines hormonal treatment because she wants to conceive. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 26 mm fibroid that appeared to indent the cavity, and a subsequent saline infusion sonohysterogram confirms a submucosal fibroid with more than half of its volume within the cavity and a normal outer myometrial margin. Her haemoglobin is 104 g/L (115-155).

data_table.Examination: Bulky uterus approximately 8 week size, mobile and non-tender, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Saline infusion sonohysterogram: 26 mm submucosal fibroid with more than 50% intracavitary component, remainder of cavity normal; haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 11 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Hysteroscopic resection of the fibroid performed transcervically under general anaesthesia
Gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist therapy for six months to shrink the fibroid
Laparoscopic myomectomy with layered closure of the resulting myometrial defect
Endometrial ablation with a second generation device following endometrial preparation
Uterine artery embolisation performed by interventional radiology as a day case procedure

subtopic_detail: Adnexal torsion where preserved Doppler arterial flow argues against the diagnosis
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a 24-year-old woman with eight hours of severe right iliac fossa pain that began abruptly while she was at the gym, with three episodes of vomiting. The pain has waxed and waned in intensity but has never fully settled.

Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago and a urinary pregnancy test is negative. She had a 6 cm right ovarian dermoid documented on a scan two years ago that she elected to leave alone. On examination she is tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an enlarged oedematous right ovary measuring 78 mm containing the known dermoid, with a small volume of free fluid, and the report notes that arterial and venous Doppler flow are both demonstrable within the ovary.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rebound, cervix closed with no bleeding, right adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, white cell count 13.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (<5), transvaginal ultrasound shows 78 mm oedematous right ovary containing a dermoid, free fluid present, arterial and venous Doppler flow both demonstrable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with analgesia and repeat the Doppler ultrasound in twelve hours
Request computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to exclude appendicitis first
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before operating
Proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy with a view to untwisting and conserving the ovary
Commence intravenous antibiotics for presumed pelvic inflammatory disease and review tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Assessing bleeding on tamoxifen where the usual endometrial thickness cut-off is not applicable
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman with a single episode of vaginal spotting last week. She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer three years ago and takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily, which she is due to continue for a further two years.

She went through menopause at 50 and has no other bleeding, no discharge and no pain. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion. Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 11 mm with a cystic heterogeneous appearance and poorly defined margins, and the sonographer comments that the endometrial-myometrial interface is difficult to resolve. The ovaries are normal and there is no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not palpable, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
