data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 11 mm, cystic heterogeneous appearance, indistinct endometrial-myometrial interface, ovaries normal, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Contact her oncologist to switch tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor and rescan afterwards
Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy irrespective of the measured endometrial thickness
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to assess for myometrial invasion first
Reassure her that the appearance is a recognised drug effect and repeat the scan in six months
Arrange outpatient pipelle endometrial sampling and manage according to the histology

subtopic_detail: Booking microcytosis with replete iron stores requiring haemoglobinopathy evaluation of the couple
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing booking bloods for a 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. She feels well apart from mild nausea and has no bleeding.

She was born in Australia and her parents came from southern Italy. She was told as a teenager that she was anaemic and took iron tablets for a year without any change in her blood count. Today her haemoglobin is 103 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 64 fL (80-100), mean cell haemoglobin 20 pg (27-33) and red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), with ferritin 96 micrograms/L (15-200), normal C-reactive protein and normal B12 and folate. Her partner was born in Cyprus and has not been tested.

data_table.Examination: No pallor, no jaundice, no splenomegaly, uterus not palpable abdominally
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 103 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 64 fL (80-100), mean cell haemoglobin 20 pg (27-33), red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (<5), B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis for her alone and test the partner only if hers is abnormal
Request haemoglobin electrophoresis for her and arrange testing of her partner now
Request a blood film and reticulocyte count and defer further testing to the 28 week visit
Request non-invasive prenatal testing on maternal blood to assess the fetus for this condition
Commence oral iron replacement and repeat the full blood count in four weeks to assess response

subtopic_detail: Treatment regimen for trichomoniasis diagnosed in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in an antenatal clinic. A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her second pregnancy describes 3 weeks of a frothy yellow-green discharge with vulval itch and soreness during sex. She has a single regular partner of 4 years.

She has taken no antibiotics recently and has not douched. She is not diabetic and her oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks is not yet due.

On speculum examination there is an adherent frothy discharge with punctate haemorrhages visible across the ectocervix, and the vaginal pH measures 5.5. A vaginal nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Trichomonas vaginalis and negative for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Her syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology from booking were both negative.

data_table.Examination: Adherent frothy vaginal discharge, punctate haemorrhages across the ectocervix, vaginal pH 5.5
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal nucleic acid amplification test positive for Trichomonas vaginalis, negative for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae; booking syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Tinidazole 2 g orally as a single dose for her, with the same dose given to her partner
Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal pessary at night for 6 nights, with no treatment for her partner
Metronidazole 400 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, with the same course given to her partner
Metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose for her, with the same dose given to her partner
Defer all antimicrobial therapy until after the birth, with a test of cure at 6 weeks postnatally

subtopic_detail: Suppressive regimen for culture confirmed recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends your general practice frustrated by a fifth episode of vulval itch and a thick white discharge in the past 12 months. Each episode has settled with an over-the-counter antifungal cream and then returned within 6 to 8 weeks.

She uses condoms for contraception, has had the same partner for 6 years and has taken no antibiotics in the past year. She uses a plain soap-free wash and no vaginal products.

Her glycated haemoglobin is 5.2 per cent (below 6.0) and her human immunodeficiency virus serology is negative. A high vaginal swab taken during the current episode has grown Candida albicans on culture, with speciation confirmed and no resistance reported. On examination there is vulval erythema with fissuring in the natal cleft and a thick adherent white discharge. A pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema with fissuring, thick adherent white vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab culture positive for Candida albicans with no resistance reported, glycated haemoglobin 5.2% (below 6.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluconazole 150 mg orally on days 1, 4 and 7, then 150 mg weekly for 6 months
Fluconazole 150 mg orally as a single dose to be repeated with each further episode
Boric acid 600 mg vaginal pessary at night for 14 nights, then review her symptoms
Nystatin vaginal pessary at night for 14 nights, then review her symptoms in 4 weeks
Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal pessary at night for 6 nights, repeated in the week before each period

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a first presentation Bartholin abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar on call. A 32-year-old woman presents with 4 days of increasing pain and swelling at the entrance to the vagina, now severe enough that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably.

She has never had a similar problem before. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, and has had no fever or rigors at home. Her last cervical screening test was 18 months ago and was negative for human papillomavirus.

On examination there is a tense, fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the posterior aspect of the introitus on the right, with overlying erythema but no spreading cellulitis into the labium or thigh. The swelling is exquisitely tender. There is no induration extending towards the ischiorectal fossa and no crepitus. Swabs have been taken for gonorrhoea and chlamydia nucleic acid amplification testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the right posterior introitus, overlying erythema without spreading cellulitis, no induration towards the ischiorectal fossa, no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Nucleic acid amplification swabs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral di-flucloxacillin with sitz baths and clinical review in 48 hours if no improvement
Simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic with a loose dressing and no catheter
Excision of the entire Bartholin gland under general anaesthetic on the next available list
Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter under local anaesthetic today
Marsupialisation of the abscess cavity under general anaesthetic on the next available list

subtopic_detail: Penicillin regimen for syphilis seroconversion detected on third trimester screening
stem:
You are the registrar in a regional antenatal clinic. A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy is recalled after her routine third trimester screening bloods.

Her booking serology at 10 weeks was negative for syphilis. The current sample is reactive on treponemal enzyme immunoassay, reactive on Treponema pallidum particle agglutination, and shows a rapid plasma reagin titre of 1:32.

She feels well and has no rash, no genital ulceration and no lymphadenopathy. She has had one new sexual partner in the past 5 months. She has never been treated for syphilis and has no allergies to any medication, including penicillin. Her human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology are negative and a detailed ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with normal growth and liquor volume.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no genital ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, symphysis-fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Treponemal enzyme immunoassay reactive, Treponema pallidum particle agglutination reactive, rapid plasma reagin 1:32; booking syphilis serology at 10 weeks negative; human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound today shows normal fetal anatomy, growth and liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose, with a repeat rapid plasma reagin titre in 4 weeks
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly, with a second identical dose one week later
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly as a single dose, with no further injections
Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly weekly for three doses over three weeks
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days, with a repeat rapid plasma reagin at delivery

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacotherapy after a minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 62-year-old woman attends your general practice to discuss her bone density result. Six months ago she tripped on a garden step and fractured her left distal radius, which was managed in a cast.

Her last menstrual period was at 51. She has no vasomotor symptoms now and does not want to take hormone therapy. She has never smoked, drinks two standard drinks a week, and walks 30 minutes most days. She takes no corticosteroids and has no family history of hip fracture.

Bone densitometry reports a femoral neck T-score of -2.6 and a lumbar spine T-score of -2.2. Her corrected calcium is 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 78 nmol/L (above 50), thyroid stimulating hormone is 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 90 mL/min/1.73m2 and coeliac serology is negative. She has no reflux symptoms and can sit upright after medication.

data_table.Investigations: Femoral neck T-score -2.6, lumbar spine T-score -2.2, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (above 50), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, coeliac serology negative
data_table.History: Minimal trauma distal radius fracture 6 months ago, menopause at 51, no corticosteroid use, no reflux symptoms

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
Calcium 1000 mg and colecalciferol 1000 IU daily alone, with repeat densitometry in 2 years
Menopausal hormone therapy with transdermal oestradiol and micronised progesterone daily
Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
Alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed

subtopic_detail: Uterus conserving treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding with a thickened junctional zone
stem:
A 42-year-old woman attends your gynaecology clinic with 2 years of progressively heavier periods. She now changes a super tampon hourly on her worst two days, passes clots the size of a fifty cent coin, and has taken sick leave twice this year.

Her period pain has become worse over the same period and now starts 2 days before bleeding. She has two children and does not want further pregnancies, but she is clear that she does not want a hysterectomy.

On examination the uterus is bulky, about 10 weeks in size, symmetrically enlarged and tender on bimanual palpation. Saline infusion sonohysterography shows a smooth cavity with no submucosal fibroid and an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging reports a junctional zone thickness of 14 mm. An endometrial pipelle biopsy shows benign proliferative endometrium. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115-155) and ferritin is 9 micrograms/L (30-200). Her cervical screening test is up to date and negative.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrically bulky tender uterus, approximately 10 weeks in size
data_table.Imaging: Saline infusion sonohysterography shows a smooth cavity with no submucosal fibroid, endometrial thickness 6 mm; magnetic resonance imaging junctional zone thickness 14 mm
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-200), endometrial pipelle biopsy benign proliferative endometrium

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation by the interventional radiology service
Prescribe tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily for the heaviest days of each period
Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system at the next available appointment
Refer for endometrial ablation on the next available operating theatre list
Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with tibolone add-back therapy

subtopic_detail: Investigating increased liquor volume when the glucose tolerance test and antibody screen are normal
stem: A 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is referred at 32 weeks with a symphysis-fundal height of 38 cm and an uncomfortably stretched abdomen. She has had no fever, rash or contact with unwell children.

data_table.Imaging: Deepest pocket 9.5 cm, amniotic fluid index 28 cm, estimated weight 55th centile, no hydrops; fetal stomach not seen on three attempts
data_table.Investigations: Glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks normal; antibody screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Tertiary fetal morphology ultrasound directed at swallowing and the upper gut
Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test now rather than imaging
Maternal serology for cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis and parvovirus
Admit for amnioreduction to relieve her abdominal discomfort now
Two weekly growth scans with cardiotocography, review at 36 weeks

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth for isolated reduced liquor volume with normal growth and Dopplers
stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks was scanned for a small symphysis-fundal height. She reports normal movements and denies any fluid loss. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg with no proteinuria.

data_table.Imaging: Deepest vertical pocket 1.6 cm, estimated fetal weight 40th centile tracking from 28 weeks, normal umbilical and middle cerebral artery Dopplers
data_table.Investigations: Speculum shows no pooling, amniotic fluid test negative, cardiotocograph reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Caesarean section today because of the reduced liquor volume
Increase oral fluid intake and reassess the liquor in 4 weeks
Give corticosteroids now and deliver in 48 hours when complete
Twice weekly fetal surveillance with planned birth at 36 to 37 weeks
Expectant care to 40 weeks with weekly cardiotocography

subtopic_detail: Immediate advice on an established antiepileptic drug at first presentation in early pregnancy
stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends your general practice having done a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks and 3 days ago and the pregnancy was not planned.

She has generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy and has been free of seizures for 4 years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily. Lamotrigine was stopped 6 years ago after a widespread rash requiring admission, and levetiracetam was stopped 5 years ago because of severe irritability and mood disturbance that resolved on withdrawal.

She has read about the risks of her medication overnight and has brought a printout. She is still taking the valproate and asks whether she should stop it today. She drives to work and cares for a 3-year-old niece two days a week. She takes no other medications and has not been taking folic acid.

data_table.History: Generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy, seizure free 4 years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily, previous severe rash on lamotrigine and severe mood disturbance on levetiracetam
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no focal deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate advice?

options.text: Halve the valproate dose today and arrange review at the joint clinic within 4 weeks
Continue the valproate unchanged and arrange joint obstetric and neurology review this week
Stop the valproate today, start folic acid 5 mg daily and review her again in 2 weeks
Switch her to levetiracetam today at an equivalent dose and review her again in 2 weeks
Stop the valproate today and review the situation at her 12-week nuchal translucency scan

subtopic_detail: Selecting heart failure therapy in the early postpartum period while breastfeeding is continuing
stem: A 33-year-old woman on day 5 after a normal vaginal birth is readmitted with orthopnoea and waking gasping at night. She had no hypertension in pregnancy and computed tomography excluded pulmonary embolism. She is breastfeeding and keen to continue.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min, BP 104/68 mmHg, SpO2 94% on room air
data_table.Echocardiography: Dilated left ventricle, ejection fraction 32 percent, no valve lesion
data_table.Investigations: NT-proBNP 4100 ng/L (below 125), creatinine 74 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her furosemide?

options.text: Digoxin, deferring other agents until an echocardiogram in 6 weeks
Candesartan with spironolactone, switching her baby to formula
Sacubitril with valsartan and cabergoline to suppress lactation
Enalapril with metoprolol, supporting her to keep breastfeeding
A higher dose of furosemide alone while she is breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: First trimester anticoagulation choice for a mechanical mitral valve on a low warfarin dose
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar in a joint cardiac obstetric clinic. A 31-year-old woman attends at 6 weeks in an unplanned first pregnancy.

She had rheumatic fever as a child in the Pacific and underwent mitral valve replacement with a bileaflet mechanical prosthesis 7 years ago. She takes warfarin 3 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0 and has had no thromboembolic or bleeding events since surgery.

Her international normalised ratio today is 2.9 and her renal and liver function are normal. Echocardiography 3 months ago showed a normally functioning prosthesis with no regurgitation and normal ventricular function. She is in sinus rhythm. She is very anxious about the reports she has read about warfarin and asks whether she should be changed to injections for the rest of the pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Mechanical first heart sound, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.9 on warfarin 3 mg daily, renal and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiogram 3 months ago with normally functioning bileaflet mitral prosthesis and normal ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Stop warfarin and use aspirin 100 mg daily until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
Stop warfarin and use rivaroxaban 20 mg daily until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
Continue warfarin at her current dose with weekly international normalised ratio monitoring
Stop warfarin and use therapeutic enoxaparin twice daily until 12 weeks, then resume warfarin
Admit her for an unfractionated heparin infusion until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a negative oestrogen and progestogen challenge in secondary amenorrhoea after uterine instrumentation
stem: A 31-year-old woman has had no periods for 11 months and cannot conceive. She had an evacuation of retained products 14 months ago, repeated a week later, and stopped breastfeeding 10 months ago.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 5.2 IU/L, LH 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol 340 pmol/L, prolactin and TSH normal
data_table.Challenge testing: No bleed after medroxyprogesterone, nor after a subsequent oestrogen and progestogen cycle
data_table.Imaging: Thin irregular endometrial line with bright echoes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy with a view to adhesiolysis under direct vision
Anti-Mullerian hormone with a repeat follicle stimulating hormone in 6 weeks
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa to exclude a lesion
A combined oral contraceptive pill to re-establish a withdrawal bleed
A 17-hydroxyprogesterone level and free androgen index for androgen excess

subtopic_detail: Surveillance plan after velamentous cord insertion is reported at the morphology scan
stem:
You are the resident in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 29-year-old woman attends at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy to discuss her morphology scan.

The pregnancy was conceived spontaneously and has been uncomplicated. She takes pregnancy multivitamins and has no medical history. She has no bleeding, no pain and reports normal fetal movements for gestation.

The scan report describes a single fetus with growth on the 45th centile and normal anatomy. The placenta is posterior and its lower edge is 55 mm from the internal os. The umbilical cord is reported to insert into the membranes 40 mm from the placental edge, with vessels running through the membranes toward the placental disc. Colour Doppler over the internal os shows no vessels crossing it. Her blood pressure is 108/66 mmHg and urinalysis is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan at 20 weeks: single fetus, growth 45th centile, normal anatomy, posterior placenta with lower edge 55 mm from internal os, cord inserting into membranes 40 mm from placental edge, no vessels crossing the internal os on colour Doppler. Urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Arrange planned caesarean section at 35 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, with inpatient admission from 32 weeks
Arrange repeat placental localisation at 32 weeks with continued routine antenatal care and no growth scans
Arrange amniocentesis for fetal karyotype and microarray, with continued routine antenatal care thereafter
Arrange serial growth ultrasound scans from the early third trimester with continued routine antenatal care
Arrange low dose aspirin from today with continued routine antenatal care and no additional growth scans

subtopic_detail: Management of nocturnal hand paraesthesia developing in the third trimester
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks has 3 weeks of tingling and numbness in both hands that wakes her at night and eases when she shakes them. Her grip feels clumsy at work. Her fingers and ankles swell in the evenings.

data_table.Examination: Sensory blunting over the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers bilaterally; percussion over the flexor retinaculum reproduces tingling; power preserved
data_table.Investigations: No proteinuria; haemoglobin, thyroid function and platelets normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical decompression of the flexor retinaculum
Arrange a local corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
Commence oral furosemide to reduce the peripheral oedema
Arrange nerve conduction studies of both upper limbs
Provide neutral position wrist splints for night-time use

subtopic_detail: Timing of glucose tolerance testing when booking body mass index is in the obese range
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 11 weeks in her second pregnancy is 1.62 m and 98 kg. Her first baby weighed 4350 g at term and she was not tested for gestational diabetes. Her mother has type 2 diabetes.

data_table.Investigations: Body mass index 37.3 kg/m2, random glucose 5.8 mmol/L, glycated haemoglobin 39 mmol/mol (<42), no glycosuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for glucose testing?

options.text: An early glucose tolerance test now, repeated at 24 to 28 weeks
A glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks only, nothing earlier
Rely on the glycated haemoglobin now, repeating it at 24 to 28 weeks
Home fasting capillary glucose now, with a tolerance test at 28 weeks
An early glucose tolerance test now, with no repeat if it is normal

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with cyclical pelvic pain, no menses and normal secondary sexual characteristics
stem: A 14-year-old girl has never had a period and for 8 months has had lower abdominal pain for about 4 days each month. She has recently been getting up twice a night to pass small volumes of urine.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair; non-tender suprapubic mass 4 cm above the symphysis; bluish bulging membrane at the introitus
data_table.Investigations: FSH, LH and prolactin normal; pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a karyotype and serum testosterone before any intervention
Refer to a gynaecological surgeon for incision of the obstruction
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review in 3 months
Reassure that menarche can be delayed and review in 12 months
Request pelvic magnetic resonance imaging before deciding

subtopic_detail: Choosing incision angle and site when performing an episiotomy at operative vaginal birth
stem:
You are the registrar conducting an assisted vaginal birth. A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is at full dilatation at 40 weeks with the vertex at station plus 2 in the direct occipito-anterior position.

She has been pushing for 2 hours and the cardiotocograph now shows recurrent late decelerations with a baseline of 150 beats per minute and reduced variability. The consultant has confirmed that a low forceps birth is appropriate and the theatre team has been notified. She has an effective epidural in situ and has consented to an assisted birth with perineal incision if required.

The perineum is short and the head is distending it with each contraction. You decide to perform an episiotomy at crowning.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 150/min
data_table.Examination: Full dilatation, vertex station plus 2, direct occipito-anterior, short perineum distending with contractions, effective epidural in situ
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph: baseline 150/min with reduced variability and recurrent late decelerations

lead_in: Which incision technique is most appropriate?

options.text: Midline incision beginning at the posterior fourchette directed vertically toward the anus at crowning
Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 25 degrees from the midline at crowning
Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline at crowning
Mediolateral incision beginning at the posterior fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline before traction
Lateral incision beginning 2 cm lateral to the fourchette angled 60 degrees from the midline at crowning

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice for a febrile pregnant woman after high risk food exposure
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 27 weeks has 2 days of fever, muscle aches and mild diarrhoea. She ate a soft cheese platter and a prepared rockmelon salad at a work function 4 days ago. She has no urinary or respiratory symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, BP 106/64 mmHg, temperature 38.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 160 /min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 68 mg/L, urinalysis negative; blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone, adding azithromycin if cultures confirm
Oral nitrofurantoin, adding intravenous cefazolin if cultures confirm
Oral doxycycline, adding intravenous ceftriaxone if cultures confirm
Intravenous benzylpenicillin, adding gentamicin if cultures confirm
Intravenous aciclovir, adding benzylpenicillin if cultures confirm

subtopic_detail: Surveillance after maternal seroconversion to parvovirus B19 in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in a maternal fetal medicine clinic. A 30-year-old primary school teacher at 17 weeks in her second pregnancy was exposed to several children with a facial rash at work 3 weeks ago and developed joint aches in her hands 5 days ago.

She has had no fever and no rash herself. Fetal movements are not yet felt. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated.

Booking serology 8 weeks ago showed parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin G negative and immunoglobulin M negative. Repeat serology this week shows immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive. Rubella immunoglobulin G is positive from booking and her measles status is immune. An ultrasound today shows a single fetus with growth on the 50th centile, normal anatomy, an amniotic fluid index within the normal range, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and no skin oedema. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is 0.9 multiples of the median.

data_table.Investigations: Booking parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M and G both negative; current immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive. Ultrasound today: growth 50th centile, normal anatomy, normal amniotic fluid index, no ascites, pericardial effusion or skin oedema; middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity 0.9 multiples of the median

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that the fetus is unaffected and continue routine antenatal care with a growth scan at 34 weeks
Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction testing and karyotype within the next week
Administer maternal intravenous immunoglobulin now and repeat the ultrasound scan in 4 weeks
Arrange fetal blood sampling with intrauterine transfusion at the earliest available operating list
Weekly ultrasound with middle cerebral artery Doppler assessment for the next 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Interpreting discordant cytomegalovirus avidity and immunoglobulin results in the first trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in an antenatal clinic. A 26-year-old childcare worker at 13 weeks in her first pregnancy had serology sent by her general practitioner after 10 days of fatigue and mildly tender neck glands that have now resolved.

She has a well 2-year-old nephew in her care 3 days a week. She has had no rash, no sore throat and no jaundice. She takes pregnancy multivitamins only.

Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M is positive, immunoglobulin G is positive, and immunoglobulin G avidity is reported as high. Epstein-Barr virus serology shows past infection. Liver function tests, full blood count and film are within normal limits. Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M is negative. An ultrasound at 13 weeks shows a single fetus with crown rump length consistent with dates, normal nuchal translucency, and no intracranial or abdominal abnormality identified.

data_table.Investigations: Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M positive, immunoglobulin G positive, immunoglobulin G avidity high. Epstein-Barr virus serology shows past infection. Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M negative. Liver function tests, full blood count and film within normal limits. Ultrasound at 13 weeks: crown rump length consistent with dates, normal nuchal translucency, no intracranial or abdominal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Infection occurred before conception; give hygiene advice and continue routine antenatal care with a morphology scan
Primary infection has occurred in pregnancy; arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction after 21 weeks
Primary infection has occurred in pregnancy; commence oral valaciclovir and arrange serial fetal neurosonography
The results are uninterpretable; repeat the full serology panel in 3 weeks before giving any advice or counselling
Reactivation has occurred in pregnancy; arrange monthly fetal growth ultrasound and neonatal hearing assessment only

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with absent uterus on imaging and normal female androgen levels
stem:
You are the registrar in an adolescent gynaecology clinic. A 16-year-old girl attends because she has never menstruated while all her friends began years ago. She has no cyclical pain and no abdominal swelling.

She is a competitive swimmer training 6 hours a week and eats well, with a stable weight. She has no headaches and no visual symptoms, and her sense of smell is normal.

On examination breast development is Tanner stage 5, axillary and pubic hair are Tanner stage 5, and height is on the 70th centile. The external genitalia are normal in appearance with a short blind-ending vaginal dimple. Pelvic ultrasound reports no uterus identified, with two normal ovaries containing antral follicles. Follicle stimulating hormone is 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone is 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol is in the mid-follicular range, and total testosterone is 1.2 nmol/L (0.5-1.7 female reference range). Renal tract ultrasound shows a solitary right kidney.

data_table.Examination: Breast Tanner stage 5, axillary and pubic hair Tanner stage 5, height 70th centile, normal external genitalia with a short blind-ending vaginal dimple
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: no uterus identified, two normal ovaries with antral follicles. Follicle stimulating hormone 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol mid-follicular range, total testosterone 1.2 nmol/L (0.5-1.7 female range). Renal tract ultrasound: solitary right kidney

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Complete androgen insensitivity with intra-abdominal testes and absent Mullerian derivatives
Congenital absence of the Mullerian duct derivatives with normally functioning ovaries
Functional hypothalamic suppression from athletic training with reduced gonadotrophin secretion
Gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads and elevated gonadotrophin secretion from absent feedback
Transverse vaginal septum obstructing outflow above a normally developed uterine cavity

subtopic_detail: Timing of antenatal deinfibulation planning for a woman with type 3 genital cutting
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 23-year-old woman who arrived in Australia 2 years ago attends at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy, accompanied by a professional interpreter she has agreed to.

She reports that passing urine takes several minutes and that periods before this pregnancy were prolonged and painful. She has no dysuria and no fever. She has not had intercourse difficulties raised as a concern by her or her partner.

On examination, with her consent, the vulva shows a horizontal band of scar tissue covering the introitus with a posterior opening admitting one fingertip. The urethral meatus is not visible. There is no tenderness, no discharge and no infection. The uterus is consistent with dates and fetal heart tones are normal. She says she does not know what was done to her as a child and asks what this will mean for the birth.

data_table.Examination: Horizontal band of scar tissue covering the introitus with a posterior opening admitting one fingertip, urethral meatus not visible, no tenderness, discharge or infection, uterus consistent with dates, fetal heart tones normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Defer any procedure and plan deinfibulation during the second stage of labour with continuity of care arranged
Recommend planned caesarean section at 39 weeks to avoid vaginal birth, with continuity of care arranged
Discuss and offer planned antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester with continuity of care arranged
Arrange reinfibulation to be performed after the birth if she requests it, with continuity of care arranged
Refer to the child protection team and defer any discussion of the birth plan until that assessment concludes

subtopic_detail: Classifying and siting repair of a perineal injury where external sphincter fibres are partly torn
stem:
You are the registrar called to the birth suite to assess a perineal injury after a 26-year-old woman's first birth. The baby weighed 4020 g and was born by vacuum extraction with a mediolateral episiotomy for a prolonged second stage.

The midwife has applied pressure and bleeding is controlled. The woman has a working epidural and is comfortable.

With her consent you examine in lithotomy in the birth suite with good lighting. The episiotomy extends through the perineal body. Digital rectal examination shows intact rectal mucosa and intact anal epithelium. On pill-rolling the external anal sphincter between index finger and thumb, you find the torn fibres involve less than half the thickness of the external sphincter across its width, and the internal anal sphincter appears intact as a separate pale layer. She has had no previous perineal injury and no anal incontinence.

data_table.Examination: Mediolateral episiotomy extending through the perineal body; rectal mucosa and anal epithelium intact; external anal sphincter torn through less than half its thickness; internal anal sphincter intact; bleeding controlled; epidural working

lead_in: How should this injury be classified and repaired?

options.text: Second degree tear involving the perineal body, repaired in the birth suite by an appropriately trained clinician
Third degree tear subclassified as 3b, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
Third degree tear subclassified as 3c, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
Third degree tear subclassified as 3a, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
Fourth degree tear involving the anorectal complex, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician

subtopic_detail: Switching antithyroid drug between trimesters when hepatic and teratogenic risks conflict
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 13 weeks with Graves disease has taken propylthiouracil since 5 weeks, switched from carbimazole by her general practitioner. She feels well, drinks no alcohol and has no history of liver disease.

data_table.Thyroid: Free thyroxine upper end of the pregnancy range, TSH 0.03 mIU/L, TSH receptor antibody 8.2 IU/L
data_table.Liver: ALT 186 then 204 U/L 4 days later (<40), AST 152 U/L; hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue propylthiouracil at the current dose with close monitoring
Stop all antithyroid drugs now and monitor thyroid function
Arrange radioactive iodine ablation after the first trimester
Add oral prednisolone to the current propylthiouracil dose
Switch back to carbimazole and monitor liver function

subtopic_detail: Responding to a falling lamotrigine concentration with breakthrough seizures in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in a joint obstetric medicine clinic. A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy has focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation, seizure free for 3 years on lamotrigine 300 mg daily before conception.

She has had two generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the past 5 weeks, the most recent while driving, and has surrendered her licence. She confirms she has not missed doses and a pill count supports this. She takes folic acid 5 mg daily and has no other medications and no vomiting.

Her pre-pregnancy trough lamotrigine concentration was 28 micromol/L. A trough sample taken today is 11 micromol/L. Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and magnesium are within normal limits, and she has no rash. Blood pressure is 108/64 mmHg with no proteinuria. Ultrasound today shows growth on the 40th centile with normal amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Trough lamotrigine 11 micromol/L today versus 28 micromol/L pre-pregnancy. Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and magnesium within normal limits. No proteinuria. Ultrasound: growth 40th centile, normal amniotic fluid and umbilical artery Doppler
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 300 mg daily, folic acid 5 mg daily; adherence confirmed by pill count

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by serial concentrations, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
Continue the current lamotrigine dose and repeat the trough concentration in 4 weeks
Add sodium valproate to the current lamotrigine dose, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
Switch from lamotrigine to levetiracetam over 4 weeks, with a planned postpartum dose reduction
Add a regular clobazam dose to the current lamotrigine, with a planned postpartum dose reduction

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological lactation suppression after stillbirth in a normotensive woman
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman on the ward. She gave birth two days ago at 34 weeks following an intrauterine fetal death, and is due for discharge tomorrow.

Her breasts have become firm, hot and painful overnight and milk is leaking through her clothing. She tells you she finds this 'unbearable to live with' and asks whether anything can be given to stop it. She has thought about donating milk and has decided against it.

Her blood pressure has been between 108/64 and 118/72 mmHg throughout the pregnancy and since birth, and her booking and postnatal blood pressure records contain no readings above 130/80 mmHg. She has no history of depression or psychosis, takes no regular medication and is not planning to feed a future infant in the coming weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1°C
data_table.Breast examination: Bilaterally firm, warm and tender with spontaneous leakage; no focal mass, no erythematous wedge, no fluctuance
data_table.History: Blood pressure never above 130/80 mmHg antenatally or postnatally; no psychiatric history; no regular medications

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Prescribe bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally twice daily for a fourteen day course
Prescribe cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose with supportive breast measures
Prescribe oestrogen therapy for one week with firm breast support and ice packs
Advise firm breast support and analgesia alone and avoid any drug treatment
Advise regular expression of milk to comfort and review her again in one week

subtopic_detail: Duration of the magnesium sulfate infusion given for fetal neuroprotection before imminent preterm birth
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar called to the birth suite for a 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 28 weeks and 3 days. She arrived two hours ago saying she has had 'tightenings coming every three minutes' and a gush of fluid.

Speculum examination confirms ruptured membranes and vaginal examination finds the cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced with the vertex at the ischial spines. Contractions are palpably strong and regular and the midwife anticipates birth within a few hours.

She received the first dose of betamethasone six hours ago. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 150/min with normal variability and no decelerations. Her reflexes are normal, urine output is 60 mL per hour and renal function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C, fetal heart rate 150/min
data_table.Vaginal examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced, vertex at the ischial spines, membranes ruptured
data_table.Medications given: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly six hours ago
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 54 micromol/L (45-90), urine output 60 mL/hour, deep tendon reflexes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional treatment to give now?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously then 1 g per hour for 24 hours after the birth
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously then 1 g per hour until birth or for 24 hours
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously as a single dose with no maintenance infusion
Nifedipine 20 mg orally then 20 mg every six hours to prolong the pregnancy
A second course of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly given 24 hours apart

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy stratified by peak total bile acid concentration
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in a day assessment unit reviewing a 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 35 weeks and 2 days. She describes three weeks of itching that is worst on her palms and the soles of her feet and keeps her awake, and says she has scratched until she bleeds.

There is no rash apart from excoriations and no abdominal pain. Her urine and stools are of normal colour and she has had no nausea or vomiting.

Blood pressure and urinalysis are normal and fetal growth is on the 45th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers. Fasting total bile acids taken this morning are 118 micromol/L, having been 46 micromol/L two weeks ago. A viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies are negative and liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8°C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations with no primary rash; no right upper quadrant tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Total bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 19), previously 46 micromol/L two weeks ago; alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L (less than 30); bilirubin within normal limits
data_table.Other results: Viral hepatitis serology and liver autoantibodies negative, liver ultrasound normal
data_table.Fetal assessment: Estimated fetal weight on the 45th centile, umbilical artery Dopplers normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan induction of labour at 39 weeks gestation
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan induction of labour at 38 weeks gestation
Arrange weekly cardiotocography and plan induction of labour at 40 weeks
Start ursodeoxycholic acid and plan induction of labour within the next week
Arrange weekly bile acid testing and plan spontaneous labour at term

subtopic_detail: Non-hormonal control of ovulatory heavy menstrual bleeding in a woman actively trying to conceive
stem: A 29-year-old woman has 2 years of heavy periods, flooding through a tampon and pad within an hour on her worst days. Her cycles are regular with no intermenstrual bleeding. She is trying to conceive and declines anything that would prevent pregnancy.

data_table.Ultrasound: Normal sized uterus, endometrial thickness 7 mm, no fibroid or polyp, normal ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 103 g/L, ferritin 7 microgram/L; thyroid, coagulation and von Willebrand studies normal

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system and start oral iron
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and start oral iron
Norethisterone from day 5 to day 26 of each cycle, with iron
Refer for endometrial ablation, with oral iron beforehand
Tranexamic acid during menstruation, with oral iron

subtopic_detail: Choice and duration of hormone replacement after biochemical confirmation of premature ovarian insufficiency
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. She says her periods 'just stopped' eight months ago and that she is waking three or four times a night drenched in sweat and feels dry and sore with intercourse.

She has never been pregnant and has an intact uterus. She takes no medications and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

A urine pregnancy test is negative. Follicle stimulating hormone measured four weeks apart is 58 IU/L and 62 IU/L with an oestradiol of 42 pmol/L on both occasions. Prolactin and thyroid function are within normal limits and a karyotype and fragile X premutation screen have been requested. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 58 IU/L then 62 IU/L four weeks apart (follicular 3-10); oestradiol 42 pmol/L on both occasions (follicular 110-400)
data_table.Other results: Urine pregnancy test negative; prolactin and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.History: Intact uterus, nulliparous, no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, body mass index 23 kg/m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oestrogen with a progestogen and continue it until about the age of 51
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review her again in six months
Start alendronate weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation for bone health
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor to control the vasomotor symptoms
Arrange bone densitometry and defer any treatment until the result becomes available

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment of endometrial hyperplasia without atypia in a woman wishing to keep her uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 44-year-old woman in clinic with the result of an endometrial biopsy. She was referred with two years of heavy, prolonged and irregular periods that soak through a pad every hour on her worst days.

She has two children and has completed her family but tells you she 'really does not want an operation' and would like to keep her uterus if that is safe.

Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2. Transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 16 mm with no focal lesion and normal ovaries. A pipelle biopsy reports endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. A full blood count shows haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155) with a ferritin of 9 microgram/L (15-200), and her thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 16 mm, no focal lesion, normal ovaries
data_table.Histology: Pipelle biopsy reports endometrial hyperplasia without atypia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), ferritin 9 microgram/L (15-200), thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Arrange total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy on the next list
Start cyclical oral norethisterone for 10 days each month and resample at 6 months
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system and resample the endometrium at 6 months
Arrange endometrial ablation and repeat the endometrial sampling again at 6 months
Advise weight loss alone and repeat the endometrial sampling again at 12 months

subtopic_detail: Action on a borderline fetal scalp lactate result with a persisting pathological cardiotocograph
stem: A 27-year-old woman in her first labour at 39+4 weeks is 7 cm dilated with the vertex at the spines. Oxytocin has been stopped, she is in the left lateral position and has had a 500 mL bolus, with no change in the trace.

data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 155 /min, variability 3 /min, repetitive late decelerations for 40 minutes
data_table.Fetal blood sample: Scalp lactate 4.4 mmol/L (normal below 4.2, borderline 4.2 to 4.8, abnormal 4.8 or above)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthetic
Continue conservative measures and repeat the sample in two hours
Apply a fetal scalp electrode and continue without further sampling
Continue conservative measures and repeat the sample in 30 minutes
Start oxytocin to accelerate labour and reassess at full dilatation

subtopic_detail: Switching antihypertensive therapy at the first antenatal visit for a woman on a renin-angiotensin blocker
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 33-year-old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Dating by her last menstrual period puts her at 7 weeks and 1 day, and she says this pregnancy was not planned.

She has taken ramipril 5 mg daily for four years for essential hypertension diagnosed at age 29, and has taken it every day including this week. She takes no other medication and has never smoked.

Her blood pressure today is 142/92 mmHg, repeated after five minutes as 144/90 mmHg. Urinalysis shows no protein. Renal function, electrolytes and a full blood count are within normal limits and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. She asks whether she needs to change anything about her tablets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 142/92 mmHg repeated at 144/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 5 mg orally daily for four years, taken daily including this week
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for protein; renal function, electrolytes and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Gestation: 7 weeks and 1 day by last menstrual period

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her antihypertensive treatment?

options.text: Continue ramipril until the end of the first trimester then change to labetalol
Stop ramipril today and withhold all antihypertensive treatment until 20 weeks
Stop ramipril today and start oral labetalol, titrating to a target below 140/90
Stop ramipril today and start oral atenolol, titrating to a target below 140/90
Halve the ramipril dose today and start low dose aspirin at 100 mg each night

subtopic_detail: Recognition of scar dehiscence during labour after caesarean when an epidural masks the pain
stem: A 34-year-old woman in her second labour at 40+1 weeks, after a previous caesarean, has a working epidural and an oxytocin infusion. Fifteen minutes ago she began describing a constant burning abdominal ache breaking through the epidural.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 /min (was 88), BP 96/54 mmHg, fetal heart 70 /min for 4 minutes
data_table.Examination: Vertex risen from the spines to 2 cm above; fresh blood at the introitus; uterus tense

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give a tocolytic, reposition her and continue labour with monitoring
Call for immediate laparotomy and transfer her to theatre now
Fetal blood sampling to clarify the significance of the trace
Increase the epidural top-up and reassess the pain in ten minutes
Increase the oxytocin and plan an assisted birth at full dilatation

subtopic_detail: Stopping rule when a trial of vacuum extraction in theatre fails with repeated cup detachment
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar conducting a trial of instrumental birth in theatre for a 28-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 41 weeks. She has an epidural that has been topped up to a surgical block, the bladder has been emptied and the anaesthetist and paediatric team are present.

She has been fully dilated for three hours with two hours of active pushing. The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 170/min with absent variability and recurrent variable decelerations.

On examination the head is at station plus 1 with the occiput in the left transverse position. There is caput of 2 cm and the parietal bones override and cannot be reduced. You have applied a posterior vacuum cup twice with correct placement over the flexion point; on each pull the cup detached with no descent of the presenting part.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2°C, fetal heart rate 170/min
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 170/min, absent variability, recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Vaginal examination: Station plus 1, occiput left transverse, caput 2 cm, overriding parietal bones that do not reduce
data_table.Instrumental attempts: Vacuum cup applied twice over the flexion point; detachment on each pull with no descent
data_table.Setting: Theatre, surgical epidural block, bladder emptied, anaesthetic and paediatric teams present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply Kielland rotational forceps to complete the birth in the operating theatre
Reapply the vacuum cup at higher pressure for one further pull in the theatre
Perform manual rotation to occiput anterior and reapply the vacuum cup afterwards
Continue maternal pushing for a further hour with close continuous fetal monitoring
Abandon the instrumental attempt and proceed to caesarean section immediately

subtopic_detail: Secondary amenorrhoea with cyclical pain and a negative progestogen challenge after postpartum curettage
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman referred with eight months of absent periods. She says she gets 'the same cramps I always got before a period, but nothing ever comes'.

She gave birth vaginally fourteen months ago. At day twelve postpartum she had heavy bleeding and underwent uterine curettage for retained products, followed by a course of antibiotics. Her periods returned briefly two months later, became progressively lighter over three cycles, and then stopped.

She is not breastfeeding and is using condoms. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Follicle stimulating hormone is 5.8 IU/L, oestradiol 340 pmol/L, prolactin and thyroid function are within normal limits, and she has no galactorrhoea or visual symptoms. A 10 day course of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate produced no withdrawal bleeding at all.

data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 5.8 IU/L (follicular 3-10), oestradiol 340 pmol/L (follicular 110-400), prolactin and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Progestogen challenge: Ten days of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate produced no withdrawal bleeding
data_table.Obstetric history: Vaginal birth 14 months ago; uterine curettage for retained products at day 12 postpartum with antibiotics
data_table.Symptoms: Cyclical lower abdominal cramping without any bleeding; no galactorrhoea or visual symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange diagnostic hysteroscopy with adhesiolysis under general anaesthetic
Arrange a karyotype and a fragile X premutation screen before any procedure
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review her again in six months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with gadolinium contrast
Start cabergoline and repeat the serum prolactin measurement again in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Perineal trauma reclassified on per rectum examination after an initial assessment of a second degree tear
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar asked to review perineal trauma in the birth room. A 24-year-old woman in her first pregnancy gave birth twenty minutes ago by forceps for a prolonged second stage, with a right mediolateral episiotomy, and the baby weighed 4180 g.

The midwife has assessed the trauma as a second degree tear and has drawn up local anaesthetic to repair it in the room. The woman has an epidural in place that remains effective.

You examine her with good lighting and an assistant. The episiotomy extends through the perineal muscles towards the anal margin. On per rectum examination with the index finger in the anal canal and the thumb on the perineum, you can feel a defect in the external anal sphincter that involves more than half of its circumference. The anorectal mucosa is intact and the internal anal sphincter is felt to be continuous.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Birth details: Forceps birth for prolonged second stage, right mediolateral episiotomy, birth weight 4180 g
data_table.Perineal examination: Episiotomy extending through the perineal muscles towards the anal margin
data_table.Per rectum examination: External anal sphincter defect involving more than half its circumference; internal anal sphincter continuous; anorectal mucosa intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfer her to theatre for repair of the sphincter under regional anaesthesia
Repair the perineal muscles in the birth room under local anaesthetic infiltration
Leave the tear to heal by secondary intention and arrange physiotherapy review
Repair the vaginal epithelium only and arrange colorectal review in six weeks
Transfer her to theatre for a defunctioning colostomy and delayed sphincter repair

subtopic_detail: Ascending motor block with bradycardia after an epidural top-up for caesarean section
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 39 weeks had her epidural topped up 6 minutes ago with 20 mL of lidocaine 2 percent with adrenaline. Her hands tingled, then her arms felt heavy; her voice is weak and she cannot breathe deeply.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 /min, BP 68/34 mmHg, RR 8 /min, SpO2 94% on oxygen
data_table.Block: Sensory level C6 bilaterally with absent grip strength
data_table.Negatives: No seizure, metallic taste, tinnitus or perioral numbness; no rash

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Treat as anaphylaxis with intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg and fluid
Intravenous lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg for local anaesthetic toxicity
Sit her fully upright to limit spread and give high flow oxygen
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g and prepare for operative birth
Intubate and ventilate her now, supporting circulation with metaraminol

subtopic_detail: Sequencing glucocorticoid and thyroid hormone replacement in postpartum hypopituitarism with hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 29-year-old woman who is five weeks postpartum. Her partner says she has been 'dragging herself around' for a month and has vomited repeatedly today and is now muddled about the date.

Her birth was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of about 4 litres from uterine atony, requiring eight units of red cells and a uterine balloon tamponade. She never produced any breast milk despite persistent attempts with a lactation consultant, and has had no vaginal bleeding of any kind since the lochia settled.

She is drowsy but rousable with sparse axillary hair. Investigations are shown. A computed tomography scan of the brain shows no haemorrhage, no mass and no hydrocephalus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58/min, blood pressure 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 35.9°C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Endocrine results: 9 am cortisol 42 nmol/L (200-650), free thyroxine 6.1 pmol/L (10-20), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography of the brain shows no haemorrhage, mass or hydrocephalus
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, sparse axillary hair

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous levothyroxine now and start hydrocortisone in the morning
Give intravenous hydrocortisone now and add levothyroxine after twenty four hours
Give 3 per cent hypertonic saline 150 mL and restrict her fluid to a litre daily
Give intravenous desmopressin now and restrict her fluid intake to a litre daily
Give oral tolvaptan now and restrict her fluid intake to one litre each day

subtopic_detail: first line management of involuntary pelvic floor contraction preventing penetration
stem: A 26-year-old woman has never been able to tolerate vaginal penetration, describing burning and involuntary tightening whenever it is attempted, including with tampons. She has no dyspareunia at other times and no history of sexual assault.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture with no fissuring or lichenoid change; cotton swab test at the vestibule negative; visible involuntary levator contraction on attempted speculum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Examination under general anaesthetic to exclude a vaginal septum
Refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded dilator therapy
Topical lidocaine 5 percent to the vestibule before intercourse
Nightly topical oestrogen cream for six weeks, then reassess
Swabs for candida and bacterial vaginosis with empirical fluconazole

subtopic_detail: sequencing analgesia and hormonal therapy for painful periods in an adolescent not seeking contraception
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl with her mother. For two years she has had cramping lower abdominal pain starting a few hours before each period and lasting two days. She misses one or two school days each cycle. She is not sexually active and does not want contraception.

Her menarche was at 12 years, cycles are regular at 29 days, and bleeding lasts five days with no flooding or clots. The pain is central and does not occur between periods. She has no dyschezia, no urinary symptoms and no pain with exercise. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g when the pain becomes severe, usually several hours after it starts, with little effect. Abdominal examination is unremarkable and she declines pelvic examination, which you do not pursue.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no mass; secondary sexual characteristics appropriate for age; no examination of the pelvis performed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer her to a gynaecologist for a diagnostic laparoscopy to look for peritoneal deposits and adhesive disease
Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound scan to assess the ovaries and the posterior compartment before commencing any treatment
Increase her paracetamol to a regular four times daily dose across the whole period and add a heat pack for symptom relief
Start regular naproxen beginning the day before bleeding and continuing for the first two days of each period
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously and reassess her symptom control after three months of therapy

subtopic_detail: immediate response when a pregnant woman discloses partner violence at a routine visit
stem:
You are the doctor conducting a routine 28 week antenatal visit in a metropolitan clinic. When you ask the standard screening questions with the woman alone, she tells you that her partner has pushed her against a wall twice in the last month and controls the household money and her phone. She has not told anyone before. She says she does not want to leave him and does not want police involved.

She is 31 years old in her second pregnancy. Symphysis fundal height is appropriate, the fetus is active and blood pressure is within normal limits. She has an old bruise on the left upper arm. Her partner is in the waiting room and has attended every visit so far. She asks you not to write anything in her handheld pregnancy record because he reads it.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height appropriate for gestation; fetal movements present; resolving bruise on the left upper arm; no abdominal tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Acknowledge the disclosure, assess immediate safety and risk to any children, and offer a warm referral to a specialist service
Arrange an urgent ultrasound for placental abruption and admit her to the antenatal ward for continuous cardiotocographic monitoring
Invite her partner in to discuss the relationship together so that both perspectives can be heard before any plan is made
Record the disclosure in her handheld record so that every clinician she meets is informed and can respond consistently
Explain that you must contact police because the assault occurred while she was pregnant and the fetus may have been at risk

subtopic_detail: managing a dilated fluid filled tube before assisted reproductive treatment
stem: A 33-year-old woman has 3 years of primary infertility after pelvic inflammatory disease at 24. She ovulates regularly and her partner's semen analysis is normal. She has decided to proceed with in vitro fertilisation.

data_table.Imaging: Hysterosalpingogram: dilated non-filling right tube, patent left tube. Ultrasound: persistent 4 cm sausage-shaped right adnexal structure separate from the ovary
data_table.Investigations: Ovarian reserve age appropriate; normal uterine cavity

lead_in: What should be recommended before her embryo transfer?

options.text: Proceed to transfer without tubal surgery, as the other tube is patent
Hysteroscopic proximal tubal occlusion with a device, confirmed on imaging
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy, or proximal occlusion if adhesions prevent it
Laparoscopic salpingostomy with adhesiolysis to restore patency
Aspiration of the tubal fluid at oocyte retrieval, with doxycycline

subtopic_detail: hormone replacement duration and dose in a young woman with gonadal dysgenesis
stem: A 19-year-old woman with 45,X gonadal dysgenesis completed pubertal induction and takes oestradiol with cyclical progestogen, with regular withdrawal bleeds. She stopped her tablets 4 months ago because she feels well and cannot conceive naturally anyway.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram with aortic root measurement normal; body mass index 26 kg/m2; uterus present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her hormone therapy?

options.text: Switch to unopposed transdermal oestradiol, as progestogen is no longer needed
Take a combined oral contraceptive pill instead, as it is simpler
Take a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D instead of hormones
Stop treatment now, with annual bone density scanning instead
Continue oestrogen with progestogen until about 51 years of age

subtopic_detail: antibiotic selection when postnatal collapse follows a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection
stem: A 29-year-old woman 36 hours after a normal vaginal birth has become acutely unwell over 3 hours with severe lower abdominal pain, vomiting and a widespread red rash. Her 3-year-old had a sore throat last week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 136 /min, BP 82/44 mmHg, RR 30 /min, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Blanching truncal rash, tender uterus, offensive lochia, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 2.8 x10^9/L, lactate 5.4 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Intravenous aciclovir with ceftriaxone for possible disseminated viral infection
Intravenous benzylpenicillin with clindamycin, alongside urgent surgical review
Intravenous ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole as triple therapy
Intravenous vancomycin with ceftriaxone, deferring any further agent
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, escalating if she does not improve

subtopic_detail: empirical therapy for a febrile pregnant woman with a food exposure and no localising signs
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 29 weeks has 3 days of fever, myalgia, headache and loose stools. She ate soft cheese and a prepackaged salad platter 5 days ago; two other guests developed diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 38.6 degrees C, pulse 108 /min, fetal heart rate 158 /min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 62 mg/L, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Send stool for culture and polymerase chain reaction and manage her supportively
A single intramuscular ceftriaxone dose with outpatient review in 24 hours
Betamethasone and nifedipine tocolysis with observation on the antenatal ward
Blood cultures and high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin
Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone, adding metronidazole if tender

subtopic_detail: definitive treatment choice after hormonal therapy fails in diffuse uterine wall disease
stem: A 44-year-old woman has 4 years of progressively heavier, more painful periods with a constant dragging pelvic ache. She has completed her family. A levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tranexamic acid and continuous norethisterone have all failed, and the device is correctly sited.

data_table.Ultrasound: Globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, subendometrial striations and myometrial cysts, no discrete fibroid
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L, ferritin 8 microgram/L; endometrial biopsy benign secretory

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Total hysterectomy with ovarian conservation, after iron replacement
Second generation endometrial ablation with ultrasound at 6 months
Uterine artery embolisation with clinical review at 3 months
A new intrauterine system with 6 months of a gonadotrophin agonist
Hysteroscopic resection of the affected myometrium with follow-up

subtopic_detail: triage of a complex adnexal mass after menopause using a combined risk assessment
stem: A 63-year-old woman has 6 weeks of bloating, early satiety and a larger waistband. Her last period was at 51 years, with no postmenopausal bleeding and no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

data_table.Ultrasound: 7 cm right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections, septations over 3 mm, marked internal Doppler flow, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: CA125 310 kU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic cystectomy
Request germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing before deciding on referral
Refer directly to gynaecological oncology for staging and planning
Repeat the CA125 and ultrasound in twelve weeks to see if they change
Arrange ultrasound guided biopsy of the solid component first

subtopic_detail: acting on a non-invasive prenatal screen that fails twice for insufficient placental deoxyribonucleic acid
stem: A 38-year-old woman in her second pregnancy had non-invasive prenatal screening at 10 weeks and again at 13 weeks; both returned no result for insufficient fetal fraction. Her body mass index is 41 kg/m2 and she takes enoxaparin. She declined first trimester combined screening and is now 14 weeks.

data_table.Ultrasound: 13 weeks: single viable fetus, dates consistent, nuchal translucency 1.4 mm, no structural abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: The nuchal translucency and normal anatomy make further testing unnecessary
Arrange a second trimester quadruple test and decide on that risk
Arrange transabdominal chorionic villus sampling this week
Repeat the screen a third time at 16 weeks, when fetal fraction rises
Repeated failure itself carries aneuploidy risk; offer amniocentesis

subtopic_detail: recognising decompensated thyrotoxicosis during labour and choosing the sequence of drug therapy
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 39 weeks has laboured for 8 hours and is now agitated, confused and vomiting. She has Graves disease and stopped propylthiouracil in the second trimester.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min in atrial fibrillation, BP 96/48 mmHg, temperature 39.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Smooth goitre with bruit, fine tremor, cervix 6 cm dilated
data_table.Investigations: Free thyroxine raised, thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological sequence?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia, antithyroid drugs afterwards
Propranolol and propylthiouracil first, then iodine an hour later, with hydrocortisone
Potassium iodide immediately, then propylthiouracil and propranolol afterwards
Amiodarone for the atrial fibrillation, then carbimazole and hydrocortisone
Broad spectrum antibiotics and paracetamol for presumed chorioamnionitis

subtopic_detail: observation period and immunoglobulin dosing after blunt abdominal injury in the third trimester
stem: A 25-year-old woman at 31 weeks was the restrained driver in a side impact collision 40 minutes ago and walked from the vehicle. There is seatbelt bruising across the lower abdomen, with no bleeding or fluid loss.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, BP 118/74 mmHg, fetal heart rate 142 /min
data_table.Blood group: O RhD negative, antibody screen negative at booking
data_table.Monitoring: Thirty minutes of cardiotocography: normal, with three irregular tightenings

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give anti-D only if fetal cells appear
Betamethasone and nifedipine tocolysis, with overnight observation
Discharge now with written advice on bleeding, pain and fetal movements
Continue cardiotocography for 4 hours, Kleihauer test and give anti-D
Urgent ultrasound for retroplacental clot, discharging if it is normal

subtopic_detail: anticoagulation choice in early pregnancy for a woman with a prosthetic heart valve
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 6 weeks has a mechanical bileaflet mitral valve and takes warfarin 4 mg daily, with an international normalised ratio stable at 2.5 to 3.5. She is well, with crisp prosthetic sounds and no murmur.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography 6 months ago: normal prosthetic gradients and left ventricular function

lead_in: What anticoagulation do you recommend for the rest of the first trimester?

options.text: Continue warfarin at her current daily dose throughout the first trimester
Stop warfarin for prophylactic dose enoxaparin once daily with monitoring
Stop all anticoagulation until 12 weeks and add low dose aspirin
Stop warfarin for inpatient unfractionated heparin by infusion
Stop warfarin and start a direct oral anticoagulant instead

subtopic_detail: counselling a couple with a completed family about permanent contraception and the clearance interval afterwards
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a couple who have decided their family is complete after three children. She is 38 and he is 40.

She has migraine with aura, so she stopped the combined pill five years ago. A copper intrauterine device inserted after her last birth was expelled within two months and she declines a further device. They have been using condoms and want something permanent, and both say they are certain they want no more children. Neither has a contraindication to surgery. They ask you which option carries the lower risk and what they need to do afterwards.

data_table.History: Three previous births, family complete, migraine with aura, previous expulsion of a copper intrauterine device
data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, body mass index 26 kg/m2 for her and 27 kg/m2 for him
