lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic tubal occlusion for her as the safer of the procedures
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device for her before making any referral
Refer for vasectomy and continue contraception until semen analysis is clear
Refer for vasectomy and stop other contraception once the wound has healed
Advise a further trial of condoms as the failure rates are broadly comparable

subtopic_detail: request for pertussis vaccination in a woman who received a dose during a pregnancy eighteen months earlier
stem:
You are the doctor in an antenatal clinic seeing a 29-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first child is 14 months old.

She received a pertussis containing vaccine at 30 weeks in that pregnancy and asks whether she really needs another one so soon, saying she read that boosters last ten years. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, her anomaly scan was normal, and she has no allergies and no history of a reaction to vaccination. She plans to breastfeed and her partner and her mother, who will provide childcare, ask whether they need anything.

data_table.History: Gravida 2 para 1, pertussis containing vaccine given at 30 weeks in the previous pregnancy 18 months ago, no vaccine allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her own pertussis vaccination?

options.text: Defer vaccination as a dose within the last five years remains protective
Check pertussis serology and vaccinate only if the antibody level is low
Give the vaccine after birth so the newborn is protected through breast milk
Give the vaccine at 36 weeks so antibody levels peak closer to the birth
Give a pertussis containing vaccine now, whatever the dose 18 months ago

subtopic_detail: isolated third trimester fall in platelets with a normal booking count, normal blood pressure and no proteinuria
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy after routine bloods showed a low platelet count.

She feels well, has no bruising, no petechiae, no bleeding gums and no epigastric pain or visual symptoms. Her booking full blood count at 10 weeks showed platelets of 178 x10^9/L. Her blood pressure has been 105/65 to 115/70 mmHg throughout the pregnancy and her urine dipstick today shows no protein. She takes no medication other than a pregnancy multivitamin and has no personal or family history of a bleeding disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 95 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), blood film shows no schistocytes and no platelet clumping, alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (<35), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein to creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol (<30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 20 mg daily and review the platelet count in one week
Arrange urgent birth by caesarean because of the risk of maternal haemorrhage
Transfuse one unit of platelets before any further antenatal procedures today
Repeat the full blood count with a film in two weeks and continue routine care
Start intravenous immunoglobulin and refer for bone marrow examination now

subtopic_detail: booking visit glycaemic assessment when obesity and a previous large infant raise the chance of undiagnosed pre-existing diabetes
stem:
You are the doctor running a booking clinic. A 33-year-old woman attends at 10 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first baby weighed 4.4 kg at 39 weeks and she was never told she had diabetes in that pregnancy, although she recalls declining the sugary drink test.

Her body mass index today is 41 kg/m2. Her mother developed type 2 diabetes at 48. She has no polyuria, no thirst and no weight loss, and her urine dipstick shows no glucose or ketones. She is taking folic acid and iodine. She asks what testing she needs and when.

data_table.History: Body mass index 41 kg/m2, previous infant 4.4 kg at 39 weeks, mother with type 2 diabetes, no glucose tolerance testing in the previous pregnancy
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for glucose and ketones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate glycaemic testing plan?

options.text: Measure HbA1c now and arrange the 75 g glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks
Arrange the 75 g glucose tolerance test at 28 weeks and take no action now
Start metformin now given the body mass index and the previous large baby
Measure a random blood glucose at each antenatal visit from 20 weeks on
Arrange fasting glucose monthly from now until the third trimester test

subtopic_detail: continued smoking in the first trimester after behavioural support has reduced but not stopped consumption
stem:
You are the doctor in an antenatal clinic reviewing a 24-year-old woman at 12 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has smoked since she was 16.

Four weeks ago you gave her brief advice, referred her to the telephone quit service and she has engaged with it. She has cut down from 15 to 8 cigarettes a day but has not been able to stop, and she describes strong cravings within an hour of waking. She is distressed about the effect on the baby and asks whether there is anything she can take. She has no history of depression or seizures, takes no regular medication, and her nausea is mild and does not prevent her eating.

data_table.History: 8 cigarettes per day, reduced from 15, first cigarette within one hour of waking, engaged with telephone quit service for four weeks, no history of depression or seizures

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to help her stop?

options.text: Advise continued gradual reduction without medication until after the birth
Offer intermittent dose nicotine replacement with continued behavioural support
Start varenicline at the standard adult dose with weekly telephone follow up
Start bupropion and arrange review of her mood at two and at four weeks
Offer an electronic nicotine device as a safer substitute during pregnancy

subtopic_detail: reduced amniotic fluid volume at forty one weeks with normal growth, normal Dopplers and a reassuring trace
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the day assessment unit. A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends at 41 weeks and 1 day for routine post-dates assessment. She reports normal fetal movements and no contractions, fluid loss or bleeding.

Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal growth on serial measurement. The scan performed an hour ago shows an estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile, a single deepest vertical pocket of 1.8 cm, and normal umbilical artery Doppler indices with positive end diastolic flow. Her cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 135 beats per minute with normal variability, accelerations and no decelerations. On vaginal examination the cervix is 1 cm dilated, 1.5 cm long, mid position and soft, with the head at station minus 2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 135/min
data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile, single deepest vertical pocket 1.8 cm, umbilical artery Doppler normal with positive end diastolic flow, cardiotocograph normal
data_table.Examination: Cervix 1 cm dilated, 1.5 cm long, mid position, soft, vertex at station minus 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in three days and continue awaiting spontaneous labour
Recommend caesarean birth today because of the reduced amniotic fluid volume
Recommend induction of labour now, beginning with cervical ripening today
Arrange twice weekly cardiotocography and review again at 42 weeks completed
Encourage maternal oral hydration and rescan the fluid volume in one week

subtopic_detail: immunosuppression review before conception in a woman with a stable kidney graft
stem:
You are the doctor in a preconception clinic. A 29-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant three years ago for reflux nephropathy asks about becoming pregnant.

She has had no rejection episodes in the last two years and her graft function has been stable. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisolone 5 mg daily, plus amlodipine for blood pressure. She uses condoms for contraception. Her last transplant clinic letter records a stable creatinine, no proteinuria and a therapeutic tacrolimus level. She is up to date with cervical screening and her rubella and varicella serology are immune.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2, urine protein to creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (<30), haemoglobin 121 g/L (115-155), tacrolimus level within target range
data_table.Medications: Tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisolone 5 mg daily, amlodipine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her medication before she conceives?

options.text: Continue all current immunosuppression and start high dose folic acid before conceiving
Stop tacrolimus and continue mycophenolate with prednisolone in the pregnancy
Advise that pregnancy is contraindicated after solid organ transplantation
Continue the current medication and monitor graft function each trimester only
Change mycophenolate to azathioprine and confirm stability over three months

subtopic_detail: request to stop a biologic agent in mid pregnancy while inflammatory bowel disease is in remission
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a joint medical and obstetric clinic. A 31-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy has ileocolonic Crohn disease that has been in remission for two years on infliximab every eight weeks.

She read online that biologic drugs cross the placenta and wants to stop her next infusion, which is due in a fortnight. She has no abdominal pain, is opening her bowels twice a day without blood, and has gained weight appropriately. Her most recent faecal calprotectin was 42 micrograms/g and her inflammatory markers were normal. Her previous flare, before starting the biologic, required admission and a course of intravenous corticosteroid.

data_table.Investigations: Faecal calprotectin 42 micrograms/g (<50), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), haemoglobin 119 g/L (115-155), albumin 34 g/L (32-45 in pregnancy)
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, fundal height consistent with dates, fetal movements normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Stop infliximab now and restart it once she has recovered after the birth
Switch to oral methotrexate for the remainder of the pregnancy and afterwards
Stop infliximab and monitor with faecal calprotectin every four weeks instead
Continue infliximab unchanged because active disease is the greater risk
Switch to prednisolone alone, tapering it once the third trimester begins

subtopic_detail: acute severe limb and back pain in the third trimester in a woman with a haemoglobinopathy and a haemoglobin at her usual baseline
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite assessment area. A 27-year-old woman at 29 weeks in her first pregnancy has six hours of severe pain in her lower back and both thighs, which she says is exactly like the crises she had as a teenager.

She has homozygous sickle cell disease and takes folic acid and prophylactic phenoxymethylpenicillin. She stopped hydroxycarbamide before conceiving. She is afebrile with a clear chest and no cough or pleuritic pain, and her oxygen saturation is 96 per cent in room air. Paracetamol at home has not helped. Her haemoglobin today is 74 g/L, which matches her documented baseline of 72 to 78 g/L. The cardiotocograph is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 145/min
data_table.Examination: Severe tenderness over the lumbar spine and both thighs, chest clear with equal air entry, abdomen soft with no uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 74 g/L (baseline 72-78 for this patient), reticulocytes 320 x10^9/L (20-100), white cell count 12.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 52 micromol/L (45-90), C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (<5), cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of her pain?

options.text: Start intravenous fluids and titrated morphine with close respiratory monitoring
Start intravenous fluids and regular intramuscular pethidine for the pain
Transfuse two units of red cells to correct the haemoglobin before analgesia
Start regular oral ibuprofen with paracetamol and review again in four hours
Arrange urgent caesarean birth as the pain indicates fetal compromise is present

subtopic_detail: heavy bleeding with subfertility and a small cavity-distorting fibroid with patent tubes and a normal semen analysis
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in an outpatient clinic. A 36-year-old woman has had two years of heavy periods with flooding and clots, and has been trying to conceive for 18 months without success.

Her cycles are regular at 28 days and she has no dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and a hysterosalpingo-contrast-sonography study last month showed both tubes patent. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 2.5 cm fibroid indenting the endometrial cavity by more than half its diameter, a normal myometrium elsewhere, normal ovaries with a good antral follicle count, and no features of adenomyosis.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, transvaginal ultrasound showing a 2.5 cm submucosal fibroid indenting the cavity, tubal patency confirmed, partner semen analysis normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device to control the bleeding first
Arrange hysteroscopic resection of the fibroid that indents the cavity
Arrange uterine artery embolisation to reduce the size of the fibroid now
Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months and review
Proceed directly to in vitro fertilisation without treating the fibroid now

subtopic_detail: seizure prophylaxis choice in severe pre-eclampsia at term when the woman has a neuromuscular junction disorder
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite. A 32-year-old woman at 37 weeks and 2 days in her first pregnancy is admitted with a two day frontal headache. Her blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg on two readings 30 minutes apart and her protein to creatinine ratio is 65 mg/mmol.

She has generalised myasthenia gravis diagnosed at 24, treated with pyridostigmine and azathioprine, and has had no crisis for three years. She has mild fatigable ptosis by the evening but normal swallow, speech and respiratory effort today, with a forced vital capacity of 3.2 L. Her platelets, liver enzymes and creatinine are normal and the cardiotocograph is reassuring. The consultant is 20 minutes away and asks you to start treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate baseline 140/min
data_table.Examination: Mild fatigable ptosis, normal speech and swallow, forced vital capacity 3.2 L, brisk reflexes without clonus, no right upper quadrant tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L (<35), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45-90), urine protein to creatinine ratio 65 mg/mmol (<30), cardiotocograph reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate plan?

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate loading and maintenance with hourly review
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate at half the usual rate with level monitoring
Treat the blood pressure and use levetiracetam instead of magnesium for cover
Treat the blood pressure alone and withhold any seizure prophylaxis entirely
Give an intravenous diazepam infusion for prophylaxis and treat the pressure

subtopic_detail: pubic and sacroiliac pain with difficulty turning in bed at twenty eight weeks and a soft uterus
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks has a month of grinding pain low at the front when she rolls over in bed and climbs stairs. She can walk 200 metres before stopping.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender uterus, antalgic waddling gait
data_table.Provocation: Positive posterior pelvic pain provocation test on the right, tender over the symphysis pubis
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative, straight leg raise negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for cardiotocography and intramuscular betamethasone
Request a pelvic radiograph to measure the symphysis pubis width
Refer to women's health physiotherapy for a support belt and advice
Arrange transvaginal measurement of the cervical length today
Prescribe regular oral diclofenac and advise complete bed rest

subtopic_detail: nocturnal hand numbness waking a woman at thirty two weeks with normal power and normal blood pressure
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks wakes two or three times a night with both hands numb and shakes them until the feeling returns, worse on the right.

data_table.Sensory: Reduced light touch over the right thumb, index and middle finger pulps
data_table.Motor and provocation: Abductor pollicis brevis power 5 out of 5; percussion over the flexor retinaculum reproduces the tingling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before starting any treatment
Refer to hand surgery for carpal tunnel decompression this pregnancy
Start oral pyridoxine and a low dose diuretic for fluid retention
Fit neutral wrist splints worn overnight and review after birth
Refer for a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel

subtopic_detail: fever and myalgia after soft cheese at twenty six weeks with no localising source of infection
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 26 weeks has felt feverish and achy for 2 days with headache and loose stools that have settled. She ate soft cheese at a wedding 4 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 /min, BP 104/62 mmHg, temperature 38.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 165 /min
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, uterus soft and non-tender, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 68 mg/L; midstream urine no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral cefalexin and review the midstream urine result
Send a stool culture and manage her symptomatically with paracetamol
Start oral azithromycin and arrange ultrasound for fetal wellbeing
Take a high vaginal swab and start intravenous metronidazole
Take blood cultures and start high dose intravenous benzylpenicillin

subtopic_detail: palpitations and weight loss three months after birth with a suppressed thyrotropin and no eye signs
stem: A 33-year-old woman 12 weeks after her first birth has palpitations on exertion, heat intolerance and 5 kg of unintended weight loss while fully breastfeeding. She has a fine tremor and a small smooth painless goitre, with no lid retraction, proptosis or pretibial change.

data_table.Thyroid function: TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 28 pmol/L (10-20), free T3 7.1 pmol/L (3.5-6.0)
data_table.Antibodies: Thyroid peroxidase antibody strongly positive, thyrotropin receptor antibody negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start propranolol for symptoms and repeat thyroid function in 6 weeks
Start carbimazole and refer to endocrinology for ongoing care
Arrange radioactive iodine uptake scanning and stop breastfeeding
Start thyroxine and recheck thyroid function in 3 months
Refer for total thyroidectomy after medical pretreatment

subtopic_detail: heavy painful periods with a diffusely bulky tender uterus and no focal lesion on imaging
stem: A 42-year-old woman has 3 years of progressively heavier, more painful periods, flooding through a pad in an hour on her worst days, with a dragging ache starting a week before bleeding. She has completed her family and has no intermenstrual bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Smooth symmetrically enlarged tender uterus of about 10 weeks size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Ultrasound: Globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, indistinct junctional zone, no fibroid, endometrium 6 mm
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L, ferritin 9 microgram/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Tranexamic acid alone, reviewing a bleeding chart in six months
A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system after counselling
Referral for uterine artery embolisation as first line
A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months
Hysteroscopic resection of the abnormal endometrium

subtopic_detail: household chickenpox contact at sixteen weeks in a woman with no recalled history of the illness
stem:
You are the general practitioner telephoned by a 27-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her 4-year-old nephew, who stayed at her house for two nights and shared meals with her, developed a blistering rash yesterday and has been diagnosed with chickenpox. She last saw him 18 hours ago.

She grew up overseas, has no recollection of ever having had chickenpox and her mother is not contactable to confirm. Her antenatal booking bloods recorded rubella immunity and a negative hepatitis B surface antigen but no varicella serology was requested. She is well, has no rash and no fever, and she has taken no immunosuppressive medication. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated with a normal first trimester screen, and she asks whether there is anything she should be doing today rather than waiting for her next appointment in three weeks.

data_table.Exposure: Two nights of household contact with a child whose vesicular rash appeared yesterday, last contact 18 hours ago
data_table.Immune history: No recalled history of chickenpox, no varicella serology on the booking panel
data_table.Booking serology: Rubella immune, hepatitis B surface antigen negative
data_table.Current status: No rash, no fever, no immunosuppressive medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her and arrange a detailed fetal morphology scan at twenty weeks
Give zoster immunoglobulin now without waiting for any serology result back
Request urgent varicella serology and give zoster immunoglobulin if seronegative
Give the varicella vaccine today and repeat the dose four weeks later on
Start oral aciclovir today and continue it for the next seven days straight

subtopic_detail: breakthrough focal seizures at twenty four weeks in a woman stable on lamotrigine before conception
stem: A 26-year-old woman at 24 weeks with focal epilepsy was seizure free for 3 years on lamotrigine 300 mg daily before conception. She has had two seizures in the past fortnight and adherence is confirmed.

data_table.Drug levels: Trough lamotrigine 2.1 mg/L against a preconception baseline of 4.6 mg/L
data_table.Assessment: BP 106/64 mmHg, no proteinuria; normal fetal growth and Dopplers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch her from lamotrigine to levetiracetam over the next two weeks
Maintain the current dose and reassess her seizures after birth
Add nightly clobazam and repeat an electroencephalogram this month
Increase the lamotrigine dose guided by serial serum levels
Add low dose sodium valproate for the rest of the pregnancy

subtopic_detail: maternal rash and joint pains at eighteen weeks after an outbreak of slapped cheek at a primary school
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old primary school teacher at 18 weeks. Three weeks ago several children in her class had bright red cheeks and were sent home, and ten days ago she developed aching hands and knees along with a lacy pink rash on her upper arms that has now faded. She feels well today.

Her parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M is positive and immunoglobulin G is positive, on a sample taken three days ago, and the booking sample from 10 weeks has been retrieved and tested as immunoglobulin G negative. Her full blood count shows haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155) with a normal white cell count and platelet count. Ultrasound today reports a structurally normal fetus with a normal liquor volume, no ascites, no pericardial effusion and no skin oedema. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg with no proteinuria and she is afebrile. She asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg with no proteinuria, afebrile, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Serology: Parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive, with a booking sample at 10 weeks that was immunoglobulin G negative
data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155) with normal white cell and platelet counts
data_table.Ultrasound: Structurally normal fetus, normal liquor volume, no ascites, pericardial effusion or skin oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management?

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction within the next week
Reassure her and continue routine antenatal care with no additional imaging
Give intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother to prevent vertical transmission
Arrange fortnightly growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler assessment only
Begin serial middle cerebral artery Doppler surveillance for the next twelve weeks

subtopic_detail: maternal toxoplasma seroconversion at fourteen weeks with a structurally normal fetus on ultrasound
stem:
You are the maternal fetal medicine registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman at 14 weeks who was investigated for three weeks of cervical lymphadenopathy and fatigue. She keeps two cats, empties the litter tray herself and has been gardening without gloves at a new house.

Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M is positive and immunoglobulin G is positive with a low avidity index, and her stored booking serum from 7 weeks is immunoglobulin G negative on retesting in the same reference laboratory. Her full blood count and liver function tests are normal and she is human immunodeficiency virus negative. Ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with normal biometry, no intracranial calcification, normal ventricles and a normal liquor volume. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mmHg and she is afebrile. She is distressed and asks what can be done to protect the baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, afebrile, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Serology: Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M positive, immunoglobulin G positive with low avidity, booking serum at 7 weeks immunoglobulin G negative
data_table.Other investigations: Normal full blood count and liver function tests, human immunodeficiency virus negative
data_table.Ultrasound: Structurally normal fetus with normal biometry, no intracranial calcification, normal ventricles and liquor volume
data_table.Exposure history: Two cats with owner-managed litter tray, gardening without gloves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start spiramycin now and arrange amniotic fluid testing after eighteen weeks
Start pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid immediately this week
Repeat the serology in four weeks and take no further action in the interim
Offer termination of pregnancy given the risk of severe fetal damage now
Start azithromycin and arrange monthly ultrasound surveillance instead of this

subtopic_detail: acute focal abdominal pain over a known uterine mass at twenty two weeks with a soft uterus between episodes
stem: A 36-year-old woman at 22 weeks has 18 hours of constant burning right-sided abdominal pain that she localises with one finger. An intramural uterine mass measured 7 cm in the first trimester and 11 cm two weeks ago.

data_table.Examination: Focal tenderness over a firm right uterine mass; uterus soft between palpations
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein 32 mg/L; cardiotocograph reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange uterine artery embolisation to devascularise the mass now
Admit for analgesia, hydration and conservative management with review
Arrange laparotomy and myomectomy to remove the mass today
Start intravenous antibiotics for a presumed intra-amniotic infection
Give nifedipine tocolysis and intramuscular betamethasone today

subtopic_detail: seven centimetre ovarian cyst with fat and calcification in a nulliparous woman with normal tumour markers
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 24-year-old nulliparous woman referred after a scan arranged for six months of intermittent dull left iliac fossa discomfort. She has regular cycles, uses condoms for contraception, and has never been pregnant. She would like children in the future.

Transvaginal ultrasound describes a 7 cm left ovarian cyst containing an echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing, layered echogenic material with a fluid level, and no solid vascular papillary projections on colour Doppler. The right ovary is normal and there is no free fluid in the pelvis. CA125 is 18 units/mL (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase, alpha fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotrophin are all within their reference intervals, and a urinary pregnancy test is negative. On examination the abdomen is soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding, and her vital signs are within normal limits. The cyst measured 6.6 cm on a scan performed nine months earlier at another practice.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no guarding
data_table.Ultrasound: 7 cm left ovarian cyst with a shadowing echogenic focus, layered echogenic material with a fluid level, no vascular papillary projections, normal right ovary, no free fluid
data_table.Tumour markers: CA125 18 units/mL (less than 35), lactate dehydrogenase, alpha fetoprotein and beta human chorionic gonadotrophin within reference intervals
data_table.Serial imaging: Cyst measured 6.6 cm nine months earlier

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to gynaecological oncology for staging laparotomy and omental biopsy
Perform ultrasound guided aspiration of the cyst and send fluid for cytology
Perform laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy preserving the remaining ovarian tissue
Perform laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy to avoid intraoperative spillage
Observe with six monthly ultrasound surveillance and repeat tumour markers

subtopic_detail: recurrent endometrioma in the only remaining ovary of a woman with a low antimullerian hormone
stem: A 34-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 2 years. She had a left salpingo-oophorectomy at 26 and a right cystectomy at 30 for a 5 cm endometrioma. She has severe dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia.

data_table.Ultrasound: 4 cm right ovarian cyst with ground glass echoes and no solid component; left adnexa absent
data_table.Ovarian reserve: Anti-Mullerian hormone 3.1 pmol/L (8-30), antral follicle count 3, day 3 FSH 12 IU/L (3-9)
data_table.Other: Patent right tube, normal semen analysis

lead_in: What would you recommend first?

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months
Laparoscopic ablation of the cyst wall with bipolar diathermy
Continuous combined oral contraception, reviewing in one year
Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation without further surgery
Repeat laparoscopic cystectomy of the cyst before treatment

subtopic_detail: young woman with bleeding after intercourse and a red ring around the cervical opening on speculum
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old woman who has had light bleeding after sex on about six occasions over the past four months. It is bright red, lasts a few hours, and is not associated with pain. She has been taking a combined oral contraceptive pill for two years and has no intermenstrual bleeding otherwise.

She has one regular partner of three years and no history of sexually transmitted infection. Her cervical screening test four months ago was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. On speculum examination the vagina is healthy with no discharge, and there is a symmetrical circumferential area of red velvety tissue extending from the external os onto the surrounding cervix, which bleeds lightly when touched with the swab. There is no visible growth or ulceration, the cervix is smooth in outline, and bimanual examination is non-tender with no adnexal mass. A self collected vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is negative.

data_table.Examination: Circumferential red velvety area around the external os that bleeds on contact, no growth or ulceration
data_table.Bimanual: Mobile non-tender uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass or cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus testing negative four months ago, chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat empirically with doxycycline for two weeks and repeat the swabs after completion
Refer urgently for colposcopic assessment of the cervix with directed biopsy of the area
Repeat the cervical screening test today as a clinician collected sample and await results
Arrange cryotherapy or diathermy ablation of the cervix at her next available appointment
Explain the finding, offer a change to a non oestrogen method, and review in three months

subtopic_detail: frothy yellow green vaginal discharge with motile organisms reported on a self collected swab
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman with three weeks of an offensive yellow green vaginal discharge and soreness on passing urine. She describes the discharge as frothy and says it has an unpleasant smell that has not responded to an over the counter antifungal pessary.

She has a new male partner of two months and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last cervical screening test was negative eighteen months ago and she is not pregnant, confirmed by a urinary test today. On speculum examination there is an adherent frothy discharge coating the vaginal walls and the vaginal pH measured with indicator paper is 5.5. The cervix appears inflamed with scattered punctate haemorrhages. Bimanual examination reveals no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness and a normal sized mobile uterus. A self collected vaginal swab reports Trichomonas vaginalis detected by nucleic acid amplification, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected.

data_table.Examination: Adherent frothy yellow green discharge, vaginal pH 5.5, cervix with punctate haemorrhages
data_table.Bimanual: No cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness, mobile normal sized uterus
data_table.Investigations: Trichomonas vaginalis detected on nucleic acid amplification, chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected, urinary pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a single dose of oral fluconazole and review her symptoms again in two weeks
Prescribe intravaginal clotrimazole for six nights and advise avoidance of soaps and bubble baths
Prescribe oral metronidazole for her and arrange treatment of her current sexual partner
Prescribe intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral azithromycin and repeat testing in three months
Prescribe intravaginal metronidazole gel nightly for five nights without partner treatment

subtopic_detail: smooth red finger of tissue protruding through the cervical opening found at a routine screening visit
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a routine cervical screening test on a 47-year-old woman. She mentions that she has noticed some spotting between periods over the last six months, which she had put down to approaching menopause, and occasional light bleeding after sex.

Her periods remain regular at 28 days and are not heavy. She has two children, takes no hormonal treatment, and her previous screening tests have all been negative. On speculum examination there is a smooth red finger of tissue about 15 mm long protruding through the external os on a narrow stalk. It bleeds lightly when the swab brushes it. The remainder of the cervix looks normal with no ulceration or irregularity, and the vaginal walls are healthy. Bimanual examination reveals a mobile anteverted uterus of normal size with no adnexal masses, and the human papillomavirus result returns negative for oncogenic types.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated 15 mm red lesion protruding through the external os, bleeding on contact
data_table.Bimanual: Mobile anteverted uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Human papillomavirus testing negative for oncogenic types

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Avulse the lesion in the treatment room today and discard it after the bleeding settles
Refer urgently under the suspected cancer pathway for examination under anaesthesia and staging
Reassure her that these are benign findings and repeat her screening test in five years
Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate the bleeding and review in six months
Refer for removal of the lesion with histopathology and assessment of the endometrial cavity
